teile.einleitung: Sometimes it says in the shop or in the online shop: **sold out**. That means there are none left. You have to wait until new ones arrive or look somewhere else.
wichtigste: Sold out means that all the items have already been sold.
This happens when many people want something at the same time.
The shop often gets new stock later.
You can wait, look in another shop or reserve something.
Tickets for concerts or matches sometimes sell out quickly.

abschnitte.text: A shop only has a certain amount of each product in **stock**. When all the items have been sold, the product is **sold out**. In an online shop it then often says “not available” or “out of stock”. The shop can only sell again when a new **delivery** arrives. That can take a few days or even weeks.

Something sells out when many people want it at the same time. This is called high **demand**. It happens, for example, with a new game, before Christmas or with a famous concert. Sometimes the manufacturer cannot deliver enough because parts are missing. Then there is less **supply** than people want to buy.

When something is sold out, you need **patience**. You can ask when new stock is coming or **reserve** the product. Sometimes another shop still has some. You can also think about whether you really need it. Be careful with people who resell sold-out things for much more money: it is rarely worth it.

gewusst: For very popular concerts, the tickets are sometimes sold out after just a few minutes.

teile.einleitung: Customer reviews help you judge a product when shopping online. But not all reviews are genuine: some are bought or fake.
wichtigste: Customer reviews show what others think of a product.
Some reviews are bought or fake.
Fake reviews make a product look better.
Many different, detailed opinions are more reliable.
Independent tests also help you decide.

abschnitte.text: When shopping online, you cannot touch a product. That is why many people look at the **stars** and comments of other buyers. Good reviews lead to more sales. That is exactly why some sellers try to influence the reviews.

There are companies that write reviews for money. Sometimes customers get a product free if they give five stars. Bad reviews for competitors also happen. In Switzerland, something like this can break the **Unfair Competition Act**.

Lots of very short, enthusiastic reviews within a short time are suspicious. You should also be careful if they all sound almost the same. Genuine reviews often mention **pros and cons** and describe exactly how the product was used. It helps to read the middling and bad reviews too.

As well as reviews, there are **independent tests**, for example by consumer magazines. Friends or family can also share their experiences. If you compare several sources, you make better decisions. A single review says little.

gewusst: Some platforms mark reviews from people who really bought the product there as a “verified purchase”.
There are computer programs that look for patterns in order to find fake reviews.

teile.einleitung: Loan interest is the price you pay for borrowed money. That is why anyone who takes out a loan has to pay back more than they received.
wichtigste: Interest is the price of borrowed money.
It is given as a percentage per year.
The higher the interest and the longer the term, the more expensive the loan.
In Switzerland, the Federal Council sets a maximum interest rate for consumer loans.
There is also interest when you save; then you receive it.

abschnitte.text: When a bank lends money, it cannot use it for anything else during that time. There is also the risk that it will not get it back. That is why it charges **interest**. So interest is the price of borrowing, rather like rent for money.

Interest is usually given as a **percentage per year**. At 8 per cent interest, a loan of 1000 francs costs about 80 francs a year. If you pay back in instalments, the amount you owe becomes smaller over time. Then the interest you pay each month falls too.

If you **save**, the bank pays you interest. If you **borrow**, you pay the bank interest. The interest on loans is almost always higher than the interest on savings. A large part of the bank’s income comes from this difference.

For consumer loans, the **Federal Council** sets a maximum interest rate. The contract must state the **effective annual interest rate**, which also includes fees. With mortgages for houses, interest is usually much lower than with consumer loans. This is because the house serves as security.

gewusst: With its policy rate, the Swiss National Bank influences how high interest rates in Switzerland are in general.
Even in ancient Mesopotamia there were rules about how much interest you could charge for borrowed grain.

teile.einleitung: The same product can cost different amounts in different shops. If you compare the prices, you find the cheaper offer and save money. You can do this with simple sums.
wichtigste: The same things do not cost the same everywhere.
If you compare prices, you can save money.
You find the lower price by comparing the numbers.
If a pen costs 2 francs in shop A and 3 francs in shop B, shop A is cheaper.
With different pack sizes, the unit price helps.
It is not only the price that counts, but also the quality.

abschnitte.text: Every shop sets its own **prices**. That is why a pen can cost 2 francs in one shop and 3 francs in another. 2 francs is less than 3 francs. So in **shop A** the pen is cheaper. If you buy it there, you save 1 franc. That does not sound like much, but with lots of purchases it adds up.

The easiest way is to compare **the same product**: same brand, same size. Then you look to see which price is lower. Today you can also compare prices on the internet. If the packs are different sizes, the **unit price** on the price tag helps. It shows, for example, what 100 grams or a litre costs.

abschnitte.titel: It is not only the price that counts
abschnitte.text: The cheapest product is not always the best choice. A cheap pen that breaks quickly may end up more expensive. The **journey** to the shop counts too: a long trip is not worth it to save one franc. If you compare cleverly, you pay attention to **price and quality**. And sometimes the best saving is not to buy something at all.

gewusst: In Switzerland, shops must display the prices of their goods clearly.
Many shops have special offers on certain days. If you know this, you can shop accordingly.

teile.einleitung: The Rappen, or centime, is the small unit of the Swiss franc: 100 Rappen make one franc. That is why the coins worth less than a franc are called Rappen. The name has a surprising history that has to do with a bird.
wichtigste: One franc has 100 Rappen.
The coins below one franc are called Rappen.
Today there are coins worth 5, 10 and 20 Rappen, as well as the half-franc worth 50 Rappen.
The 1-Rappen piece was abolished in 2007, the 2-Rappen piece as early as 1978.
In French the Rappen is called centime, in Italian centesimo.
Swiss coins are minted by Swissmint in Bern.
The 10-Rappen piece has looked almost the same since 1879.

abschnitte.text: The **Rappen** is the hundredth part of a franc. If something costs 3.40 francs, that is 3 francs and 40 Rappen. It is abbreviated to Rp. or Rp; on price tags you often only see the number after the point. In French-speaking Switzerland people say **centime**, in Ticino centesimo and in Romansh rap.

Today there are four coins below one franc: 5 Rappen, 10 Rappen, 20 Rappen and the **half-franc**, which is worth 50 Rappen. The 5-Rappen piece is golden in colour and made of aluminium bronze. The other coins are silvery and made of a mixture of copper and nickel. The 5, 10 and 20-Rappen coins show the head of **Libertas**, a figure who represents freedom.

The name dates from the Middle Ages. In Freiburg im Breisgau, coins were minted with an eagle on them, which people mockingly called a **raven** (Rabe). Over time, the word Rabe or Rappe became the name of the coin. In 1403 several towns on the Upper Rhine joined together in the Rappen Coin League, which issued these coins together.

Since 1850 the franc has been the single currency of the whole of Switzerland, and ever since it has been divided into 100 Rappen. There used to be 1 and 2-Rappen pieces as well. The 2-Rappen piece was withdrawn from circulation in 1978, the **1-Rappen piece** in 2007. Making them cost more than the coins were worth, and hardly anyone needed them any more.

Because there are no longer any 1 or 2-Rappen coins, amounts paid in cash are **rounded** to 5 Rappen. If your shopping costs 7.32 francs, you pay 7.30 francs at the till. With 7.33 francs, on the other hand, it would be 7.35 francs. With a card or Twint, however, the amount is charged exactly to the Rappen.

All Swiss coins are made by **Swissmint**, the federal mint in Bern. The Swiss National Bank then puts them into circulation. Millions of new Rappen coins are minted every year. Each coin shows the year it was minted, which is why some people collect coins from particular years.

begriffe.erklaerung: The money that is used in a country; in Switzerland, the franc.
A factory where coins are made.
A female figure who represents freedom and can be seen on Rappen coins.
Adjusting an amount to a simpler number, for example to the nearest 5 Rappen.

gewusst: The 10-Rappen piece is considered one of the oldest coins in the world still in circulation with almost the same design, because its look dates from 1879.
The half-franc is worth 50 Rappen but is not called a 50-Rappen piece.
In everyday life in German-speaking Switzerland, the 20-Rappen piece is also called a “Zwänzgi”.

teile.einleitung: Net pay is the money that actually arrives in your account at the end of the month. It is less than the wage in the contract, because contributions to social insurance are deducted first.
wichtigste: Gross pay is the whole wage before deductions.
Net pay is the wage after deductions.
Gross minus deductions equals net.
Deductions include, for example, AVS/IV/EO and unemployment insurance.
Deductions are calculated as a percentage of gross pay.
With 1000 francs gross and 6.4 per cent deductions, 936 francs net are left.

abschnitte.text: The word **gross** (brutto) means “whole”; **net** (netto) means “clean” or “what is left over”. The **gross pay** is stated in the employment contract. The employer deducts contributions from it and pays them to the social insurance schemes. What remains is the **net pay**. With this money you then pay the rent, food and all your other expenses.

For all employees, **AVS/IV/EO** is deducted. On top of that there is **unemployment insurance** (ALV). Anyone who works at least 8 hours a week for the same employer often also pays for **non-occupational accident insurance**. Above a certain income, the **pension fund** is added. For apprentices with a small wage, the deductions are therefore often smaller than for adults with a full wage.

Deductions are usually given as a **percentage**. An example: the gross pay is 1000 francs, and the deductions together are 6.4 per cent. 6.4 per cent of 1000 francs is 64 francs. 1000 minus 64 gives **936 francs net pay**. The formula is: gross minus deductions equals net.

In Switzerland, for most people **taxes** are not deducted from their wages. You pay them yourself later, after the tax return. You also pay **health insurance** separately. So anyone making a budget should not only look at their net pay. It is worth putting money aside for taxes every month.

gewusst: The words “brutto” and “netto” come from Italian.
Goods also have gross and net: the gross weight includes the packaging, the net weight does not.

teile.einleitung: How do you divide up your pay sensibly? The **50-30-20 rule** is a simple rule of thumb for this. It divides your net income into three parts: needs, wants and saving.
wichtigste: 50 per cent of net income is meant for necessities.
30 per cent is for wants and free time.
20 per cent is for saving or paying off debts.
The rule is a guide, not a law.
It is based on net pay, meaning pay after all deductions.
In Switzerland, rents and health insurance are often so high that you have to adapt the rule.

abschnitte.text: Half of your **net income** is meant for **necessities**. These include **rent**, food, **health insurance**, travel to work and taxes. These are expenses you can hardly do without. If you need more than half for these, you should check where you can save.

Just under a third may be spent on **wants**. These are things that give you pleasure but are not necessary: going out, hobbies, holidays, new clothes or streaming subscriptions. This part makes sure that a budget is not only about doing without. It helps you stick to the plan.

A fifth goes into the **future**. You put it into a **savings account**, build up a **reserve** for emergencies or pay off **debts**. In Switzerland you can also pay into **pillar 3a** for this. Many experts recommend putting the savings amount aside right at the beginning of the month.

The 50-30-20 rule is a **guide**. With low pay or high rents, 50 per cent is often not enough for needs. Then the part for wants becomes smaller. Anyone who lives with their parents, on the other hand, can save more. The most important thing is to have a plan at all.

gewusst: The rule was made popular by the US politician Elizabeth Warren together with her daughter in a book from 2005.
Budget advice services in Switzerland offer budget templates that are adapted to Swiss costs.

teile.einleitung: Many subscriptions have a minimum contract term. This means you have to pay for a certain period, even if you no longer use the service. That is why it is worth looking closely before signing.
wichtigste: The minimum contract term is the period during which you have to pay for a subscription.
A 12-month minimum term means paying for at least a year.
Cancelling earlier is often not possible or costs a fee.
Typical examples are mobile phone contracts, gym memberships or magazine subscriptions.
Many subscriptions renew automatically if you do not cancel in time.
The notice period is stated in the contract.

abschnitte.text: With a subscription you pay regularly, for example every month. With a **minimum contract term** you promise to keep the subscription for a certain period. 12 or 24 months are common. During this time you have to pay every instalment, even if you no longer need the service. In return you often get a lower price or a cheap phone.

If you want to end a subscription, you have to **cancel** it. There is a **notice period** for this, for example two months before it runs out. If you miss this deadline, many contracts renew **automatically**, often for another year. That is why it is wise to write the end date in your diary or on your phone. You should cancel in writing and keep a confirmation.

Before signing a contract, it is worth looking at the **small print**. Important questions are: How long does the contract run? What does it cost in total? When and how can I cancel? With a subscription for 30 francs a month over 24 months, you pay 720 francs altogether. Sometimes an offer without a minimum term is a little more expensive per month, but more flexible.

gewusst: For young people under 18, the parents usually have to agree to contracts.
Free trial subscriptions also often turn into paid ones automatically if you do not cancel them in time.

teile.einleitung: Artificial scarcity is a sales trick: an offer is made to seem scarce or about to end. The idea is that customers buy quickly without thinking for long.
wichtigste: Artificial scarcity creates time pressure or a feeling that something is scarce.
Examples are “Only 2 left!” or a countdown.
You are meant to buy straight away instead of thinking it over.
Often the offer is not nearly as scarce as it looks.
If you stay calm and compare, you make better decisions.

abschnitte.text: People do not want to miss out. When something seems scarce, it seems more valuable. Online shops use this with messages like “Only 2 left!” or a **countdown**. This trick is called **artificial scarcity**.

Under **time pressure** you think less carefully. You no longer ask yourself whether you really need the product or whether it is cheaper elsewhere. That is exactly what the sellers want. Experts also speak of **dark patterns**, which are tricks in the design of websites.

abschnitte.titel: Spotting it and seeing through it
abschnitte.text: Sometimes the countdown simply starts again from the beginning on your next visit. Or it always says “only 2 left”, no matter when you look. Claims like these are often not honest. In Switzerland, the **Unfair Competition Act** bans misleading information when selling.

A good rule is to sleep on it for a night. You can compare the price in other shops. If the offer is gone tomorrow, a similar one usually comes along soon. If you do not let yourself be rushed, you only buy what you really want.

gewusst: The feeling of missing out is also known by the English abbreviation “FOMO”.
Sentences like “12 people are looking at this right now” are also meant to create pressure.

teile.einleitung: A debt advice service helps people who can no longer pay their bills. Together with the people affected, experts get an overview of all the debts and draw up a plan for how they can be reduced. In Switzerland there are advice centres like this in every region.
wichtigste: Debt advice centres help people with debts.
First, an overview of all debts, income and expenses is made.
Then the experts draw up a plan with the person for paying off the debts.
Non-profit advice services are usually free or cheap.
The advisers often also negotiate with the creditors.
The earlier you get help, the better debts can be reduced.
Be careful with companies that promise to make you debt-free quickly for an expensive fee.

abschnitte.text: A **debt advice service** is a specialist office that people with money problems can turn to. Social workers and budget experts work there who know about debts, debt enforcement and the law. They listen without judging and are bound by **confidentiality**. The aim is to bring order back into the person’s finances.

Many people with debts have lost track and no longer open their post. In the advice session, all bills, reminders and debt enforcement papers are collected first. Then a **budget** is drawn up that shows all income and expenses. That way you can see how much money is left each month for paying back.

Together, a plan for **paying off the debts** is made. The advice service negotiates with the creditors about affordable instalments or partly cancelling the debt. Sometimes a **debt settlement** is possible, in which all creditors receive part of the money. It is important that no new debts arise during this time.

In Switzerland there is the umbrella organisation **Schuldenberatung Schweiz**, which lists recognised advice centres. Many are run by cantons, municipalities or charities such as Caritas. Budget advice services also help with planning finances. For young people there are also services in schools and at youth advice centres.

On the internet, some companies advertise with the promise of getting rid of debts quickly. They often charge high fees in advance, and the debts can even get bigger as a result. Reputable, **non-profit** advice centres do not promise miracles. They work openly and usually free of charge or for a small contribution.

begriffe.erklaerung: Paying back and reducing debts.
A plan under which all creditors receive part of their money and the debts are then settled.
The advisers may not tell anyone what you confide in them.
Working for the good of the community and not to make a profit.

gewusst: Many people only seek help when they have already been in debt for years, even though early advice would be much easier.
In Switzerland there is also a kind of personal bankruptcy, but afterwards the debts remain as certificates of loss.
Some advice centres offer online calculators with which you can test your budget yourself.

teile.einleitung: Every person needs some things to live: food, drink, clothes and a home. These are called **needs**. Other things are fun but not necessary: these are **wants**.
wichtigste: Needs are things you need to live.
They include food, drink, clothes and a roof over your head.
Shoes that fit are also a need, because you need them every day.
Wants are fun but not necessary.
Anyone who plans their money thinks about needs first.
Safety, friendship and learning are also important needs.

abschnitte.text: Every person has to **eat** and **drink**, otherwise they become ill. We need **clothes** so that we do not get cold, and a **home** where we sleep and feel safe. These are **basic needs**. They are the same for all people in the world. Health and warmth in winter are part of them too.

Not everything is easy to tell apart. **Shoes** that fit are something you need every day to walk well: that is a **need**. The fifth pair of trainers in your favourite colour, on the other hand, is a **want**. **Stickers**, sweets or a **trip to the cinema** are also fun but not necessary. A good question is: “Can I live well without it?”

People do not only need things they can touch. We also need **safety**, **friends** and **family** who love us. **Learning** and **playing** are also important so that children develop well. The researcher **Abraham Maslow** arranged needs in a pyramid. At the bottom are food and sleep, and higher up friendship and recognition.

Anyone who plans their money thinks about **needs** first. Parents, for example, first pay the rent and for food. Only what is left over is for **wants**. This helps make sure the money is enough for the most important things. If you have wants, you can save up for them.

gewusst: In the Convention on the Rights of the Child, the United Nations set out that all children have a right to food, health, education and play.

teile.einleitung: With wage garnishment, part of a person’s wages is held back directly to pay off debts. The debt enforcement office instructs the employer to pay this part to the office instead of to the employee. The subsistence minimum remains protected, however, so that the person can go on living.
wichtigste: With wage garnishment, part of the wages is held back for debts.
It is ordered by the debt enforcement office.
The employer pays the garnished amount directly to the debt enforcement office.
The subsistence minimum remains protected and is not garnished.
In Switzerland, wage garnishment lasts at most one year.
If debts remain unpaid, the creditors receive a certificate of loss.

abschnitte.text: With **wage garnishment**, the state takes part of a person’s income in order to pay debts with it. It is the most common form of seizure in Switzerland. Not only wages can be garnished, but also pensions or other regular income. The aim is for the **creditors** to receive at least part of their money.

First a creditor makes a **request for debt enforcement** to the debt enforcement office. The debtor receives a payment order and can raise an objection within 10 days. If the debtor does not pay and does not object, the creditor can ask for the debt enforcement to continue. Then an official from the debt enforcement office comes and carries out the **seizure**.

The debt enforcement office calculates the person’s **subsistence minimum**. This includes a basic amount for food and clothes, the rent, health insurance and the costs of getting to work. Only the part of the wages above this amount is garnished. If someone earns no more than the subsistence minimum, nothing can be taken from their wages.

The debt enforcement office tells the **employer** what amount has been garnished. The employer must pay this part directly to the office every month. For the people affected this is often unpleasant, because the boss finds out about the debts. But the employer may not dismiss someone simply because of wage garnishment.

In Switzerland, wage garnishment lasts at most **one year**. If the debts have still not been paid after that, the creditors receive a **certificate of loss from the seizure**. With it they can start debt enforcement again later, and the debt only expires after 20 years. Anyone affected by a seizure can find help at a debt advice centre.

begriffe.erklaerung: When the debt enforcement office takes money or belongings in order to pay debts.
The minimum amount you need to live on, which cannot be seized.
The official procedure for recovering unpaid debts.
A document about debts that could not be paid.

gewusst: With wage garnishment, sometimes even part of the 13th month’s salary is garnished.
A seizure remains visible in the debt enforcement register, which can make it harder to find a flat.
If the wages fall during the garnishment, the debt enforcement office must adjust the garnished amount.

teile.einleitung: A small loan is a loan for a fairly small amount that you pay back in instalments. For things you want, such as a new games console, it is usually not a good idea, because the interest makes the purchase more expensive.
wichtigste: A small loan is borrowed money that you pay back with interest.
The interest makes a purchase more expensive.
For things you want, it is wiser to save first.
The Consumer Credit Act protects borrowers in Switzerland.
You can cancel a loan agreement within 14 days.
Loans can quickly lead to debt.

abschnitte.text: With a **small loan** you get money straight away and pay it back in monthly instalments. On top of that comes the **interest**, which is the price of borrowing. A games console for 500 francs therefore ends up costing considerably more. And if you no longer need it, you still have to keep paying.

If you save up for something you want, you pay no interest. In a savings account you even get a little extra. While saving you also have time to think about whether you really want the thing. Many wishes are no longer so important after a few weeks.

In Switzerland the **Consumer Credit Act** applies. The bank must check whether you can pay the loan back. There is a **maximum interest rate**, and **aggressive advertising** for loans is banned. After signing, you can still cancel the agreement for 14 days.

If you have several loans, you quickly lose track. When the instalments are higher than what is left over, **debt** builds up. Young adults are affected particularly often. You can get help from a **debt advice service**, which is free in many cantons.

gewusst: In Switzerland, loans to minors are not valid without the parents’ consent.
Many debt advice services in Switzerland report that problems often start with small amounts such as unpaid phone bills.

teile.einleitung: Many employees in Switzerland are paid not twelve but **thirteen monthly salaries** a year. The **13th month's salary** usually comes once a year, often in December. If you plan for it wisely, you will have fewer money worries.
wichtigste: The 13th month's salary is an extra month's pay each year.
It is usually paid in December, sometimes in two parts.
It is not required by law but is set out in the employment contract or collective labour agreement.
AHV and other contributions are also deducted from the 13th month's salary.
It is wise to use it for annual bills, reserves or savings goals.
It is not money that you have available every month.

abschnitte.text: The **13th month's salary** is extra pay that comes on top of the normal monthly salary. So anyone who gets it receives 13 instead of 12 monthly salaries a year. Whether there is one is set out in the **employment contract** or in a **collective labour agreement**. There is no law in Switzerland that requires it for everyone. But it is very common.

The 13th month's salary is usually paid with the **December salary**. Some companies pay half in summer and half in December. Anyone who starts or leaves a job during the year often gets a share, depending on how long they have worked. As with the normal salary, **social insurance contributions** are deducted.

Because the 13th month's salary only comes once, you should not plan to spend it on everyday things. It is good for **annual bills** such as taxes, car insurance or a yearly subscription. You can also use it to build up a **reserve** for unexpected expenses or to put money aside for a **savings goal** such as a holiday. This takes pressure off the monthly budget.

abschnitte.titel: Not to be confused with a bonus
abschnitte.text: The 13th month's salary is something different from a **bonus**. A bonus often depends on how well the company or the person has done and is not always certain. The 13th month's salary, on the other hand, is firmly agreed if it is in the contract. That is why you can plan with it more reliably.

gewusst: In March 2024, Swiss voters said yes to a 13th AHV pension. It is to be paid from 2026.
Anyone who divides their annual salary by 12 in their budget, even though they get 13 salaries, thinks they are richer each month than they really are.

teile.einleitung: Prepaid, or pay as you go, means “paid in advance”. With a mobile phone, you first top up credit and can then use it for calls, messages or surfing the internet. That way you always know exactly the most you will spend.
wichtigste: Pay as you go means: pay first, then use.
You top up credit, for example with a card from a shop or online.
Once the credit is used up, there are no further costs.
With a contract, on the other hand, you pay a fixed amount every month and receive a bill.
Pay as you go helps you keep costs under control.

abschnitte.titel: How pay as you go works
abschnitte.text: With a pay-as-you-go offer you have a **SIM card** that you put money onto. This money is called **credit**. Every call, every message and every data package is deducted from it. When the credit is empty, you can only receive calls or you have to top up again. In Switzerland you have to register with an ID document when you buy a pay-as-you-go card.

abschnitte.titel: Pay as you go or contract?
abschnitte.text: With a **contract** you pay the same every month, no matter how often you use the phone. A contract is often linked to an agreement that runs for a certain time. Pay as you go is **flexible**: you can stop at any time and do not have to cancel. If you use a lot of internet, a contract is sometimes cheaper. If you do not make many calls, pay as you go often saves money.

For a first phone, many families choose pay as you go. There are no nasty surprises with a high bill. You learn to manage with a fixed amount. Even so, it is worth checking from time to time how much credit is left. Paid services or purchases in apps can also use up the credit quickly.

gewusst: The “pay first” principle does not only exist for phones, but also for prepaid credit cards or gift cards.
Even with a pay-as-you-go phone, credit can expire if you do not use the card for a very long time. This is stated in the provider’s terms.

teile.einleitung: A discount is a price reduction. The price is lowered by an amount or by a percentage. If you can calculate percentages, you can quickly see how much you really save.
wichtigste: A discount means: the price becomes lower.
Discounts are often given as a percentage, for example 25 %.
25 % is a quarter, 50 % is a half, 10 % is a tenth.
With a 25 % discount on 40 francs, you save 10 francs and pay 30 francs.
A discount is only worth it if you really need the thing.

abschnitte.text: The German word **Rabatt** comes from Italian and means deduction. Shops give discounts in the **sales**, with special offers or for loyal customers. There is also the **bulk discount**: if you buy a lot, you pay less per item. Sometimes you get a discount with a voucher or a code too.

Per cent means “out of a hundred”. So 25 % means 25 out of 100, which is a **quarter**. A jumper costs 40 francs. A quarter of 40 is 10. So you save 10 francs and pay **30 francs**. With 10 % you simply divide by 10: of 40 francs, that is 4 francs.

Big signs saying “minus 50 %” are meant to grab your attention. You then quickly buy something you do not need at all. That way you have not saved anything, but spent money. It is also worth comparing prices in different shops. Sometimes a product is just as cheap elsewhere without a discount.

gewusst: A discount for paying a bill quickly is called a **cash discount** (Skonto), for example 2 % for payment within 10 days.

teile.einleitung: You are in debt when you have to pay back money to someone that you borrowed or have not yet paid. Small debts are sometimes normal, but when they grow and you can no longer pay them, they become a big problem. If you know the warning signs, you can react early.
wichtigste: Debts are amounts of money that you have to pay back or still have to pay to someone.
Unpaid bills, loans and payments by instalments are forms of debt.
One warning sign is when you pay bills with new loans.
Interest, reminder fees and debt enforcement costs are often added to debts.
In Switzerland, taxes and health insurance premiums are among the most common debts.
Anyone who is over-indebted can no longer pay their debts from their income.
Debt advice centres help for free or at low cost.

abschnitte.text: **Debts** arise when you borrow money or buy something and have not yet paid for it. If a friend lends you 10 francs, you owe her 10 francs. An unpaid phone bill or a bank loan are also debts. The person who is owed money is called the creditor; the person who owes money is called the debtor.

abschnitte.titel: How the debt trap comes about
abschnitte.text: It often starts harmlessly with a phone contract, online shopping or a payment by instalments. If bills are not paid on time, **reminder fees** and interest are added. Some people then take out a new loan to pay old bills. That way the debts keep on growing, and people speak of a **debt spiral**.

One clear warning sign is when you pay bills with new loans. Other signs are reminders that pile up, or letters that you no longer open because you are afraid. Anyone who overdraws their account every month or borrows money from friends should also be careful. The earlier you react, the easier the problem is to solve.

In Switzerland, unpaid **taxes** and health insurance premiums are the most common debts. Many young adults get into debt when starting work, because they underestimate their expenses. Anyone who does not pay their debts can face debt enforcement proceedings. An entry in the debt enforcement register later makes it harder, for example, to find a flat.

The most important tool against debt is a **budget** that shows what you take in and spend. You should only buy what you can already pay for. For taxes, it is worth putting some money aside every month. And if you notice that your money is not enough, you should get help early from a debt advice service.

Anyone who can no longer pay their debts is **over-indebted**. Then it helps to talk to the creditors and agree on payments by instalments. Debt advice centres help to make a plan. Debts are no reason to be ashamed; what matters is that you do something about them.

begriffe.erklaerung: A person who owes someone money.
A notice that a bill has not yet been paid, often with a fee.
When you have so many debts that you can no longer pay them back.
When debts keep growing because of new loans and fees.

gewusst: States also have debts, but compared with many other countries, Switzerland has fairly little.
The debt brake in the Federal Constitution was approved by the people in 2001 and is meant to prevent the federal government from taking on too much debt.
In ancient Rome, people who did not pay their debts could even be sold into slavery.

teile.einleitung: An impulse buy is a spontaneous purchase that you make without thinking about it first. You see something, want it straight away and pay, even though you had not planned it at all. Retailers know this effect very well and use it cleverly.
wichtigste: An impulse buy is a spontaneous, unplanned purchase.
It often happens because of a feeling, such as desire, boredom or stress.
Shops deliberately place sweets and small items at the till.
Online shops also lure you with discounts, countdowns and one-click buying.
Impulse buys can quickly blow your budget.
A simple counter-strategy is to sleep on it for a night before buying.

abschnitte.text: With an **impulse buy** you decide within seconds to buy something. Typical examples are a chocolate bar at the till, a T-shirt in the sale or a game in an online shop. Often you regret the purchase later because you did not really need the thing. Experts then speak of a **bad buy**.

Our brain reacts strongly to **rewards**. When we see something nice, the brain releases messenger substances that create a good feeling. This feeling is stronger than calm thinking about the price. Especially when you are tired, hungry or sad, you buy on impulse more easily.

In the retail trade, the waiting area at the till is also called the **pester zone**, because that is where children ask their parents for sweets. Basic foods such as milk are often at the back of the shop, so that you have to walk past lots of other products. Red price tags, “today only” and “special offer” create time pressure. Online, you are lured by countdowns, messages like “only 2 left” and saved payment details.

A proven rule is the **24-hour rule**: you wait a day before buying something you had not planned. Often the wish has already gone by then. A shopping list that you stick to also helps. If you only take as much cash with you as you really need, you cannot spend too much.

Individual impulse buys are often small, but together they cost a lot of money. If you often buy on impulse, you have less at the end of the month for important things or for saving. In the worst case, impulse buys paid in instalments or on invoice lead to **debt**. A household account book shows how much you spend on purchases like these.

begriffe.erklaerung: A purchase you regret later because you do not need the thing.
The area at the till with sweets and small items.
Waiting a day before an unplanned purchase and only then deciding.
All the measures companies use to try to sell their products.

gewusst: Many supermarkets play calm music so that customers walk more slowly and buy more.
Experience shows that people who go shopping hungry put more into their trolley.
The sweets in the pester zone are deliberately placed at children’s eye level.

teile.einleitung: With a part-time job, teenagers earn their first money of their own, for example by babysitting, mowing lawns or delivering newspapers. You learn a lot about work and about handling money.
wichtigste: A part-time job is a small job alongside school.
Typical examples are babysitting, gardening, walking dogs or delivering newspapers.
In Switzerland, young people may do light work from the age of 13.
During term time, young people’s working hours are limited.
It is wise to save part of the money and spend part of it.
School always comes first.

abschnitte.titel: Your first money of your own
abschnitte.text: Many teenagers would like to treat themselves to something special, such as a bike, a game or clothes. With a **part-time job** they can earn the money for it themselves. Popular jobs are **babysitting**, mowing lawns, walking dogs, delivering leaflets or giving tutoring. The Swiss Red Cross (SRC) offers babysitting courses. There you learn what to look out for with small children.

In Switzerland, the **Employment Act** protects young people. From the age of 13, young people may do **light work** that does not harm their health or their schooling. During term time they may only work a few hours a week. Dangerous work is forbidden. For a regular job, under-18s usually need their parents’ consent.

Mia earns 40 francs from babysitting. She can spend it all or save it all. The wisest thing is to **divide it up**: for example, save 20 francs and spend 20 francs. That way she can treat herself now and still work towards a bigger **savings goal**. A **savings account** or a piggy bank helps to put the money aside for later.

A part-time job does not only bring money. You learn to be **punctual** and **reliable**. You notice how much work lies behind an amount of money. This helps you shop more thoughtfully later. A part-time job can also be an advantage when looking for an apprenticeship. But it is important that there is still enough time for school, homework and rest.

gewusst: If you earn money as a teenager, you soon notice how many hours of work a new phone costs.
Young people who are employed are also entitled to holidays.

teile.einleitung: A budget is a plan that shows how much money you have available and what you want to spend it on. When your family plans a day out and thinks about how much money there is for it, it is making a budget. With a budget you keep track and avoid debt.
wichtigste: A budget is a plan for income and spending.
It helps you keep track of your own money.
A distinction is made between fixed costs such as rent and variable costs such as free time.
A good budget also includes an amount for saving.
Municipalities, cantons and the Confederation also make a budget every year.
Budget advice Switzerland offers templates and tips for families and young people.
Anyone who sticks to a budget is less likely to get into debt.

abschnitte.text: A **budget** is an overview of the money that comes in and the money you want to spend. **Income** is, for example, wages, pocket money or presents. **Spending** is everything you pay for, from your mobile phone to a trip to the cinema. The aim is for spending not to be greater than income.

**Fixed costs** are expenses that stay the same every month, such as rent, health insurance or a mobile phone contract. **Variable costs** change, for example for food, clothes or free time. There are also irregular expenses such as holidays, presents or dentist's bills. It is best to put a small amount aside for these every month.

You can practise making a budget even with your pocket money. Write down how much you get and what you spend it on, for example in a small notebook or an app. If you are saving for something bigger, such as a bike, you put a fixed amount aside every month. That way you can see exactly when you will be able to afford your goal.

With a budget, families plan their spending on housing, food, insurance and free time. **Budget advice Switzerland** publishes sample budgets that show how much money other households typically spend. A popular rule of thumb is the 50-30-20 rule: half for necessities, 30 per cent for wants and 20 per cent for saving. Anyone moving out of home for the first time should definitely make a budget.

Municipalities, cantons and the Confederation also draw up a budget every year, which is often called an **estimate** there. Parliament decides what the money is spent on, for example schools, roads or the army. In many municipalities, the municipal assembly votes directly on the budget. The Confederation spends more than 80 billion francs every year.

begriffe.erklaerung: Money that you receive.
Money that you pay out.
Costs that come up regularly at the same level.
Another word for the budget of a municipality, a canton or the Confederation.

gewusst: The word budget comes from the Old French “bougette”, a small leather bag for money.
Switzerland has a debt brake in its constitution, which forces the Confederation not to spend more than it takes in over the long term.
Many people underestimate how much money they spend on small things such as snacks or drinks when they are out.

teile.einleitung: An **agreement** is something that two or more people settle with each other. Especially when it comes to money, clear agreements help to avoid arguments. If you lend something, you should agree when it will come back.
wichtigste: In an agreement, two or more people come to an understanding.
When lending, you should agree when the money will come back.
Clear agreements prevent arguments.
You can also write an agreement down.
If you keep to agreements, people trust you.

abschnitte.text: In an **agreement**, two or more people say what applies. For example: “I'll lend you 5 francs, and you'll give them back to me on Friday.” Both are happy with this. Then everyone knows where they stand. Adults make agreements all the time too, for example with their employer or their landlord.

Sometimes you forget exactly what was agreed. That is why it can help to **write the agreement down**: who, how much, by when. A short note or a message on your mobile is enough. For larger amounts, adults write a **contract** that both sign. This is an agreement with fixed rules.

Anyone who keeps to an agreement is **reliable**. Others are then happy to trust them again. If you cannot keep an agreement, you say so early and honestly. Then you can find a new solution together, for example a later date.

gewusst: In Switzerland, even without a signature, a spoken agreement can be a valid contract, for example when shopping in a shop.

teile.einleitung: Some bills only come once a year, but they are big. So that they do not suddenly empty your account, you put part of the amount aside every month. This is called a provision (Rückstellung).
wichtigste: A provision is money you set aside for a later bill.
Typical annual bills are taxes, insurance or the radio and television licence fee.
You divide the annual amount by 12 and put this part aside every month.
That way the money is ready when the bill arrives.
Provisions belong in every good budget.

abschnitte.text: Some expenses do not come up every month. **Taxes**, **health insurance** if paid annually, other **insurance** or the **radio and television licence fee** often only come once or a few times a year. If you forget them in your budget, you suddenly have too little money. Then all that is left is to get into debt or pay the bill late.

You write down all the annual bills and add them up. You divide this amount by **12**. If, for example, an insurance policy costs 600 francs a year, you put **50 francs** aside every month. It is best to transfer the money to a separate **savings account**. That way you do not spend it on other things by mistake.

With provisions, you do not get a fright when a big bill lands in the letterbox. The money is already there. For unexpected expenses too, such as a dentist’s bill or a broken bike, a small **emergency fund** is worth having. Budget advice services recommend building provisions firmly into your budget.

gewusst: Companies also make provisions. In their accounts this is an important technical term.

teile.einleitung: Premium-rate services are offers by phone or text message that cost more than a normal message. They include, for example, prize draws, voting in TV shows or subscriptions for ringtones. The costs go straight onto the phone bill.
wichtigste: Premium-rate services cost more than a normal text message or a normal call.
They often use short codes or numbers beginning with 090.
The extra costs are charged to the phone bill.
Sometimes you take out a subscription with a text message without noticing.
You can have premium-rate services blocked by your mobile provider.
Always check the price before sending.

abschnitte.text: A **premium-rate service** is a service that is paid for through the mobile network. For example, you send a text message to a **short code** with four or five digits. Or you call a number that begins with **0900** or **0901**. As well as the normal costs, the provider charges an extra amount. This is taken from your phone bill or your pay-as-you-go credit.

Typical examples are prize draws, voting in TV programmes, games or horoscopes by text message. A single message can cost a few francs. If you take part often, you quickly pay a lot of money. **Text message subscriptions** are particularly dangerous: you then get messages regularly, and each one costs something. To end such a subscription, you usually have to send “STOP” to the same number.

The price must be stated in the advert. Read it carefully before you send anything. Parents can have **premium-rate services blocked** by the mobile provider. In Switzerland, providers must offer such a block free of charge. If you do not understand a bill, ask the provider. If there is a dispute, the telecommunications ombudsman, **Ombudscom**, can help.

gewusst: With the cost control in your mobile provider’s app, you can see at all times what money has been spent on.
Mobile games also have expensive extra purchases that can be paid for through the phone bill.

teile.einleitung: Roaming is when you use your mobile phone abroad. The phone then connects to the network of a foreign provider. Without a suitable package, this can be very expensive.
wichtigste: Roaming means using your phone abroad on foreign networks.
Your own provider pays the foreign network and passes the costs on to you.
Without a package, mobile data in particular can cost a lot.
With a roaming package, Wi-Fi or with mobile data switched off, the bill stays low.
Before travelling, it is worth checking the prices with your provider.

abschnitte.text: The English word **roaming** means wandering around. At home your phone is connected to your provider’s network. Abroad, this network does not exist. That is why the phone automatically connects to a **foreign network**. The foreign network charges money for this use, and your provider passes the cost on to you.

**Mobile data**, meaning surfing the internet, is often particularly expensive. Apps download data in the background without you noticing. Calls that you answer abroad can also cost money. Switzerland is not part of the EU. The EU rule that roaming in EU countries is charged at domestic prices therefore does not automatically apply to Swiss providers.

Before your holiday, ask your provider about a **roaming package**. With it, a certain amount of data is paid for in advance. On your phone you can switch off **mobile data** or **data roaming**. In the hotel or café you use **Wi-Fi**. Many providers send a text message with the prices when you arrive in a country, and you should read it.

gewusst: Even near the border in Switzerland, your phone can accidentally connect to a foreign network.

teile.einleitung: A banknote can tear, end up in the washing machine or burn. In many cases, however, the money is not lost: damaged notes can be replaced.
wichtigste: A damaged banknote is not automatically worthless.
You can take it to a bank.
The Swiss National Bank is responsible for Swiss notes.
If enough of the note is left, you usually get a replacement.
You should keep even small pieces and not throw them away.

abschnitte.text: Banknotes in Switzerland are issued by the **Swiss National Bank**, SNB for short. It also replaces damaged notes. You can take a damaged note to a bank, which passes it on, or directly to the National Bank. It is important to bring all the pieces.

The National Bank checks how much of the note is still there. If more than half is left, there is usually a replacement. A note that has been through the washing machine can often still be exchanged too. Very small remains in which no note can be recognised are not replaced.

Burnt or very badly damaged notes can also be handed in. Experts at the National Bank examine them closely. But anyone who has destroyed a note on purpose in order to get a replacement cannot expect any money. Suspicious cases are checked carefully.

Swiss banknotes come in different series. Since 2020, notes from the sixth series onwards can be exchanged at the National Bank with no time limit. So if you find old notes in an old drawer, you should not throw them away. However, you can no longer pay with them in shops.

gewusst: The current Swiss banknotes are not made of paper alone, but of a composite material with a plastic layer in the middle.
The Swiss National Bank has its seats in Bern and Zurich.

teile.einleitung: The PIN is a secret number with which you prove that a bank card really belongs to you. PIN stands for “personal identification number” and works like a password made of digits. Anyone who knows your PIN and has your card can control your money, which is why it is so important.
wichtigste: The PIN is a secret number code, usually made up of four to six digits.
You need it at cash machines and often when paying by card in a shop.
You must not tell anyone your PIN, not even friends or people claiming to work for a bank.
Anyone who has the PIN and the card can withdraw money or pay without you noticing.
After several wrong attempts, the card is usually blocked.
A real bank never asks for your PIN by phone, text message or email.
If the card is lost, you must have it blocked by the bank immediately.

abschnitte.text: The **PIN** is a secret combination of numbers that belongs to a bank card, a credit card or a mobile phone. It usually consists of four to six digits. The card is the key, so to speak, and the PIN is the lock that goes with it. Only when both match does the machine give out money.

At a **cash machine**, in Switzerland often called a Bancomat, you always have to enter your PIN. It is also often required when paying in a shop with a debit card, especially for larger amounts. For small amounts you can often pay contactlessly without a PIN. Phones and SIM cards also have their own PIN.

Anyone who finds or steals your card and knows your PIN can withdraw money from your **account**. This often happens without you noticing until you look at your bank statement. If you passed on the PIN yourself, the bank usually does not have to make good the loss. That is why the PIN is considered one of the most important secrets in handling money.

Learn your PIN by heart and never write it on the card or keep it in your purse. When typing it in, hold your hand over the keypad so that nobody can watch. Fraudsters sometimes try to get the PIN through **phishing**, meaning fake messages. But a bank never asks for your PIN, neither on the phone nor by email.

If you enter the PIN wrongly several times, usually three times, the card is **blocked**. This protects against thieves who simply guess. If the card is lost or stolen, call the bank’s card-blocking number straight away. You will then get a new card and usually a new PIN as well.

The first cash machines appeared from 1967, first in London. So that only the right person got money, a secret code was needed. That is how the PIN became a fixed part of banking. Today many devices also use fingerprints or face recognition.

begriffe.erklaerung: A secret number that belongs to your card, like a password made of digits.
The usual word in Switzerland for a cash machine.
Fraud with fake messages to get hold of secrets such as passwords or a PIN.
The bank makes a card unusable so that nobody can pay with it any more.

gewusst: Many people choose birthdays or 1234 as their PIN, which is why thieves try exactly these numbers first.
The world’s first cash machine was put into operation at a bank in London in 1967.
At many banks you can change your PIN yourself at the machine to a number you can easily remember.

teile.einleitung: Pester products (Quengelware) are sweets and small items placed right by the till in a shop. They are positioned so that children in particular see them and want them. Many children then pester until their parents buy something.
wichtigste: Pester products are usually by the till.
They are often sweets, chewing gum or small toys.
The goods are placed exactly at children’s eye level.
While waiting in the queue, you have time to look at them.
The aim is spontaneous purchases that you had not planned at all.

abschnitte.text: At the till you often have to wait. During this time you look around. Shops put small, cheap things there that you quickly pick up. Because they do not cost much, you hardly think about it. Purchases like these are called **spontaneous purchases** or **impulse buys**. That is why the area by the till is sometimes also called the **pester zone**.

Shops think very carefully about where each product goes. Expensive or popular products are often at eye level. For children, that means lower down on the shelf. Things you need every day, like milk or bread, are often right at the back. That way you walk past lots of other goods. This approach is part of **marketing**, meaning everything that is meant to boost sales.

A **shopping list** helps you buy only what you really need. You can also agree beforehand whether there will be something sweet or not. If you notice that something is tempting you, ask yourself: Did I want this before? That way you can see through the tricks and decide for yourself.

gewusst: Some shops have tills without sweets so that families can pay in peace.

teile.einleitung: An in-app purchase is a purchase you make directly inside an app or a mobile game. Whether it is “gems”, “coins” or new characters: it costs real money, so you should ask your parents first. Many games are free at the start and make their money precisely from purchases like these.
wichtigste: In-app purchases are purchases inside an app or a game.
Game currencies such as gems or coins cost real money.
Children should always ask their parents before making an in-app purchase.
Many free games are financed through in-app purchases.
Payment is often made through the account in the App Store or Google Play Store.
On phones and tablets you can block in-app purchases or protect them with a password.

abschnitte.text: An **in-app purchase** takes place directly in an app, without having to go to a shop or a website. You can use it to buy, for example, new levels, costumes for game characters or a subscription with extra features. In games you often buy a **virtual currency** such as gems, diamonds or coins. But behind each of these currencies there is real money.

Many games are free to download; this is called **free-to-play**. The companies that make them still earn money, because some of the players buy extras. Often the game is designed so that without buying anything you have to wait a long time or play very often. With money it goes faster, and that is exactly what is meant to tempt you into buying.

Some games sell **loot boxes**, which are surprise boxes with random contents. You do not know beforehand whether you will get something rare or just something worthless. This is similar to gambling and can be addictive. Some countries, such as Belgium, have therefore banned paid loot boxes.

On iPhones, Android devices and games consoles you can block in-app purchases in the settings. Parents can make it so that every purchase has to be confirmed with a **password** or with their approval. Prepaid gift cards help to limit spending. That way there are no nasty surprises on the bill.

Children and young people under 18 may only spend smaller amounts of their **pocket money** without their parents’ consent. If a child has spent a lot of money without permission, the parents can contact the provider. Some stores refund the money in such cases, but there is no guarantee. It is best to agree clear rules within the family for buying things on the internet.

begriffe.erklaerung: Play money such as gems or coins that you buy with real money.
Games that are free but offer purchases within the game.
A surprise box in a game with random contents.
An online shop where you download and pay for apps.

gewusst: The makers of some well-known mobile games earn billions every year, even though the games can be downloaded for free.
Game currencies are often sold in odd-sized packs so that it is hard to work out the real price.
Belgium has classified paid loot boxes as gambling and banned them.

teile.einleitung: A household has many expenses every month, for example for the flat, food and electricity. So that the money is enough, a family plans these costs in a budget.
wichtigste: Fixed costs, such as the rent, come up every month.
On top of that there are expenses that vary, such as food or clothes.
Health insurance and taxes are big items in Switzerland.
A budget shows what the money is needed for.
You should put some money aside for unexpected expenses.
Housing is the biggest expense for many households.

abschnitte.text: **Fixed costs** are expenses that are the same every month. They include the rent, health insurance premiums, other insurance and subscriptions. They have to be paid before you spend money on anything else. For many families, the flat or house is the biggest item in the budget.
**Variable costs** differ from month to month. They include food, clothes, free time and outings. This is where a family can most easily save. If you shop carefully, you have more money left over.

In a **budget** you write down all income and spending. That way you can see whether the money is enough and where you can save. In Switzerland, for example, budget advice services help with templates and tips. Taxes, which come once a year, are also best planned for monthly.

Sometimes the washing machine breaks down or a dentist’s bill arrives. For cases like these a **reserve** is important. If you save a small amount every month, you will not get into difficulties so quickly. Children can help too, by saving electricity and water.

gewusst: According to the Federal Statistical Office, Swiss households spend the largest share of their consumer spending on housing and energy.
In Switzerland, health insurance premiums have to be paid per person, children included.

teile.einleitung: A debt spiral comes about when you pay old debts with new loans. Because every loan costs interest, the debts keep growing. Like a spiral, it turns downwards.
wichtigste: In a debt spiral you take out new loans to pay old debts.
Every new loan brings extra interest.
The debts grow instead of getting smaller.
In the end, a large part of the money goes on interest alone.
Budget advice services and debt advice centres offer help.

abschnitte.text: Someone cannot pay a bill and takes out a **loan**. Now they have to pay back the loan plus **interest**. If the money is not enough for that, they take out another loan. So each step becomes more expensive. The debts get bigger and bigger, and less and less money is left to live on.

Interest is the price of borrowed money. With **consumer loans** and **credit cards** it is often high. If you cannot pay the interest, it is sometimes added to the debt. Then you pay **interest on interest**. That is why a debt grows quickly if nothing is paid back.

The most important step is: take on **no new debts** to pay old ones. An honest **budget** shows how much you can pay off each month. Then you talk to the creditors about a payment plan. Debt advice centres help to find a way out.

gewusst: In Switzerland, the Federal Council sets a maximum interest rate for consumer loans so that loans cannot become as expensive as lenders like.

teile.einleitung: One click on “Try it free”, and suddenly bills arrive every month: that is a **subscription trap**. A hidden contract is concluded that costs money regularly. If you read the small print, you can protect yourself well.
wichtigste: A subscription trap is a hidden contract that costs money regularly.
Free offers, prize draws or trial subscriptions are often used as bait.
The costs and the length of the contract are hidden in the small print.
Subscription traps exist on websites, in apps and by text message.
Before you click, it is worth checking the price, the length and how to cancel.
If you have problems, your parents or a consumer protection organisation can help.

abschnitte.text: A **subscription trap** lures you with something that looks free or very cheap. This can be a **free trial**, a prize draw, a horoscope or a game. Anyone who clicks “Next” takes out a **subscription** without noticing. After that, bills arrive every month or every week. Often you only notice when money is missing.

In subscription traps, the **costs** and the **length** of the contract are often in small or grey print or right at the bottom of the page. You often have to give your address or mobile number, even though something is supposed to be free. A trial subscription sometimes renews automatically if you do not **cancel** in time. If you look carefully, you will find these details in the **small print**.

Subscription traps are not only found on websites but also in **apps** and by **text message**. Sometimes tapping on an advert is enough, and the costs are charged to your **mobile phone bill**. That is why it is wise to ask your parents before you sign up for anything. Many mobile providers can block such payments.

Before every click: check the **price**, the **length** and how to **cancel**. If you have fallen into a trap anyway, you should not simply pay, but you should not simply ignore everything either. It is better to get help from your parents or from a **consumer protection organisation**. They often have template letters for such cases. In Switzerland too, prices must be stated clearly.

gewusst: Many subscription traps are designed so that the confirm button is large and colourful but the price is hardly visible.
Anyone under 18 is generally only allowed to sign larger contracts with their parents' consent.

teile.einleitung: A household account book is a record of all income and spending, so you can keep track of your money. In it you write down how much money comes in and what it is spent on. That way you quickly notice where the money is actually going.
wichtigste: A household account book records all income and spending.
It helps you keep track of your own money.
You can keep it on paper, in a spreadsheet or with an app.
After a few weeks you can see what you spend the most money on.
A household account book is the basis for a personal budget.
You can keep a small household account book even with your pocket money.

abschnitte.text: A **household account book** is a list in which you note every movement of money. On one side is the **income**, such as pocket money, wages or presents. On the other side is the **spending**, for example on snacks, clothes or your phone. At the end of the month you work out what is left over.

It is best to write down every expense straight away, otherwise you forget small amounts. Receipts from the shop help with this. You sort the expenses into **categories** such as food, free time, clothes or saving. If you keep at it regularly, you will have a clear picture after just one month.

In the past, many families kept a real book with columns for each day. Today many people use a spreadsheet on the computer or a **budgeting app** on their phone. Some banks even show the spending on your account automatically sorted into categories. You still have to note cash spending yourself, though.

From the figures in the household account book you can make a **budget**, which is a plan for the future. You decide how much you want to spend on each category every month. In Switzerland, for example, Budgetberatung Schweiz offers sample budgets for young people and families. That way you can also save on purpose for a bigger goal such as a bike.

Many people are amazed at how much money goes on small things like drinks or apps. A household account book makes these **money guzzlers** visible. It helps to avoid debt, because you notice early on when money is getting tight. You also learn to decide more consciously what really matters to you.

begriffe.erklaerung: Money you receive, for example wages or pocket money.
Money you pay for something.
A plan for how much money you want to spend on what.
A group into which you sort similar expenses.

gewusst: Even on old farms, income and spending were noted in books so that the family would get through the winter.
People who keep a household account book often discover subscriptions they no longer use at all.
Small daily expenses of 3 francs add up to more than 1000 francs a year.

teile.einleitung: You fall into a debt trap when you have more and more debts and can hardly get out. It often starts with taking on new debts to pay old ones. Interest and fees make everything even worse.
wichtigste: A debt trap often arises when you pay old debts with new ones.
On top of that come interest, reminder fees and debt enforcement costs.
As a result the debts get bigger instead of smaller.
Common causes are buying in instalments, loans, phone bills and online purchases.
Anyone in debt can get help from a debt advice service.

abschnitte.text: It often starts with small amounts: an unpaid phone bill, something bought in instalments, an online purchase on **invoice**. If you cannot pay, **reminder fees** are added. Some people then take out a **loan** to settle the old bills. But the loan costs **interest**. In the end you have more debt than before.

One warning sign is when your money has already run out before the end of the month. Anyone who no longer opens bills or ignores reminders is also in danger. If a bill is not paid for a long time, **debt enforcement proceedings** can follow. An entry in the **debt enforcement register** can later make it harder, for example, to find a flat.

It is important not to look away. A **budget** shows where the money goes. You can often agree **payment by instalments** with the creditors without taking out new loans. In Switzerland, many cantons have **debt advice centres** that help for free or at low cost. The earlier you get in touch, the easier it is.

gewusst: Many adults who are in debt took on their first debts when they were young, often because of phones, taxes or health insurance.

teile.einleitung: Dividing up your money means not spending it all at once. You think about how long the money has to last and spread it out. That way you still have some left at the end of the week.
wichtigste: Dividing up means not spending everything at once.
You spread the money over the time it has to last.
You can spend one part and keep another.
If you divide up your money, you will still have some later.
A small plan helps with dividing up.
Adults divide up their money too; this is called a budget.

abschnitte.text: Imagine you get **4 francs** for the whole week. If you spend it all on Monday, you have nothing left until Sunday. If you **divide up** the money, you think beforehand: how much do I need today, and what will I keep? For example, you spend 1 franc and keep 3 francs. That way you still have something left for later.

A **plan** makes dividing up easier. You can write down how much money you have and what you need it for. Some children put the money into different **money boxes**: one for spending and one for saving. When one box is empty, you know straight away: now I will wait until next time.

Before you buy something, you can ask yourself: **Do I really need this?** Or do I only want it because I can see it right now? Sometimes it helps to wait a day. If you still want it then, the wish is real. That way you spend your money on things that really make you happy.

Parents usually get their **wages** once a month. With that money they have to pay the rent, food, health insurance and much more. That is why many make a **budget**. This is a plan for how the money is spread over the month. Anyone who learns as a child to divide up their **pocket money** will be good at it later.

gewusst: Budget advice Switzerland gives recommendations on roughly how much pocket money children can get at what age.
Many children first get their pocket money weekly and later, when they are older, monthly.

teile.einleitung: A bank account is an account with a bank or with Swiss Post in which you can keep and manage money safely. Your wages are paid into it, you pay bills with it and you withdraw cash from it. Many young people open their first account while they are still at school.
wichtigste: In a bank account, money is kept safely at a bank.
There are different kinds of account, for example the personal account, the savings account and the youth account.
Every Swiss account has an IBAN that begins with CH.
With a debit card or an app you can pay directly from your account.
Banks sometimes charge fees because running accounts and services costs them money.
In Switzerland, balances of up to 100,000 francs per person and bank are specially protected.
Many banks offer young people accounts without fees.

abschnitte.text: A **bank account** is like a safe store for your money at a bank. The bank keeps an exact record of how much money comes in and goes out. The money is not kept in a box of its own; the bank uses it, for example, for loans to other customers. In return you get a **balance** that you can use at any time.

You need a **personal account** or salary account for everyday life, for example for your wages, bills and standing orders. In a **savings account** you put money aside for later, and you often get a little more interest for it. For children and young people there are special youth accounts with low or no fees. Important providers in Switzerland are the cantonal banks, Raiffeisen banks, the big banks and PostFinance.

With a **debit card** you can pay in a shop or withdraw cash from a cash machine. The money is taken from your account immediately. Today bills are usually paid with a **QR-bill** in e-banking or with an app. Payment apps such as Twint are also linked to a bank account.

Banks sometimes charge **fees** because accounts, cards, security and staff cost them money. Typical charges are account fees, card fees or costs for withdrawing cash from other banks' machines. On the other hand, the bank sometimes pays **interest** on your balance because it can work with the money. It is worth comparing the offers of different banks.

Never give your PIN or your login details to anyone, not even to friends or people claiming to work for the bank. Banks never ask for passwords by email or text message; such messages are often **phishing**. Check the transactions on your account regularly so that you notice mistakes quickly. If the bank goes bust, deposit protection covers balances of up to 100,000 francs per customer.

begriffe.erklaerung: The international account number; in Switzerland it is 21 characters long and begins with CH.
The money in your account that belongs to you.
An amount that the bank pays for your money or charges for a loan.
A card with which you pay directly from your own account.
Fraudulent messages that try to get hold of your passwords.

gewusst: From 2015 to 2022 there were negative interest rates in Switzerland, and large customers even had to pay to keep money in their accounts.
The word bank comes from the Italian “banco”, the table of money changers at medieval markets.
Children can often have an account from birth, which their parents open for them.

teile.einleitung: In a price comparison you look at how much the same product costs in different shops or from different providers. There are often big differences, and if you compare, you can save a lot of money. But a good comparison looks not only at the price, but also at quantity and quality.
wichtigste: The same product can cost different amounts in different shops.
If you compare prices, you save money for other wishes.
The unit price, for example per kilo or per litre, helps you compare fairly.
Quality, guarantee and delivery costs also belong in the comparison.
On the internet, comparison websites help you compare.
Special offers and discounts are not always as cheap as they look.
Comparing is particularly worth it for expensive purchases.

abschnitte.text: In a **price comparison** you look at what a particular product costs from several sellers. This can be in the supermarket, in an electronics shop or on the internet. The same games console can cost 50 francs more in one shop than in another. If you compare, you consciously choose the best offer.

Packs are often different sizes, which is why the **unit price** is important. It shows how much a kilo, a litre or 100 grams costs. In Switzerland this price is shown in small print on the price tag of many foods. That way you notice that a jumbo pack is sometimes not cheaper at all than two small ones.

On the internet you can compare lots of prices in a few minutes. There are **comparison websites** for this, which list the offers of many retailers. But you should also take delivery costs and delivery time into account. With orders from abroad, customs duty and VAT are sometimes added.

abschnitte.titel: It is not only the price that counts
abschnitte.text: The cheapest product is not always the best. **Quality**, durability and the guarantee also matter. Shoes for 20 francs that break after two months end up costing more than a pair for 60 francs that lasts two years. Reviews from other customers can also help.

If you want something bigger, note down the prices from two or three shops. Ask yourself whether you really need the product now or whether you can wait for a **special offer**. Watch out for bait offers with big discount signs, which are sometimes not that cheap at all. And work out how many weeks of pocket money the difference adds up to.

begriffe.erklaerung: The price for a fixed quantity, for example per kilo or per litre.
A reduction that makes something cheaper.
A very cheap offer meant to lure customers into the shop.
What you pay extra to have goods delivered to your home.

gewusst: Some online shops change their prices several times a day, depending on demand.
Many Swiss people cross the border to Germany, France or Italy to go shopping, which is called shopping tourism.
Jumbo packs are not always cheaper; the unit price shows this straight away.

teile.einleitung: The price is the amount of money you have to pay for a product or a service. Whether it is an ice cream, a bus ticket or a bike, everything has a price. If you pay attention to prices, you learn what things are worth and can use your money more wisely.
wichtigste: The price tells you how much money you have to pay for something.
In Switzerland, prices are given in francs and centimes.
Prices come about through supply and demand.
A price includes costs for materials, work, transport, taxes and profit.
In Swiss shops, the price must be clearly displayed.
If you look at prices when shopping, you learn how much things cost and shop more consciously.
When prices rise in general, this is called inflation.

abschnitte.text: A **price** is the amount of money the seller asks for a product or service. It is on a price label, on a sign or on the menu. In Switzerland it is given in francs and centimes, for example 2.50 francs for a bread roll. For buyers, the price is important information for deciding whether a purchase is worth it.

Prices depend on **supply and demand**. If many people want to buy something that is rare, the price rises. If there is a great deal of a product but few buyers, the price falls. That is why strawberries are more expensive in winter than in June, when they are ripe in Switzerland.

A price is made up of many parts: raw materials, wages, rent for the shop, transport and advertising. On top of that comes **value added tax**, which goes to the state. Finally, the retailer also wants to make a **profit**. That is why, with a T-shirt costing 20 francs, often only a small part is left for the woman who sewed it.

Switzerland is considered a **high-price island**, because many products are more expensive here than in neighbouring countries. Reasons include the high wages and rents.
