A law requires shops to display their prices including VAT clearly. The federal **Price Supervisor** also makes sure that companies without real competition do not charge excessive prices.

If you go shopping with your parents and look at the prices, you learn how much things cost in everyday life. You notice, for example, that branded products are often more expensive than own brands. You also see that special offers are not always real bargains. If you know prices, you can divide up your pocket money better.

When many things become more expensive at the same time, this is called **inflation** (in Switzerland “Teuerung”). Then you can buy less with the same money. In Switzerland, the Federal Statistical Office measures inflation with the Swiss Consumer Price Index. The Swiss National Bank tries to keep prices as stable as possible.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much of something there is and how many people want to buy it.
A tax that is included in the price of almost all goods and goes to the state.
When prices rise in general and money becomes worth less.
A federal office that makes sure prices are fair.

gewusst: The magazine The Economist compares prices in different countries using the price of a Big Mac, and Switzerland is regularly one of the most expensive countries.
Prices like 9.95 francs are meant to seem cheaper, because our brain pays most attention to the first digit.
In the past, prices were often not displayed at all but negotiated at the market, which is called haggling.

teile.einleitung: Anyone employed in Switzerland is insured against accidents at work. This insurance is called occupational accident insurance. Its premium is paid entirely by the employer.
wichtigste: All employees in Switzerland are compulsorily insured against accidents at work.
The premium for occupational accident insurance is paid in full by the employer.
That is why it does not appear as a deduction on the payslip.
Occupational diseases are also insured.
The rules are in the Federal Act on Accident Insurance, UVG for short.
The largest accident insurer in Switzerland is Suva.

abschnitte.text: An **occupational accident** happens at work or on a journey you make for work. Examples are a fall from a ladder on a building site or a cut in a restaurant kitchen. Apprentices doing vocational training are also insured. **Occupational diseases** are insured too. These are illnesses caused by work, for example by dangerous dust.

The premium for occupational accident insurance is paid by the **employer** alone. That is why there is no deduction for it on the payslip. It is different with **non-occupational accident insurance**: it covers accidents in free time. Its premium is usually deducted from wages. It applies to employees who work at least 8 hours a week for the same employer.

After an accident, the insurance pays the **medical costs**, meaning the doctor, hospital and therapy. If you cannot work, there is a **daily allowance**. It is 80 per cent of the insured wages. If a permanent impairment remains after a serious accident, there may be a pension. In this way nobody has to get into financial difficulty because of an accident at work.

In many sectors, for example construction or industry, employees are insured with **Suva**. Suva is the largest accident insurer in Switzerland. Other businesses, for example offices, can choose a private insurer. Suva also works for **accident prevention**. With campaigns it explains how to work safely.

gewusst: Anyone who works less than 8 hours a week is also protected on the way to work by the occupational accident insurance.
Suva is an independent public-law institution and does not work for profit.

teile.einleitung: An investment means using money so that you get more back later. When you save, you put money safely aside; when you invest, you put money in with a risk in order to get a higher return. Companies and states also invest, for example in machines, roads or schools.
wichtigste: Investing means using money in order to earn a return in the future.
When you save, you put money safely aside; when you invest, you take a risk.
Typical investments are shares, bonds, funds and property.
The higher the possible profit, the higher the risk usually is too.
If you spread your money across many investments, you lower the risk.
Companies invest in machines, buildings or research.
Education is also considered an investment in your own future.

abschnitte.text: An **investment** is spending money today in the hope of a benefit in the future. A baker who buys a new oven wants to bake more bread with it and earn more. A private person can, for example, put their money into **shares** and hope for rising share prices and dividends. The word comes from the Latin word for “to clothe”.

When you **save**, the money sits in an account and is safe, but it usually earns only a little interest. When you invest, the money can grow more, but it can also lose value. That is why the rule is: money you will need soon belongs in a savings account. Money you will not need for many years can be invested.

**Shares** are parts of companies, and their value often goes up and down a lot. With **bonds** you lend money to a state or a company and receive interest in return. Property such as houses and flats brings in rent. Funds and ETFs bundle many investments into a single product.

The **return** shows how much an investment earns in a year, usually as a percentage. In principle: the higher the possible return, the higher the risk. Anyone who promises that you will get rich quickly without any risk is usually not trustworthy or is a fraudster. Experts advise spreading your money and thinking long term.

abschnitte.titel: Investments by companies and the state
abschnitte.text: It is not only private individuals who invest. Companies build factories, buy computers or pay for research into new products. The state invests in roads, railway lines, schools and hospitals. A well-known Swiss example is the Gotthard Base Tunnel, which opened in 2016 and cost many billions of francs.

begriffe.erklaerung: What an investment earns, usually given as a percentage per year.
A part of a company that makes you one of its owners.
A security with which you lend money to a company or the state.
The possibility that you lose money.

gewusst: If you start investing when you are young, you benefit from the compound interest effect for a particularly long time.
A good education is also considered an investment, because it can make a higher income possible later.
With the Gotthard Base Tunnel, Switzerland invested for decades in the longest railway tunnel in the world.

teile.einleitung: A consumer loan is money that you borrow from a bank, for example to buy a piece of furniture or a car, and that you have to pay back with interest. It is also called a small loan or personal loan. Consumer loans are convenient, but they can quickly lead into the debt trap.
wichtigste: A consumer loan is borrowed money for private purchases.
It must be paid back with interest, usually in monthly instalments.
Leasing, credit cards with part payment and overdrafts also count as consumer loans.
In Switzerland, the Consumer Credit Act governs these loans.
Before granting a loan, the bank must check whether you can actually pay it back.
In Switzerland, the interest on cash loans is limited to a maximum of 10 per cent.
Many people in debt have one or more consumer loans.

abschnitte.text: With a **consumer loan**, a bank or credit institution lends money to a private individual. It is used to pay for things for personal use, such as furniture, holidays, a car or a television. You have to pay the money back in **instalments** with interest. As a result, the thing you bought ends up costing considerably more than its price.

The best-known consumer loan is the **cash loan**, where you receive an amount of money straight into your account. **Leasing** a car also counts; with leasing you rent the car for several years. Anyone who makes part payments with a credit card or overdraws their account is also taking out a loan. Online shops also have offers like “buy now, pay later”.

The **Consumer Credit Act** protects customers from too much debt. Before a bank grants a loan, it must check the person’s **creditworthiness**, that is whether they can pay the instalments as well as their living costs. Since 2016 the interest on cash loans may be at most 10 per cent a year. Loans are reported to a central database so that nobody gets too many loans at the same time.

A consumer loan makes expensive wishes possible straight away, but the bill comes later. If you fall ill or lose your job, you often can no longer pay the instalments. Then reminders, debt enforcement and a **debt spiral** threaten. According to debt advice centres, young adults are particularly often affected by debt.

Before you take out a loan, you should ask yourself whether you really need the thing straight away. It is often wiser to **save** first and pay in cash later. If you still need a loan, compare the interest and total costs of different providers. If you have money worries, the free advice centres of Schuldenberatung Schweiz can help.

begriffe.erklaerung: A part payment with which you pay back a loan bit by bit.
The price you have to pay for borrowed money.
A kind of rental over several years, usually for cars.
The ability to pay back a loan without getting into difficulty.

gewusst: A loan of 10,000 francs at 10 per cent interest costs a good 1500 francs in interest over three years.
In Switzerland, aggressive advertising for consumer loans has been banned since 2016.
Anyone who takes out a loan is recorded in a central database that other banks can consult.

teile.einleitung: Every payslip in Switzerland shows the deduction for **AHV, IV and EO**. With these contributions you pay into the most important social insurance schemes. For employees, the employer and the employee each pay half.
wichtigste: AHV stands for old-age and survivors' insurance.
IV is the disability insurance, and EO is the income compensation scheme.
Employers and employees each pay half of the contributions.
In 2024 the contribution was 10.6 per cent of pay in total.
People in work pay from 1 January after their 17th birthday.
Self-employed people pay their contributions alone.

abschnitte.text: The **AHV** is the **old-age and survivors' insurance**. It pays a **pension** when you retire. If a parent dies, the children and the partner receive a survivors' pension. The AHV is the **first pillar** of the Swiss pension system. It has existed since 1948.

With the same deduction you also pay into two other insurance schemes. The **IV**, the **disability insurance**, helps people who can no longer work because of illness or an accident. The **EO**, the **income compensation scheme**, pays part of your wages, for example during military or civilian service. That is why payslips often say “AHV/IV/EO”.

For employees, the contributions are **shared**. The employer deducts one half from the wages and pays the other half on top. In 2024 the total contribution was 10.6 per cent of pay, so 5.3 per cent for each side. **Self-employed people** have no employer and therefore pay their contributions alone.

Anyone who works pays AHV contributions from **1 January after their 17th birthday**. That is why many apprentices suddenly see new deductions on their payslip in their second year. People who do not work, for example students, pay a minimum contribution from 1 January after their 20th birthday. In this way there are no **gaps in contributions** that would reduce the pension later.

The AHV works on a **pay-as-you-go system**. This means that the contributions of people in work are paid straight out again as pensions to retired people. In addition, there is money from the Confederation and from VAT. Every person has an **AHV number**, under which their contributions are collected.

gewusst: The AHV was approved by the people in 1947 and introduced in 1948.
Anyone with gaps in their contributions can pay for missing years up to five years later.

teile.einleitung: A debt enforcement register extract is a document from the debt enforcement office. It shows whether debt enforcement proceedings are running or have run against a person. Many people need one for the first time when they are looking for a flat.
wichtigste: The extract shows the debt enforcement proceedings against a person.
Landlords often ask for it when you apply for a rented flat.
You order it from the debt enforcement office where you live.
Many offices also let you order it online.
The extract costs a small fee.
It shows debt enforcement proceedings from the last 5 years.

abschnitte.titel: What do you need it for?
abschnitte.text: Anyone who applies for a **rented flat** often has to include a current extract. Landlords want to know whether someone pays their bills. A **clean extract** with no entries shows that you are reliable. Sometimes employers also ask for it, for example for jobs with a lot of responsibility for money. Banks may also want to see it for a loan.

The **debt enforcement office where you live** is responsible. If you have moved in recent years, it may make sense to ask at your previous place of residence too. Many offices let you order online, often also via the **EasyGov** portal. You have to prove your identity so that nobody can order someone else's data. The extract costs a small fee.

The extract shows the **debt enforcement proceedings** from the last 5 years, with the creditor, the amount and the current status. **Certificates of loss** can also appear. A certificate of loss is issued when there was not enough money during a seizure of assets. If there are no entries, the extract says that no proceedings are recorded. Landlords usually want an extract that is only a few weeks or months old.

It is best to pay bills on time. If you cannot pay at some point, an early conversation with the creditor helps, and paying in **instalments** is often possible. If you have money worries, many cantons offer free **debt advice**. If an unjustified debt enforcement is in the register, you can ask for it not to be disclosed under certain conditions.

gewusst: Switzerland has had its debt enforcement procedure since the Federal Act on Debt Enforcement and Bankruptcy of 1889.
An extract only ever covers the district of the debt enforcement office that issues it.

teile.einleitung: A rental deposit is an amount of money that you lodge as security when a tenancy begins and usually get back when you move out. It protects the landlord in case the tenant does not pay the rent or damages something in the flat. In Switzerland there are exact rules on how high it may be and where the money must be kept.
wichtigste: The rental deposit is security for the landlord.
You lodge it at the start of the tenancy.
For flats it may be at most three months’ rent.
The money must be held in a blocked account in the tenant’s name.
When you move out, you usually get the deposit back with interest.
Instead of paying cash, you can also take out rental deposit insurance.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who rents a flat often has to pay a **rental deposit**, also called a rent deposit. It is **security** for the landlord. If the tenant does not pay the rent or leaves damage when moving out, the landlord can take money from the deposit. If everything is in order, the tenant gets the money back.

Tenancy law in the **Code of Obligations** lays down that the deposit for flats may be at most three months’ rent. With a monthly rent of 1500 francs, that means at most 4500 francs. The money must be lodged in a **blocked account** at a bank in the tenant’s name. That way the landlord cannot simply use it.

When you move out, the flat is inspected together and a **handover report** is drawn up. It states whether there is any damage that the tenant must pay for. The tenant does not have to pay for normal wear and tear, such as slightly faded walls after many years. If both sides agree, the bank releases the money together with the interest.

To release the deposit, the bank usually needs the consent of both sides. If the landlord does not make a legal claim within one year of the end of the tenancy, the tenant can ask for the money back themselves. If there is a dispute, the **conciliation authority** for tenancy matters, which exists in every canton, can help. The procedure there is free of charge.

Many young people do not have enough money for a deposit when they first move out. Instead of lodging the money, you can take out **rental deposit insurance**. For this you pay a premium every year, which you do not get back. If there is damage, the insurance pays the landlord, and you have to pay the amount back to the insurance later.

begriffe.erklaerung: An amount of money lodged as security.
A bank account that can only be used with the consent of both sides.
A document that records the condition of the flat when moving in and out.
An office that helps when there is a dispute between tenant and landlord.

gewusst: The rental deposit belongs to the tenant, even though they cannot use it during the tenancy.
In Switzerland there is no legal upper limit on the deposit for business premises.
You should report damage that was already there when you moved in straight away, otherwise you may have to pay for it when you move out.

teile.einleitung: Inflation means that prices rise in general and you can buy less with the same money. If a bread roll costs more today than ten years ago, that is a sign of inflation. In Switzerland, the Swiss National Bank makes sure that prices stay stable.
wichtigste: Inflation means that prices rise in general.
You can then buy less with the same money.
In Switzerland, the Federal Statistical Office measures inflation with the Swiss Consumer Price Index.
The Swiss National Bank aims for inflation of less than 2 per cent a year.
The opposite of inflation is called deflation; then prices fall.
Very high inflation is called hyperinflation.
In Switzerland, people often say “Teuerung” instead of inflation.

abschnitte.text: With **inflation**, the general price level rises. So it is not just individual things that become more expensive, but many goods and services at the same time. As a result, money loses value; this is called the falling **value of money**. If you have 100 francs in your piggy bank, you can buy less with it after a few years of inflation.

Every month, the Federal Statistical Office watches the prices of a **basket of goods**. It contains the typical spending of a household, such as food, rents, clothes, electricity and transport. From this comes the **Swiss Consumer Price Index**, CPI for short. If this index rises by 2 per cent, the same basket of goods costs 2 per cent more than a year earlier.

Inflation happens, for example, when many people want to buy more than can be produced. Rising costs for energy such as oil and gas also make many products more expensive. If a central bank puts a great deal of new money into circulation, that can also push prices up. After the coronavirus pandemic and the start of the war in Ukraine, prices rose sharply in many countries from 2022.

abschnitte.titel: The role of the National Bank
abschnitte.text: In Switzerland, the **Swiss National Bank** (SNB) is responsible for stable prices. By price stability it means inflation of less than 2 per cent a year. If prices rise too much, it can raise the **policy rate**; then loans become more expensive and people spend less. Compared with other countries, inflation in Switzerland has mostly been low in recent decades.

Inflation hits people especially hard if their wages or pension do not rise as fast as prices. Savings in an account with low interest also lose purchasing power. An extreme form is **hyperinflation**, as in Germany in 1923, when banknotes worth billions were printed. Mild, steady inflation, on the other hand, is considered normal for a healthy economy.

begriffe.erklaerung: The Swiss word for rising prices, in other words inflation.
A selection of typical goods and services whose prices are compared.
The opposite of inflation: prices fall in general.
An interest rate set by the National Bank, which it uses to steer the economy.

gewusst: In Germany in 1923, a loaf of bread at times cost billions of marks, and children played with bundles of worthless money.
The Swiss franc is considered a particularly stable currency worldwide.
The basket of goods is adjusted regularly because shopping habits change; today, for example, mobile phone contracts are part of it.

teile.einleitung: A bulk discount means: if you buy more, you pay less per item. Offers like “3 for 2” look tempting. But they are only worth it if you really need everything.
wichtigste: With a bulk discount, the price per item goes down if you buy more.
“3 for 2” means: you take 3 and only pay for 2.
One item is then free, so to speak.
An offer is only worth it if you need everything.
The unit price helps when comparing.
Shops want to sell more with special offers.

abschnitte.text: With a **bulk discount**, you get a lower price if you buy a larger quantity. It comes as a **jumbo pack** or as an offer such as “3 for 2” or “2 for 1”. With “3 for 2”, a yoghurt costs, say, 1 franc. You take three but only pay 2 francs. Per item, a yoghurt then costs only about 67 centimes.

A discount only saves money if you would have bought the things anyway. If you take three yoghurts but only eat two, you have saved nothing in the end. Food can go past its date and end up in the bin. Shops know this: with special offers they want customers to **buy more** than they had planned. That is why a **shopping list** is worth it.

On many price tags, next to the price, there is a smaller amount, such as “per 100 grams” or “per litre”. This is the **unit price**. In Switzerland, the Price Indication Ordinance requires it to be shown for many packaged products. With the unit price you can see straight away whether the large pack really is cheaper. Sometimes, in fact, it is not.

gewusst: Companies also get a bulk discount when they order a great deal from a supplier.
Long-lasting things such as toothpaste or rice are better suited to jumbo packs than fresh food.

teile.einleitung: Every month, employees get a payslip. It shows how much you have earned, what is deducted and how much goes into your account at the end.
wichtigste: The payslip shows gross pay, deductions and net pay.
AVS/IV/EO is always deducted from the wages of adult employees.
Unemployment insurance (ALV) is also a fixed deduction.
Depending on the situation, the pension fund and accident insurance are added.
As a rule, you pay your health insurance premium yourself.
The employer also pays its own contributions to the social insurance schemes.

abschnitte.text: At the top of the **payslip** are the name, the month and the **gross pay**. Sometimes allowances are added, such as the **child allowance** or money for overtime. Below that come the deductions, line by line. At the very bottom is the **net pay**: this is the amount that is paid out. You should keep the payslip and check it briefly.

The **AVS** is the old-age and survivors’ insurance, and the **IV** is the disability insurance. The **EO**, the income compensation scheme, pays out, for example, during military or civilian service. These three are always deducted together. In 2024 the employees’ share came to 5.3 per cent of the wage in total. The employer pays the same amount again on top.

A small part is also deducted for **unemployment insurance** (ALV). Anyone who works at least 8 hours a week for the same employer usually pays for **non-occupational accident insurance** (NBU). Above a certain annual salary, the **pension fund** is added; this is the second pillar of retirement provision. These deductions differ a little from company to company.

The **health insurance premium** does not normally appear on the payslip. Each person takes out their own health insurance and pays the bill themselves. Most people in Switzerland also pay their taxes separately. One exception is **withholding tax**: for some foreign employees, the tax is deducted directly from their wages.

gewusst: The AVS has existed since 1948. It is Switzerland’s most important social insurance scheme.
In Switzerland, people who work pay AVS contributions from the year after their 17th birthday.

teile.einleitung: A purse (Portemonnaie) is a small pouch for money. In it you keep coins, notes and often cards too. That way you have everything together and do not lose something so quickly when you are out and about.
wichtigste: A purse is a pouch for money.
In it you keep your coins and notes together.
Many purses also have compartments for cards.
That way you do not lose your money so easily when you are out.
The word comes from French.

abschnitte.text: In a **purse**, money has its own fixed place. There is a compartment for **coins**, often with a zip or press stud. In another compartment are the **banknotes**. Many purses also have small slots for cards, such as a bank card, an ID card or a pupil’s pass. That way, when paying, you quickly find what you need.

Loose coins in your trouser pocket fall out easily. In a purse they stay **together**. It is best to carry your purse in a bag that you can close. On crowded trains or at markets you should keep a close eye on it. It is also wise not to take too much cash with you. If you lose your purse, you can ask at the municipality’s **lost property office**.

The word **Portemonnaie** comes from French. “Porter” means to carry, “monnaie” means money or coins. So a Portemonnaie is a “money carrier”. In Germany people often say **Geldbörse**; in Switzerland they usually say Portemonnaie. Some people also say “Portmonee” for short.

gewusst: Today, many lost property offices in Switzerland can also be asked online about lost items.

teile.einleitung: At the end of the month your money has already gone, and you do not really know why? Then **keeping track of your spending** helps. If you write down all your spending for a month, you can see where your money really goes.
wichtigste: Keeping track of spending means writing down what you spend money on.
It is best to note down all your spending for a month, including the small amounts.
It is often many small amounts that add up.
A household account book, a spreadsheet or an app can help.
With this overview you can make a budget.
What you write down, you can control better.

abschnitte.text: Many people know exactly how much they earn but not how much they spend. You remember big bills like the rent. But on top of that come many **small amounts**: a coffee, a snack, a subscription or a game on your mobile. On their own they are small, but together they become large. That is why there is often less money left at the end of the month than you thought.

The best way is to write down **all your spending** for a month. You can use a small notebook, a **household account book**, a spreadsheet or a **budgeting app**. It is important to note really every expense, including those paid by card or Twint. Receipts help you not to forget anything. At the end you sort your spending into groups such as food, free time or mobile phone.

After a month you can see in black and white what the money was spent on. Many people are surprised. Now you can decide where you want to save, for example on a subscription that you hardly use. From this overview a **budget** is created, meaning a plan for your money next month. That way you are back in control of your money.

Sometimes the money is not enough even though you keep track. Then it is good to talk to someone early. In Switzerland there are **budget advice services** that help with planning. They also have **budget templates** for apprentices, students and families. Your parents or a teacher can also give you tips.

gewusst: Small daily expenses add up quickly: anyone who spends 4 francs a day on a snack spends almost 1,500 francs a year on it.
Many banks automatically show in their app how much you have spent on each group of expenses.

teile.einleitung: Your mobile phone bill can be used to pay not only for calls and data but also for extra services from other companies. These can be expensive text message subscriptions or premium-rate numbers. A third-party billing block stops such services from being charged.
wichtigste: Third-party providers are companies that charge for their services through the mobile phone bill.
These include premium services such as expensive text message subscriptions or 0900 numbers.
A block stops such extra services from being charged.
You can have it set up by your own mobile provider.
The block especially protects children and young people from cost traps.
Normal calls, text messages and internet still work.

abschnitte.text: **Premium services** are paid offers that are charged to your mobile phone bill. Examples are hotlines with **0900 numbers**, text message subscriptions for games, ringtones or competitions. The company offering the service is not your own mobile provider but a **third-party provider**. The mobile provider just collects the money for them.

Sometimes a click on an advert in a game is enough, and you have already taken out a **subscription**. After that, paid text messages arrive every week. Many people only notice on their bill. Such subscriptions can quickly add up to large amounts. If you discover an unwanted subscription, you can often end it by sending a text message with the word **STOP**.

With a **third-party billing block** or premium services block, such services cannot be charged at all. You set it up with your mobile provider, in your customer account, in the app or by phone. In Switzerland, providers must offer a block **free of charge** on request. It is especially useful for children's mobile phones. Normal calls, text messages and mobile internet continue to work.

Check the bill carefully and report unclear amounts to your **mobile provider** straight away. In disputes with the provider, the **Ombudscom** arbitration service helps in Switzerland. It mediates between customers and telecoms companies. After that, it is best to set up a block straight away so that it does not happen again.

gewusst: Depending on the settings, in-app purchases in games can also be charged to the mobile phone bill.
In the settings of mobile phones, purchases can also be protected with a password.

teile.einleitung: A youth savings account is a bank account especially for children and teenagers. The money you save is safe there, and the bank often pays a little interest on top.
wichtigste: Many banks offer savings accounts for children and teenagers.
In a savings account you often get some interest.
Interest is a small amount that the bank pays for the money you save.
For young people the interest is sometimes a bit higher than with normal accounts.
Money is safer in the bank than in a money box.
Until the child comes of age, the parents usually help to manage the account.

abschnitte.text: In a **savings account** you keep money that you do not need straight away. The bank uses this money, for example for loans to other people. In return it pays **interest**. A youth savings account is often free and has no account fees.

Interest is given as a percentage. At 1 per cent interest, you get 1 franc extra on 100 francs in one year. If you leave the interest in the account, the interest grows too in the following year. This is called **compound interest**. How high the interest is depends on the bank and on the general level of interest rates.

Money in the bank cannot be lost or stolen as easily as cash at home. In Switzerland, deposits of up to 100,000 francs per person and bank are protected by **deposit protection**. For children that is more than enough. The bank statement always shows how much has been saved.

For children, it is usually the parents who open the account. Until the child comes of age, they have a say in what happens to the money. From the age of 18 you can manage the account yourself. The youth account is then often converted into a normal account.

gewusst: Albert Einstein is said to have called compound interest the eighth wonder of the world, but there is no proof that he really said it.
In recent years there have been times when banks paid almost no interest on savings accounts.

teile.einleitung: If you pay a bill late, you get a reminder. Some companies also charge a reminder fee for it. In Switzerland, however, this is only allowed if it was agreed beforehand.
wichtigste: A reminder fee is an amount you have to pay for a reminder.
In Switzerland, a reminder fee must in principle be agreed beforehand.
This is often stated in the contract or in the general terms and conditions (GTC).
Statutory default interest may be charged even without an agreement.
By law, default interest is 5 per cent a year.
If you pay on time, you do not have to pay any reminder fees.

abschnitte.text: A bill has a **payment deadline**, for example 30 days. If you do not pay, you get a **reminder**. Many companies then add a fee, perhaps 10 or 20 francs. This **reminder fee** is meant to cover the effort of sending reminders. It quickly makes a small bill more expensive.

In Switzerland, the **Code of Obligations** (OR) governs what applies when a payment is late. It says nothing about a reminder fee. That is why such a fee must in principle be agreed beforehand. This happens in the contract or in the **general terms and conditions**, the small print. So anyone who orders something or takes out a subscription should also read the terms and conditions.

**Default interest** is something different. By law, anyone who is late with a payment owes interest of 5 per cent a year. The company may charge this interest even without an agreement. With small amounts it is usually low. But the simplest thing is to pay bills on time. Then there is neither interest nor a fee.

gewusst: If you think a reminder fee is unjustified, you can query it with the company and pay only the amount of the bill.
In Switzerland, consumer protection organisations also help with questions about reminders.

teile.einleitung: With a mobile phone contract you pay a fixed amount every month for calls, messages and internet. Offers with a “free phone” sound tempting, but there is often a catch.
wichtigste: A contract costs a fixed amount every month.
Many contracts have a minimum term, for example 12 or 24 months.
A “free phone” is usually paid for through a higher monthly fee.
With pay as you go you pay in advance and have full control over the costs.
Before signing up, it is worth comparing the total costs.

abschnitte.titel: Contract or pay as you go
abschnitte.text: With a **contract** you pay monthly, usually by bill. With **pay as you go** you first top up credit and can only use as much as there is on it. For children and teenagers, pay as you go is often safer, because no surprisingly high bill can arrive. A contract can be worth it if you need a lot of internet.

abschnitte.titel: The catch with the free phone
abschnitte.text: If an expensive phone is offered “free” or for 1 franc, it is usually included in the **monthly fee**. So you pay it off month by month. On top of that there is often a long **minimum term**. If you want to leave earlier, you sometimes have to pay the remaining amount.

You should always do the sum: monthly fee times the number of months plus the price of the phone. Then you compare it with a cheap contract and a phone you buy yourself. The second option is often cheaper. Extra costs, for example for calls abroad, also belong in the calculation.

abschnitte.titel: Who is allowed to sign a contract?
abschnitte.text: A phone contract is a **legal contract**. In Switzerland, minors usually need their parents’ consent for it. Often the parents take out the contract and are then also responsible for the bill. Before signing, you should read the terms and conditions carefully.

gewusst: Using the internet abroad without a suitable package can lead to high costs, which is why providers send a warning text message.
Many providers offer special, cheaper contracts for young people.

teile.einleitung: A toy library (Ludothek) is like a library, but for games. There you can borrow board games, puzzles, ride-on toys and other toys and bring them back later.
wichtigste: In a toy library you borrow games for a certain time.
Afterwards you bring them back so that others can play with them.
Borrowing costs little or nothing at all.
You can try out lots of games without buying them.
In Switzerland there are toy libraries in many municipalities.
Volunteers often work there.

abschnitte.text: In a **toy library** there are shelves full of games: board games, card games, puzzles, building blocks, costumes and even scooters or go-karts. You choose something and take it home. After a few weeks you bring it back. Then another child may play with it. Each game has a **loan period**.

Games can be expensive. In the toy library you only pay a small **annual fee** or a small charge per game. That way you can try out lots of games. If you like one especially, you can ask for it as a present later or buy it. If you **borrow instead of buying**, you save money and need less space at home.

A game that many children use one after another is put to better use. Fewer new things have to be made. This saves **raw materials** and avoids rubbish. For this to work, care is important: you count the pieces before you bring a game back. In Switzerland, many toy libraries are run by **volunteers**, often with support from the municipality.

gewusst: The word “Ludothek” comes from the Latin “ludus”, which means game.
There are several hundred toy libraries in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: When you buy in instalments, you buy something straight away but only pay for it bit by bit in several part payments. In German this is also called buying “auf Pump”, on borrowed money. It sounds convenient, but it often costs considerably more than the normal price and can lead to debt.
wichtigste: When buying in instalments, you pay for a product in several part payments over a longer period.
The part payments are called instalments.
Interest and fees are often added, so you pay more in total.
Buying in instalments is a form of credit, meaning borrowed money.
In Switzerland, the Consumer Credit Act governs such transactions.
Before a loan is given, it must be checked whether you can afford it.
Many instalments at the same time can quickly lead into the debt trap.

abschnitte.text: When **buying in instalments**, you get the goods straight away, for example a phone, a television or a sofa. But you do not pay everything at once; you pay in monthly **instalments**. A phone costing 600 francs could, for example, be paid in 12 instalments of 55 francs each. In the end you would have paid 660 francs, so 60 francs more than the price.

If you pay in instalments, you are actually borrowing money from the seller or from a bank. For this they charge **interest**, which is a kind of rent for the money. Sometimes there are also fees for processing or for late payments. That is why buying in instalments is almost always more expensive than saving and paying later.

In Switzerland the **Consumer Credit Act** applies. It requires that before a loan is given, it is checked whether the person can actually pay the instalments. The interest must not exceed a legal upper limit. You can also still cancel a loan agreement shortly after signing it.

Today there are many new ways of paying in instalments. When shopping online, companies advertise with **buy now, pay later**. Leasing for cars or phone contracts that include a device work in a similar way. Because it is so easy, you can quickly lose track of all your commitments.

The monthly instalments look small, but several instalments together can blow your budget. If you cannot pay an instalment, reminder fees and even debt enforcement proceedings threaten. A good principle is: save first, then buy. In any case, young people under 18 may not enter into such contracts without their parents’ consent.

begriffe.erklaerung: A part payment that you pay regularly until everything has been paid off.
Money that you borrow and have to pay back later.
The price you pay for borrowed money.
You rent something for a long time in return for monthly payments, but it does not belong to you.

gewusst: The German expression “auf Pump” is colloquial and means roughly “on borrowed money”.
More than 100 years ago you could already buy sewing machines in instalments; this was one of the first examples of buying in instalments on a large scale.
In Switzerland, young adults often get into debt through phone contracts, online shopping and instalment payments.

teile.einleitung: Data protection means that personal data is protected from other people's eyes and from misuse. When shopping on the internet, this also concerns payment details such as credit card numbers. If you are careful, you protect your money.
wichtigste: Personal data includes, for example, your name, address, date of birth and payment details.
Saved payment details make shopping convenient, but they also make impulse buying easier.
In a hacker attack on a shop, saved data can be stolen.
Strong passwords and two-factor authentication protect accounts.
In Switzerland, the Data Protection Act sets out how companies must handle data.
Real companies never ask for passwords by email.

abschnitte.text: Many online shops offer to **save your card**. This is practical, because next time you only have to click. But that is exactly what makes **impulse buying** easier. If criminals manage a **data breach**, meaning a break-in into a shop's data, they can steal saved details. That is why it is best to save payment methods only with a few trustworthy providers.

In **phishing**, fraudsters send fake emails or text messages. They look like messages from a bank, Swiss Post or a shop. You are supposed to click on a link and enter your password or card number. Real companies never ask for such details in this way. If in doubt, open the website yourself in the browser instead of clicking on the link.

A good **password** is long and is only used for one single account. A **password manager** helps you store many passwords safely. Even safer is **two-factor authentication**: as well as the password, you need, for example, a code on your mobile phone. Updates for mobile phones and computers also close security gaps.

In Switzerland, the federal **Data Protection Act** applies. A revised version has been in force since 1 September 2023. It requires companies to say openly what data they collect and what for. Compliance is monitored by the **Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner**. Anyone who becomes a victim of fraud should inform their bank immediately and report it to the police.

gewusst: When paying with a mobile phone, often not the real card number is transmitted but a substitute code.
The word phishing is based on the English word “fishing”, meaning fishing for data.

teile.einleitung: Overdrawing an account means spending more money than there is in it. If the bank allows this, it lends you the missing money and charges interest for it.
wichtigste: With an overdraft, the account balance is below zero.
You borrow the missing money from the bank.
You then owe the bank money.
The bank usually charges high interest for this.
Not every bank allows an overdraft.
Youth accounts usually cannot be overdrawn at all.

abschnitte.text: Normally you can only spend money that is in your account. But some banks allow you to go below zero for a certain time. Then there is a **minus** on your bank statement. This option is called an **overdraft** or overdraft facility.

For the minus, the bank charges **overdraft interest**. It is usually much higher than the interest you get in a savings account. Sometimes there are fees as well. The longer the account stays in the red, the more expensive it becomes.

Accounts for children and teenagers usually cannot be overdrawn. If there is no money left in the account, the card simply does not work. This protects you from debt. Once you are an adult, you should ask exactly whether and how far your own account can be overdrawn.

With the bank’s app or your bank statement you can see your **balance** at any time. It helps to check regularly, especially before bigger purchases. Standing orders such as the rent should be planned for. If the account does go into the red, you should balance it out again as quickly as possible.

gewusst: In Switzerland, a maximum interest rate set by the Federal Council also applies to overdrafts.
The word “Kontokorrent” comes from Italian and means roughly “running account”.

teile.einleitung: Purchasing power means how many goods or services you can buy with a certain amount of money. A hundred francs are not worth the same everywhere and at all times. The term lets you compare how well people can live on their money.
wichtigste: Purchasing power shows how much you can buy with a certain amount of money.
If prices rise, the purchasing power of money falls.
If wages rise faster than prices, purchasing power grows.
In Switzerland, wages and prices are high compared with other countries.
The Big Mac Index compares the purchasing power of different countries in a simple way.
When you shop abroad, you often notice differences in purchasing power.

abschnitte.text: **Purchasing power** describes how much you can afford with your money. If an ice cream used to cost 2 francs and costs 3 francs today, you only get two ice creams instead of three for 6 francs. So the money has lost purchasing power. That is why what matters is not only how much money you have, but what you can buy with it.

When prices rise in general, this is called **inflation**, or in Switzerland “Teuerung”. With inflation, the purchasing power of money falls. But if wages rise as much as prices or more, you lose nothing. That is why a distinction is made between the **nominal wage**, the figure on the payslip, and the **real wage**, which takes inflation into account.

In Switzerland people earn a lot on average, but rents, food and services are expensive too. In a neighbouring country the same pizza often costs less. That is why many people from border regions go shopping in Germany, France or Italy; this is called **shopping tourism**. Economists compare countries using what is known as **purchasing power parity**.

Since 1986 the magazine “The Economist” has published the **Big Mac Index**. It compares what a McDonald’s Big Mac costs in different countries. Because the product is almost the same everywhere, the difference in price shows in a simple way whether a currency is expensive or cheap. Switzerland is regularly one of the most expensive countries.

Purchasing power helps us understand whether people are better or worse off financially. When negotiating pay rises, trade unions and employers often discuss **inflation compensation**. In Switzerland, pensions are also regularly adjusted to price changes. For you this means: savings that earn no interest slowly lose value over time.

begriffe.erklaerung: The wage with the higher prices already taken into account.
A pay rise that makes up for the higher prices.
Shopping abroad because it is cheaper there.
A comparison of how much you get for the same amount of money in different countries.

gewusst: With the Big Mac Index, currencies are compared using a hamburger.
A franc from 1950 had many times the purchasing power it has today.
Every year Swiss households spend billions of francs on shopping just across the border.

teile.einleitung: Occupational pensions are the second pillar of the Swiss pension system. Employees save money for old age in a pension fund together with their employer. While the AHV is a basic state insurance for everyone, the pension fund works through the employer.
wichtigste: Occupational pensions are the second pillar of the pension system.
The money is saved in a pension fund.
The AHV is a basic state insurance for everyone; the pension fund is an occupational scheme through the employer.
Since 1985, occupational pensions have been compulsory for most employees.
Employers must pay at least half of the contributions.
Each person builds up their own balance; this is called the funded system.
Together, the AHV and the pension fund are meant to replace about 60 per cent of previous pay.

abschnitte.text: **Occupational pensions** add to the AHV. Their aim is for people to be able to roughly keep their usual standard of living in old age. The money is invested in a **pension fund**, which is often run by a large employer, a sector of the economy or a collective foundation. The most important law on this is the Federal Act on Occupational Pensions, BVG for short.

The pension fund works on the **funded system**. Every insured person saves into their own account, a bit like a piggy bank with their name on it. The pension fund invests the money, for example in shares, bonds and property, so that it grows. On retirement you receive a pension or have part of it paid out as capital.

The **AHV** is compulsory for everyone and works on the pay-as-you-go system: young people pay the pensions of older people. In the second pillar, on the other hand, everyone saves for themselves. You are only insured in a pension fund if you are employed and earn enough. Self-employed people can insure themselves voluntarily.

Anyone who earns more than a certain minimum salary is compulsorily insured; in 2025 this was about 22,700 francs. From the age of 25, people save for old age; before that, only death and disability are insured. The employer pays at least as much as the employee. If you change jobs, you take your balance with you as a **vested benefit**.

The idea of the three pillars was written into the Federal Constitution in 1972. The BVG came into force on 1 January 1985 and made pension funds compulsory for many employees. An important figure is the **conversion rate**, which determines how much pension you get for each franc of your balance. In September 2024 the people rejected a reform that was meant to lower this rate.

begriffe.erklaerung: An institution in which employees and employers save for old age.
The Federal Act on Occupational Pensions.
The savings balance that you take with you when you change jobs.
The percentage used to convert the balance into an annual pension.

gewusst: You can draw money from the pension fund early to buy your own house or flat.
Swiss pension funds hold around 1000 billion francs in total (as of about 2023).
Anyone who leaves Switzerland for good can have their balance paid out under certain conditions.

teile.einleitung: A subscription is a contract under which you pay regularly for a service. This can be a magazine, a streaming service, a mobile phone contract or a rail pass. Subscriptions are convenient, but small monthly amounts add up to a lot of money over the year.
wichtigste: With a subscription you pay regularly, for example every month or every year.
Typical subscriptions are streaming, mobile phones, magazines, gyms or the rail General Abonnement (GA).
Small monthly amounts add up to a large sum over the year.
Many subscriptions renew automatically if you do not cancel in time.
When cancelling, you have to pay attention to the notice period.
Free trial subscriptions often turn automatically into paid subscriptions.
It is worth checking all your subscriptions regularly.

abschnitte.text: A **subscription** is a contract for a service that you receive again and again. For this you pay a fixed amount at regular intervals. In the past, subscriptions were mainly common for newspapers and magazines. Today there are subscriptions for music, films, games, cloud storage and even for clothes or coffee.

Very well known is the SBB's **General Abonnement (GA)**, with which you can use almost all trains, buses and boats for a year. With the **Half Fare travelcard** you travel at half price. There are cheaper offers for young people, for example the GA for young people. Many families also have subscriptions for their mobile phones, internet and television.

Three subscriptions at 15 francs a month each cost 45 francs a month together. Over a year that is already 540 francs. Many people forget subscriptions they hardly use any more and still keep paying. That is why a **subscription list** with all your current contracts and costs is worthwhile.

Many subscriptions renew automatically for a month or a year. If you want to cancel, you must keep to the **notice period** set out in the terms of the contract. It is best to cancel in writing or directly in your online account and keep the confirmation. Watch out with **trial subscriptions**: if you do not cancel before the free period ends, you often pay the full price afterwards.

Before taking out any subscription, think about whether you really need the service regularly. Sometimes it is cheaper to buy something individually or to share a subscription with your family. With mobile phone contracts, extra services such as in-app purchases can cause high bills. Children and young people under 18 need their parents' consent for larger contracts.

begriffe.erklaerung: A contract under which you pay regularly for a service.
The time before the end of a contract by which you have to cancel.
A subscription that you can test for a while for free or cheaply.
The contract continues if you do not cancel.

gewusst: The General Abonnement of the Swiss railways has existed for more than 100 years.
Many streaming services earn a lot from subscriptions that customers hardly use any more.
The German word for subscription, “Abonnement”, comes from French.

teile.einleitung: The three-pillar system is the Swiss pension system. It rests on three pillars: the AHV, the pension fund and private provision. The third pillar is voluntary; with it you save extra for old age and can save on taxes at the same time.
wichtigste: The Swiss pension system rests on three pillars.
The first pillar is the state AHV together with the IV; it is meant to secure the minimum needed to live.
The second pillar is the occupational pension through the pension fund.
The third pillar is voluntary private provision, with which you save extra and can save on taxes.
A distinction is made between the tied pillar 3a and the flexible pillar 3b.
The three-pillar system has been in the Federal Constitution since 1972.
Together, the first two pillars are meant to replace about 60 per cent of previous pay.

abschnitte.text: The **three-pillar system** is meant to make sure that people are financially secure in old age, in case of disability or when a relative dies. You can imagine it as a building resting on three pillars. The more stable all three pillars are, the more securely the roof stands, meaning income in old age. The principle was written into the Federal Constitution by the people on 3 December 1972.

The first pillar consists of the **AHV** and the disability insurance (IV). It is compulsory for everyone and is meant to cover basic needs. It works on the pay-as-you-go system, so today's contributions pay today's pensions. If the pension is not enough, there are also **supplementary benefits**.

The second pillar is the **occupational pension** in the pension fund. Here employees and employers save together for each individual person. Together with the AHV, it is meant to make it possible to roughly keep your usual standard of living. Since 1985 it has been compulsory for most employees.

The third pillar is voluntary **private provision**. In **pillar 3a** you save into a special account or into funds and may deduct the payments from your taxes. In return the money is tied up, and you can usually only draw it shortly before retirement. Anyone with a pension fund was allowed to pay in a maximum of about 7250 francs a year in 2025.

Anyone who starts early paying even small amounts into pillar 3a benefits for a long time from **compound interest**. The flexible pillar 3b covers all other saving, such as a savings account or life insurance. Exceptions allow pillar 3a money to be drawn earlier, for example to buy your own home or when starting your own business. It is worth comparing the offers of banks and insurers.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tied private pension provision with a tax advantage.
Flexible private saving without special rules.
Extra money from the state if the pension is not enough to live on.
Interest that you earn on interest you have already received.

gewusst: With pillar 3a you can save on taxes in every year in which you pay in.
Switzerland's three-pillar system is often held up abroad as a model.
You can open a pillar 3a account from the age of 18, as soon as you have an income on which AHV contributions are due.

teile.einleitung: An emergency fund (Notgroschen) is money you put aside for unexpected expenses. It helps when your bike breaks, a large bill arrives or you earn less for a while.
wichtigste: The emergency fund is a money reserve for emergencies.
Experts often recommend three to six months’ expenses.
It belongs in a savings account you can get at easily.
Monthly expenses times the number of months gives the target amount.
After taking money out, you top it up again.
The emergency fund comes first, then long-term investing.

abschnitte.titel: What is an emergency fund for?
abschnitte.text: Many things in life come unexpectedly: the washing machine breaks down, the dentist sends a big bill or there is a gap between two jobs. If you have a **reserve** then, you do not have to get into **debt**. An emergency fund gives you security and peace of mind. The German word comes from the **Groschen**, an old coin.

Experts often recommend a reserve of **three to six months’ expenses**. You calculate: monthly expenses times the number of months. Sara has 2,400 francs of expenses a month and would like a 3-month reserve. 3 times 2,400 gives **7,200 francs**. Young adults often start with a smaller goal, for example one month’s pay, and then build it up.

In an emergency, the money must be available **immediately** and **without loss**. That is why the emergency fund belongs in a **savings account** from which you can withdraw money at any time. **Shares** are not suitable for this, because their value goes up and down. Money in **pillar 3a** or in a **fixed-term deposit** is tied up for a longer time. It is good to keep the emergency fund in a separate account, apart from your everyday money.

abschnitte.titel: Topping up and the right order
abschnitte.text: An emergency fund is only useful if it is ready. So after an emergency expense you top it up again with a fixed **monthly amount**, for example by standing order. For people starting their careers, the order matters: **first security, then return**. Only once the reserve is in place do you invest further money for the long term. Otherwise, if there is a surprise, you have to sell investments, perhaps at just the wrong moment.

gewusst: The Groschen used to be a coin in many European countries. The word “Notgroschen” comes from it.
A standing order that goes out straight after your wages arrive helps you save without much effort.

teile.einleitung: Before a bank in Switzerland gives a consumer loan, it must check whether the person can pay it back. This is called a creditworthiness check, and it is required by the Consumer Credit Act.
wichtigste: The creditworthiness check is required by the Consumer Credit Act.
The lender must base its calculation on repayment within 36 months.
The subsistence minimum must not be touched.
Existing loans are checked with the IKO.
If the person is not creditworthy, no loan may be granted.

abschnitte.text: The lender looks at the person’s **income** and **expenses**. These include rent, health insurance, taxes and loans that already exist. It checks the existing loans with the **Consumer Credit Information Office**. This gives a picture of how much money is left over each month.

The law requires that a cash loan could be paid back within **36 months**. This applies to the calculation, even if the contract runs for longer. The **subsistence minimum** must not be touched. This is the amount a person absolutely needs to live on.

abschnitte.titel: If the check is not passed
abschnitte.text: If the check shows that the person cannot bear the loan, it must not be granted. If a lender does not stick to this, it can lose its interest and costs. In this way the law aims to prevent **over-indebtedness**. So it protects borrowers from burdens that are too heavy.

gewusst: A similar check is also required for leasing contracts, for example for a car.

teile.einleitung: When you shop online, you often have to tick a box: “I accept the terms and conditions”. In German these are called **AGB**, short for **Allgemeine Geschäftsbedingungen** (general terms and conditions). They contain the rules for the purchase, for example on delivery, payment and returns.
wichtigste: Terms and conditions are a business's general rules for its customers.
They cover, for example, delivery, payment, returns and guarantees.
Anyone who accepts the terms and conditions is bound by these rules.
It is worth reading the most important points before buying.
In Switzerland there is no general legal right to return goods bought online.
Whether you may send goods back is therefore often stated in the terms and conditions.

abschnitte.text: The **general terms and conditions** are the rules that a business sets out in the same way for all customers. They apply to many purchases, not just one. That is why they are called **general**. You usually find them right at the bottom of the website or before you pay. Anyone who ticks the box agrees to the rules.

The terms and conditions state, for example, how long **delivery** takes and what it costs. They set out how you can **pay** and when the bill is due. The rules on **returns** are also important: may you send goods back, and who pays the postage? The **guarantee** for broken things is also described there.

Many people think that you can always send back things you have bought online. But in Switzerland there is **no general right of return** for online purchases. Many shops offer it voluntarily, and this is then stated in the terms and conditions. It is different in the EU: there, online purchases generally come with a 14-day right of withdrawal.

Terms and conditions are often long and written in difficult language. You do not have to read every word, but you should read the most important points: **costs**, **delivery**, **returns** and, for subscriptions, **cancellation**. Swiss law forbids terms and conditions that put customers at an unfair disadvantage. Consumer protection organisations can help if you have questions.

gewusst: The terms and conditions of many large apps and platforms are so long that it would take you more than an hour to read them.
Shops, gyms and mobile phone providers also have terms and conditions, not just online shops.

teile.einleitung: Pillar 3a is a voluntary way of saving money for old age in Switzerland. The state rewards this with lower taxes. In return, the money stays tied up for a long time.
wichtigste: Swiss retirement provision has three pillars.
Pillar 3a is part of the third pillar, private provision.
Anyone with earned income subject to AVS contributions can pay in.
Payments up to the annual maximum can be deducted from taxable income.
Normally the money can be withdrawn at the earliest 5 years before the AVS reference age.
Early withdrawal is only allowed in special cases, for example for buying your own home.
If you start early, you benefit from compound interest for a long time.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland secures people’s old age with the **three-pillar system**. The first pillar is the **AVS**, the state provision for everyone. The second pillar is the **pension fund** through the employer. The third pillar is **private provision**, which each person decides on themselves. Pillar 3a is the “tied” part of the third pillar.

Anyone who has **earned income subject to AVS contributions**, in other words who works, can pay in. Every year the federal government sets a **maximum amount**. People who belong to a pension fund may pay in less than self-employed people without a pension fund. The payments can be deducted from **taxable income**. That way you pay less tax today.

The money is **tied up**, so you cannot simply withdraw it. Normally you may withdraw it at the earliest **5 years before the AVS reference age**. **Early withdrawal** is only possible in special cases: for a home you live in yourself, for starting your own business or if you emigrate permanently. When you withdraw the money you have to pay tax on it, but at a lower rate than on normal income.

Pillar 3a savings can be kept in a **3a account** at a bank, which pays interest. You can also invest them in **securities** such as funds. These can bring a higher return, but their value goes up and down. Because the money stays invested for many years, **compound interest** works: returns themselves bring further returns. That is why an early start is worth it, even with small amounts.

gewusst: Many apprentices and young workers can open a 3a account as soon as they get their first wages.
You may have several 3a accounts and withdraw them later in different years.

teile.einleitung: With a youth allowance (Jugendlohn), teenagers get a larger amount from their parents than with pocket money. In return they pay for certain things themselves, for example clothes, their phone or free time.
wichtigste: The youth allowance is bigger than normal pocket money.
Teenagers use it to pay for clothes, their phone or going out themselves.
That way they learn to plan with more money.
Parents and teenagers agree exactly what it covers.
A written agreement prevents arguments.
The youth allowance is usually suitable from about the age of 12.

abschnitte.text: The **youth allowance** is an idea from Switzerland. Instead of pocket money, teenagers get a fixed amount every month. From it they pay for things that the parents would otherwise pay for. Basic needs such as housing, food and health insurance remain the parents’ responsibility.

Typical expenses are **clothes**, **shoes**, the **phone**, the hairdresser, free time and going out. The older the teenagers are, the more they take on. If they buy too much at the start of the month, the money runs out at the end. That is exactly how they learn to make a **budget**.

Parents and teenagers discuss which expenses the youth allowance covers. It is best to write this down **in writing**. Then it is clear later who pays for what, and there are fewer arguments. The agreement can be adjusted regularly.

With a youth allowance you practise dividing up money, saving and setting priorities. Mistakes are allowed, because they happen with small amounts. If you learn early how to handle money, you will cope better later as an apprentice or a student. It is important that the parents do not step in every time money gets tight.

gewusst: In Switzerland there are online calculators for the youth allowance that help you decide on the amount.
Many experts recommend starting the youth allowance small and increasing the responsibility step by step.

teile.einleitung: A budgeting app is a program on your mobile phone that you use to record your income and spending. It works like a digital household account book. But you still have to do the saving yourself.
wichtigste: A budgeting app helps you keep an eye on income and spending.
You enter what you spend money on, or the app reads it from your account.
Spending is sorted into categories, for example food or free time.
Charts show where the money goes.
The app does not save for you: you have to make the decisions yourself.
For apps with access to your account, data protection is especially important.

abschnitte.text: In a budgeting app you enter every **income** and every **expense**. Some apps can be linked to your bank account and read the payments automatically. The app sorts everything into **categories**, such as mobile phone, clothes, going out or saving. At the end of the month you can see exactly how much was spent on what.

Many apps let you set a **budget** for each category. This is the maximum amount you want to spend. If you almost reach the limit, you get a warning. You can also enter a **savings goal**, for example a new bike. The app then shows how far you have got.

An app is a **tool**, not a magician. It shows the figures, but you have to save yourself. If you forget to enter spending, you get the wrong picture. You also have to enter cash by hand. A simple notebook or a spreadsheet does the same job if you prefer it that way.

Budgeting apps know a lot about your money. That is why it is worth checking who offers the app and what happens to the **data**. A secure password and, if possible, **two-factor authentication** protect the account. Free apps sometimes make money from advertising or from data. In Switzerland, for example, Budget advice Switzerland offers templates and tips on budgeting.

gewusst: Household account books on paper have existed for a very long time; the app is just their modern form.
Many banks have built an analysis of spending directly into their e-banking app.

teile.einleitung: The old-age and survivors' insurance, AHV for short, is the most important social insurance scheme in Switzerland. It is a state insurance that pays a pension in old age and is partly financed by people in work. Widows, widowers and orphans also receive money from the AHV.
wichtigste: The AHV is a state insurance that pays a pension in old age.
It is partly financed by people in work and their employers, plus money from the Confederation.
The AHV has existed since 1948; the people had approved it in 1947.
It forms the first pillar of the Swiss pension system.
The retirement age is 65 for men and is being raised step by step to 65 for women.
Widows, widowers and orphans receive a survivors' pension.
Because people are living longer and longer, there are often votes on how the AHV is financed.

abschnitte.text: The **AHV** is meant to make sure that older people have enough money to live on when they no longer work. Almost everyone who lives or works in Switzerland is compulsorily insured. It pays **old-age pensions** to retired people and **survivors' pensions** to families in which a parent or spouse has died. Together with the disability insurance (IV), it forms the first pillar.

The AHV works on a **pay-as-you-go system**. This means that the money that people in work pay in today is paid straight out again to today's pensioners. Employees and employers each pay half of the contribution, which is deducted from wages. In addition, money from the Confederation and part of VAT go into the AHV.

As early as the national strike of 1918, people demanded an old-age insurance. The people clearly approved the AHV on 6 July 1947, and it came into force on 1 January 1948. Since then it has been adjusted in many revisions. In 2024 the people accepted an initiative for a **13th AHV pension**, which will be paid from 2026.

Anyone in work pays contributions from 1 January after their 17th birthday. People who do not work, such as students, have to pay a minimum contribution from the age of 20. Every person receives an **AHV number**, which begins with 756. If years of contributions are missing, the pension is reduced later, which is why paying contributions without gaps is important.

People in Switzerland today live much longer than in 1948, so they also draw a pension for longer. At the same time, the large generations born after the war, the **baby boomers**, are retiring. As a result there are fewer and fewer people in work for every pensioner. With the AHV 21 reform, the retirement age for women is being raised step by step from 64 to 65 between 2025 and 2028.

begriffe.erklaerung: Money that you receive regularly when you are retired.
Today's contributions pay for today's pensions.
Widows, widowers and orphans whose relative has died.
The state pension provision from the AHV and IV.

gewusst: The AHV number has 13 digits and is also on the health insurance card.
With a turnout of almost 80 per cent, the 1947 AHV vote had one of the highest turnouts in Swiss history.
The AHV is also paid to people who have moved abroad after retiring.

teile.einleitung: Accidents do not only happen at work, but also during sport, at home or on holiday. For accidents like these in your free time, Switzerland has non-occupational accident insurance, NBU for short.
wichtigste: NBU insures accidents in your free time.
You are covered by it if you work at least 8 hours a week for the same employer.
The premium is usually deducted from your wages.
Occupational accidents are paid for by the employer through occupational accident insurance.
If you work less, you are insured for accidents in your free time through your health insurance.
The rules are set out in the Accident Insurance Act (UVG).

abschnitte.text: If you break your leg skiing or fall off a ladder at home, you have had a **non-occupational accident**. This is the name for all accidents that do not happen at work. **Non-occupational accident insurance** (NBU) then pays, for example, for the doctor, hospital and part of your wages if you cannot work. It is part of the compulsory accident insurance for employees.

Whether you are insured against accidents in your free time through your employer depends on your working hours. Anyone who works **at least 8 hours a week** for the same employer is insured through the NBU. The **premium** for it is usually deducted from the wages. Anyone who works less is only insured against occupational accidents. Accidents on the way to work then also count as occupational accidents.

In Switzerland, everyone must be insured against accidents. People who do not have NBU, for example children, pupils or pensioners, are insured through their **health insurance**. Anyone who has NBU through their employer can exclude **accident cover** from their health insurance. That way you save on premiums. But if you lose or change your job, you must include accident cover again in good time.

The best-known accident insurer is **Suva**. It mainly insures employees in industry, construction and trades. Other companies insure their employees with private insurers. The rules for this are set out in the **Accident Insurance Act** (UVG). The employer bears the costs of occupational accidents; the NBU is usually paid for by the employees.

gewusst: After a job ends, you remain insured through the NBU for about another month.
In Switzerland, more accidents happen in people’s free time than at work.

teile.einleitung: The data allowance is the amount of data that you may use with your mobile phone over the mobile network. Many contracts only include a certain allowance per month. When it is used up, the internet becomes slower or it costs extra.
wichtigste: Data is measured in megabytes (MB) and gigabytes (GB).
Many mobile phone contracts include a fixed data allowance per month.
When it is used up, the speed is slowed down or extra data costs money.
Videos and streaming use especially large amounts of data.
On Wi-Fi, what you use does not count towards your mobile data allowance.
Abroad, mobile internet can become expensive through roaming.

abschnitte.text: Every time your mobile phone loads something from the internet, **data** is transferred. A message needs only a little, a video a great deal. It is measured in **megabytes** and **gigabytes**. One gigabyte is around 1000 megabytes. The data allowance in your contract says how much you may use over the mobile network each month.

Different things happen depending on the contract. Often the speed is heavily **slowed down**, and the internet is then very slow. With other contracts, extra data is **charged**, and the bill becomes higher. Some contracts offer unlimited data, but they usually cost more. It is worth choosing a contract that suits how much you use.

**Videos**, streaming films and online games use the most data. Music streaming and video calls also use a lot. Text messages and emails without large attachments, on the other hand, use little. Many apps load data in the background, for example for updates. In the settings you can choose for such updates only to be loaded on **Wi-Fi**.

On your mobile phone and in your provider's app you can see how much of your **data allowance** has already been used. At home and at school it is best to use Wi-Fi. Be careful **abroad**: mobile internet via **roaming** can cost a lot outside your contract. That is why you should find out before your holiday what is included in your contract.

gewusst: A byte consists of 8 bits, the smallest unit of information.
Video quality makes a big difference: a film in high resolution needs many times more data.

teile.einleitung: In economics, diversification means investing money not in one place but spread out. In this way you spread the risk: if one investment does badly, others may make up for the loss. A well-known saying puts it like this: don't put all your eggs in one basket.
wichtigste: Diversification means spreading money across different investments.
You invest money in a spread-out way to spread the risk.
Anyone who puts everything into a single company can lose everything if it goes bankrupt.
You can spread money across companies, sectors, countries and types of investment.
Funds and ETFs are easy ways to spread money widely.
In 1952 the economist Harry Markowitz explained scientifically why spreading makes sense.
Companies also diversify by offering different products or serving different markets.

abschnitte.text: **Diversification** comes from the Latin word for variety. It means dividing your money among many different **investments**. Imagine you carry all your eggs in one basket and trip: then they are all broken. If you spread them across several baskets, most of them stay whole when you fall.

Every investment has its own **risk**; for example, a company may run into problems or a sector may fall into a crisis. Not all investments fall at the same time. If the shares of a travel company fall, the shares of a food producer may rise. Thanks to the mix, the total value goes up and down less.

You can spread money across different companies, but also across sectors such as technology, health or energy. Spreading across several countries and currencies is also important. You can also mix different **asset classes**, meaning shares, bonds, property and cash. A **fund** or an ETF often bundles hundreds of companies into a single product.

In 1952 the American economist **Harry Markowitz** published modern portfolio theory. He showed with mathematics that a good mix can lower risk without greatly reducing returns. For this he received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1990. But the idea of spreading is much older: traders in earlier centuries already spread their goods across several ships.

When the airline Swissair collapsed in 2001, many shareholders lost all the money they had invested. When Credit Suisse came to an end in 2023, investors also lost a lot. Those who had spread their money widely felt such losses much less. That is why Swiss pension funds also spread their money across many investments at home and abroad.

begriffe.erklaerung: Spreading money across different investments.
