The danger when too much money is in a single investment.
A pot in which the money of many investors is invested together in many companies.
All the investments that a person or company owns.

gewusst: The saying “Don't put all your eggs in one basket” exists in many languages.
The principle is also familiar from collecting Panini stickers or trading cards: several small swapping partners are safer than a single one.
Diversification does not protect against all losses, because in big crises almost all shares often fall at the same time.

teile.einleitung: “Buy now, pay later” is a payment method offered by many online shops. It is convenient, but you still have to pay, and on time.
wichtigste: You get the goods straight away and pay later or in instalments.
Payment must be made by a certain deadline.
Anyone who misses the deadline has to pay reminder fees or interest.
The offer tempts people into buying things they cannot afford.
It is easy to lose track of several unpaid bills.
Unpaid bills can lead to debt enforcement proceedings.

abschnitte.text: When paying in an online shop, you choose “pay later” or “pay by invoice”. The goods are delivered, and you receive an **invoice** with a deadline, often a few weeks. With some offers you can also split the amount into **instalments**. Behind the offer there is often a separate company that collects the money for the shop.

Because you do not have to pay straight away, the purchase feels **cheaper** than it is. So you quickly buy more than you can afford. If you have several unpaid bills, it is easy to lose track. If you miss a deadline, **reminder fees** are added. With instalment payments, **interest** may be charged.

If a bill stays unpaid for a long time, it is often handed over to a **debt collection agency**. Then further costs are added. In the worst case, the creditor starts **debt enforcement proceedings**. These then appear in the debt enforcement register and can, for example, make it harder to find a flat. In this way small purchases can quickly turn into **debts**.

Before you click on “pay later”, you should ask yourself: do I already have the money now? If not, it is usually better to wait. Make a note of unpaid bills with their **due date**. Anyone who needs help can find free **debt advice** in many cantons.

gewusst: In Switzerland, paying by invoice was a popular payment method long before online shopping.
For young people under 18, such offers are usually not available at all because they are not yet of age.

teile.einleitung: The Consumer Credit Act, KKG for short, is a Swiss federal law meant to protect people when they take out small loans, leasing and credit card debt. Among other things, it provides a right of withdrawal, with which you can cancel a small loan you have taken out within a short period. Banks must also check whether you can actually pay the loan back.
wichtigste: The Consumer Credit Act (KKG) protects consumers when it comes to loans.
It applies to loans from 500 to 80,000 francs.
You can cancel a consumer loan agreement within 14 days.
Before granting a loan, banks must check creditworthiness.
The maximum interest rate is limited and set by the Federal Council.
Loans must be reported to a central information office.
The current law has been in force since 2003.

abschnitte.text: The **Consumer Credit Act** is a Swiss federal law that has applied since 1 January 2003. It governs loans that private individuals take out for their own consumption. These include **cash loans**, leasing contracts for cars and credit cards with part payment. The law does not, however, apply to mortgages on houses.

Anyone who has taken out a consumer loan can cancel it in writing within **14 days**. You do not have to give a reason; this is called the **right of withdrawal**. Any money already received must then be returned. This gives you time to think over a hasty decision again calmly.

Before a loan is granted, the lender must check the person’s **creditworthiness**. It works out whether the person can pay the instalments without falling below the subsistence minimum. It assumes that a cash loan can be paid back within 36 months. If a bank grants a loan without checking properly, it can lose the interest and even the money it lent.

All consumer loans are reported to the **Consumer Credit Information Office**, IKO for short. That way other lenders can see whether someone already has loans. The Federal Council sets a **maximum interest rate**; since 2016 it has been 10 per cent for cash loans and 12 per cent for overdrafts and credit cards. Higher interest is banned.

abschnitte.titel: Advertising and protection of young people
abschnitte.text: Since 2016, **aggressive advertising** for consumer loans has been banned. What counts as aggressive was laid down by the credit industry in its own agreement. In any case, minors cannot take out a loan agreement without their parents’ consent. The aim is that young people in particular do not fall into a debt trap.

begriffe.erklaerung: The right to cancel a contract within a set period without giving a reason.
The highest interest that a lender may charge.
The information office to which all consumer loans are reported.
A loan where the money is paid out to you directly.

gewusst: Before 2016, the withdrawal period for consumer loans was only 7 days.
The KKG only applies to loans of 500 francs or more; smaller amounts are not covered.
Banks that grant a loan without checking risk losing all the money they lent.

teile.einleitung: Debt enforcement (Schuldbetreibung) is an official procedure in Switzerland that someone can use to recover unpaid debts. If you do not pay a bill, the creditor can start debt enforcement proceedings against you at the debt enforcement office. In everyday life people usually just say “Betreibung”.
wichtigste: Debt enforcement is an official procedure for recovering unpaid debts.
The debt enforcement office where the debtor lives is responsible.
The rules are set out in the Federal Act on Debt Enforcement and Bankruptcy, SchKG for short.
The first step is the payment order.
You can raise an objection to a payment order within ten days.
In the end the office can seize wages or belongings, but the subsistence minimum remains protected.
Debt enforcement proceedings are listed in the debt enforcement register, which harms you when, for example, you are looking for a flat.

abschnitte.text: **Debt enforcement** is the official way to claim money that someone owes. The person who is owed money is called the **creditor**; the person who owes money is called the debtor. The rules are set out in the Federal Act on Debt Enforcement and Bankruptcy of 1889. The debt enforcement is carried out by the debt enforcement office of the municipality or region.

First the creditor makes a request for debt enforcement at the office. The office then sends the debtor a **payment order**, often delivered in person. It states how much money is being claimed. In Switzerland anyone can start debt enforcement proceedings without first proving that the claim is correct.

If you do not agree with the claim, you can raise an **objection** within ten days. This is a simple challenge that needs no reason. The debt enforcement is then stopped for the time being. The creditor must then prove in court that they really are owed the money.

If no objection is raised or the court rules in the creditor’s favour, the debt enforcement continues. The office can then carry out a **seizure**, meaning it takes wages or valuable belongings. Seized items are auctioned, and the creditor is paid with the proceeds. What you absolutely need to live on, the subsistence minimum, may not be seized.

If there is still not enough money, the creditor receives a **certificate of loss**. With it they can claim the debt again later if the debtor has more money. A certificate of loss only expires after 20 years. For companies listed in the commercial register, debt enforcement can also lead to bankruptcy.

Every debt enforcement case is entered in the **debt enforcement register**. Landlords and employers often ask for an extract from this register. Anyone with entries there finds it harder to get a flat. That is why it is important to pay bills on time or to talk to the creditor early if there are problems.

begriffe.erklaerung: A person or company to whom you owe money.
An official letter demanding payment of a debt.
A challenge to debt enforcement if you dispute the debt.
The office takes wages or belongings in order to pay debts.
The money you absolutely need to live on, which is protected.

gewusst: The Swiss debt enforcement system is almost unique in the world, because you can start proceedings against someone without a court judgement.
Common reasons for debt enforcement in Switzerland are unpaid taxes and health insurance premiums.
The debt enforcement law, SchKG, is more than 130 years old and has been revised several times since then.

teile.einleitung: People who work get money for it. This money is called wages, or pay. With it, adults pay for rent, food, clothes and much more for themselves and their family.
wichtigste: Wages are the money you get for your work.
Most employees get their wages once a month.
Wages are usually paid into a bank account.
Gross pay is the whole wage; net pay is what is left after deductions.
Many employees in Switzerland get a 13th month’s salary.
Women and men are entitled to equal pay for equal work.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who works for a company, a hospital or a municipality is **employed**. The person makes their time and skills available. In return the **employer** pays wages. What you earn is stated in the **employment contract**. With the wages the family pays for rent, food, health insurance and holidays.

Many people get a **monthly salary**. It is the same every month, even if a month is shorter. Others receive **hourly pay**: they get money for every hour they work. In Switzerland, many companies pay a **13th month’s salary**. There is then an extra month’s pay at the end of the year or spread over the year.

**Gross pay** is the wage stated in the contract. Contributions to social insurance, for example to the AVS, are deducted from it. What then arrives in the account is called **net pay**. So it is always a bit smaller. How much is deducted is shown on the **payslip**.

In Switzerland there is no minimum wage for the whole country. But some cantons have introduced their own **minimum wage**. In many industries, **collective labour agreements** set the minimum that must be paid. These agreements are negotiated jointly by employers and trade unions. The Federal Constitution requires women and men to earn the same for work of equal value.

gewusst: The word “salary” comes from the Latin “sal”, meaning salt. Salt used to be very valuable.
Pocket money is not a wage, because you do not get it for doing work.

teile.einleitung: With leasing, you rent a car for a certain period and pay monthly instalments for it. The residual value is the amount the car is supposed to be worth at the end of the contract. It affects how high the monthly instalments are.
wichtigste: The residual value is the estimated value of the car at the end of the contract.
It is fixed when the leasing contract is signed.
The lower the residual value, the higher the monthly instalments.
The higher the residual value, the lower the instalments.
At the end you give the car back or can sometimes buy it for the residual value.

abschnitte.text: With **leasing**, the car does not belong to the person who drives it, but to the **leasing company**. You may use it for an agreed period, for example three or four years. For this you pay a **leasing instalment** every month. Often you also have to pay a deposit at the start. A car loses value over time, and it is exactly this loss of value that you pay for with the instalments.

The **residual value** is the amount the car is supposed to be worth at the end. The instalments mainly cover the difference between the price when new and the residual value, plus interest. If the residual value is **low**, the difference is large and the instalments become **higher**. If the residual value is set high, the instalments are lower.

If you drive more kilometres than agreed or return the car damaged, you often have to **pay extra**. Ending the contract early can also be expensive. In Switzerland, the **Consumer Credit Act** applies to many private leasing contracts. Among other things, it requires a check of whether you can pay the instalments.

gewusst: Leasing usually includes fully comprehensive insurance, which costs extra.

teile.einleitung: Once a year, employees get a salary certificate from their employer. It sums up the whole year’s pay on one sheet. You need it above all for your tax return.
wichtigste: The salary certificate shows the wages for a whole year.
The employer must issue it, usually at the start of the new year.
It shows gross pay, deductions and net pay.
You enclose it with your tax return.
The same form is used throughout Switzerland.
If you had several jobs, you get a salary certificate from each employer.

abschnitte.titel: One sheet for the whole year
abschnitte.text: Every month there is a payslip. The **salary certificate** adds up all these months. It shows how much you earned in the whole year and how much was deducted for AVS, IV, EO, unemployment insurance and the pension fund. The employer usually sends it in January or February. If you change jobs, you also get one when you leave.

In Switzerland, adults fill in a **tax return** every year. In it you have to state how much you earned. The salary certificate is the proof of this. You enclose it with the tax return or upload it online. That way the **tax office** can check the information.

The salary certificate does not only show money. It also states whether you may use a **company car** privately or get free meals. Benefits like these also count as income. **Expenses**, meaning money for costs you had at work, are listed too. The form is the same throughout Switzerland, so that all cantons can read it in the same way.

gewusst: The salary certificate is often called “Form 11”.
You should keep salary certificates for a few years, because you may still need them later.

teile.einleitung: A shopping list is a list of everything you want to buy in the shop. It helps you not to forget anything. And it helps you save, because you only buy what you really need.
wichtigste: A shopping list shows what you need to buy.
With a list you buy fewer things that you do not need at all.
Shops are laid out so that you feel like buying more.
Before writing the list, you check what you still have at home.
If you shop when you are not hungry, you buy fewer things on impulse.
Fewer unnecessary purchases also mean less food in the bin.

abschnitte.text: With a **shopping list** you know exactly what you need to get. That way you do not forget anything important and do not have to go to the shop twice. Above all, you make fewer **impulse purchases**, meaning things you only buy because they happen to be there. This is good for your **budget**. You can write it on paper or keep it on your mobile phone.

Shops are cleverly laid out. Sweets are often by the **till**, where you have to wait. Basic foods such as milk are sometimes right at the back, so that you walk past lots of other things. Expensive products are often placed at **eye level**. With a list, you are less easily distracted.

Before writing the list, look in the **fridge** and the store cupboard. That way you do not buy anything twice. A **meal plan** for the week is helpful: then you know which ingredients you need. If you buy less, you also throw away less. This helps against **food waste**.

It is best **not to go shopping hungry**, because then more ends up in the trolley. **Special offers** are only worth it if you really need the product. Comparing the price per kilo or per litre shows what is cheaper. In Switzerland this is usually shown on the price label.

gewusst: The price per kilo or litre on the label is called the unit price and makes packs of different sizes comparable.
In Switzerland, a large part of food waste is produced in private households.

teile.einleitung: When shopping, you need to do sums: What does everything cost together, is my money enough, and how much change will I get back? With a few simple rules it is quite easy.
wichtigste: One franc has 100 centimes.
Before buying, you add up the prices.
If the total is bigger than your money, it is not enough.
You work out the change like this: amount paid minus price.
Two times 50 centimes is one franc.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland you pay with **francs** and **centimes** (Rappen). One franc has **100 centimes**. There are coins worth 5, 10 and 20 centimes, as well as half a franc, 1, 2 and 5 francs. So an apple for 50 centimes costs half a franc. Two apples cost 50 plus 50 centimes, which is 100 centimes or **1 franc**.

If you want to buy several things, you first **add up** all the prices. An exercise book costs 3 francs, a rubber costs 2 francs. Together that is 5 francs. If you only have 4 francs, you are 1 franc short. Then you have to choose one of them or save a bit more.

If you pay with more money than something costs, you get **change** back. You work out: amount paid **minus** price. An ice cream costs 3 francs, and you give 5 francs. 5 minus 3 is 2. So you get **2 francs** back. It is always worth quickly counting your change.

gewusst: The smallest coin in Switzerland today is the 5-centime piece. The 1-centime piece was abolished in 2007.

teile.einleitung: Value added tax, VAT for short (MWST in German), is a tax charged on most goods and services and included in the selling price. Every time you pay for an ice cream, a book or a haircut, a small part goes to the federal government. It is one of Switzerland’s most important sources of income.
wichtigste: Value added tax is included in the price of most goods and services.
It has applied in Switzerland since 1995 and replaced the earlier goods turnover tax.
Since 2024 the standard rate has been 8.1 per cent.
A reduced rate of 2.6 per cent applies to food, books and medicines.
A special rate of 3.8 per cent applies to hotel stays.
Companies pay the tax to the Federal Tax Administration.
Value added tax is the federal government’s biggest source of income.

abschnitte.text: **Value added tax** is a tax on consumption. It is charged on almost everything you buy, from clothes and bikes to mobile phone contracts. In the shop you usually do not see it, because it is already included in the price. But the **receipt** often shows how much VAT is contained in the amount.

The tax gets its name because it is charged on the **value added** at each stage. A farmer sells wheat to a mill, the mill sells flour to the bakery, and the bakery sells bread to you. Each company accounts for the tax on its sales and may deduct the tax it has already paid on its purchases; this is called **input tax deduction**. In the end, the customer bears the whole tax.

Since 1 January 2024 the **standard rate** has been 8.1 per cent. For everyday necessities such as food, books, newspapers and medicines, a **reduced rate** of 2.6 per cent applies. For hotel stays there is a special rate of 3.8 per cent. Some services, such as medical treatment, school teaching or renting a flat, are exempt from the tax.

Value added tax was introduced in 1995 and replaced the **goods turnover tax**, which had existed since 1941. At first the standard rate was 6.5 per cent. Because the tax is written into the Federal Constitution, every increase in the rate has to be approved by the people and the cantons. The latest increase, in 2024, helps to finance the AVS.

Compared with the rest of Europe, Swiss VAT is very low; in Germany, for example, the standard rate is 19 per cent. Even so, it brings the federal government billions of francs every year. Companies only have to register with the **Federal Tax Administration** once their annual turnover reaches 100,000 francs. That is why small businesses such as a kiosk with little turnover often do not have to account for VAT.

begriffe.erklaerung: The value a company adds to a product by processing it.
The usual tax rate, which is 8.1 per cent in Switzerland.
Companies may deduct the tax they paid when buying.
The federal authority that collects taxes such as VAT.

gewusst: A croissant to take away is taxed at 2.6 per cent, but if you eat it at a table in a café it is taxed at 8.1 per cent.
Switzerland has one of the lowest VAT rates in the whole of Europe.
Tourists from abroad can have the VAT on certain purchases refunded when they leave Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: If you do not pay your debts, debt enforcement proceedings can be started against you. If you still do not pay, the debt enforcement office can take money or belongings to settle the debts. This is called seizure (Pfändung).
wichtigste: Seizure is a step in debt enforcement proceedings.
It follows if you raise no objection and do not pay.
The debt enforcement office can seize assets or part of your wages.
The person always keeps the subsistence minimum.
Bankruptcy usually only applies to people and companies in the commercial register.
If you cannot pay everything, the creditor gets a certificate of loss.

abschnitte.text: It all starts with an unpaid bill. The creditor, meaning the person or company you owe money to, can start debt enforcement proceedings at the **debt enforcement office**. You then receive a **payment order**. If you do not agree, you can raise an **objection** within 10 days. If you do not do so and do not pay either, the creditor can ask for the proceedings to **continue**. For private individuals, **seizure** then usually follows.

With a seizure, someone from the debt enforcement office comes round or asks the person to come in. They look at what **assets** there are: money in the account, valuable things or a car. Very often part of the **wages** is seized. The employer then pays this part directly to the debt enforcement office. Such wage garnishment lasts at most one year.

Nobody may have everything taken away. The debt enforcement office calculates the **subsistence minimum**. This is the money you need for housing, food, health insurance and the bare essentials. Only what is above it is seized. Important belongings such as a bed, clothes or tools needed for work may not be seized either. They are called **exempt items** (Kompetenzstücke).

If what is seized is not enough to pay all the debts, the creditor receives a **certificate of loss**. It shows how much is still owed. The debts have not disappeared because of it. A certificate of loss remains valid for 20 years. Debt enforcement proceedings and seizures are listed in the **debt enforcement register**. That is why it is worth seeking help early from a **debt advice service** if you have money problems.

gewusst: The rules on seizure are set out in the Federal Act on Debt Enforcement and Bankruptcy, SchKG for short.
Every municipality or region in Switzerland has a debt enforcement office responsible for it.

teile.einleitung: In a guarantee, one person commits to paying another person's debts if that person cannot pay. The person who gives the guarantee is called the guarantor. A guarantee is a great sign of trust, but it can become expensive.
wichtigste: In a guarantee, someone promises to pay another person's debts if that person cannot pay.
The person who gives the guarantee is called the guarantor.
In Switzerland, guarantees are governed by the Code of Obligations.
Strict formal rules apply to private individuals so that nobody gives a guarantee lightly.
With a joint and several guarantee, the creditor can demand money directly from the guarantor.
Guarantees can put a strain on friendships and families if problems arise.
The state also sometimes gives guarantees, for example for loans to companies.

abschnitte.text: A **guarantee** is a contract between the guarantor and a **creditor**, for example a bank. The guarantor promises to pay someone else's debts if that person cannot manage it. The person for whom the guarantee is given is called the **principal debtor**. In this way someone can get a loan or a flat who might otherwise be turned down.

abschnitte.titel: How does it work in Switzerland?
abschnitte.text: Guarantees are governed by the **Code of Obligations**. For private individuals, a guarantee must be made in writing and state the maximum amount for which you are liable. For more than 2000 francs it even needs to be officially certified by a notary. If the guarantor is married, the spouse usually also has to agree in writing.

abschnitte.titel: Simple and joint and several guarantees
abschnitte.text: With a **simple guarantee**, the creditor must first try to get the money from the principal debtor. Only if that does not work does the guarantor have to pay. With a **joint and several guarantee**, on the other hand, the creditor can go straight to the guarantor. That is why banks usually ask for a joint and several guarantee.

Anyone who gives a guarantee can lose a lot of money, and in the worst case even end up in debt. The old German saying “Bürgen soll man würgen” (roughly: guarantors should be throttled) warns against giving a guarantee lightly. Only sign a guarantee if you could pay the amount yourself if necessary. For rented flats there are often alternatives today, such as **rent deposit insurance**.

The Confederation and the cantons also give guarantees. During the Covid pandemic in 2020, the Confederation guaranteed emergency loans to thousands of Swiss companies so that banks could lend them money quickly. There are also guarantee cooperatives in Switzerland that help small companies and trades. In this way young businesses without much wealth can also get a loan.

begriffe.erklaerung: The person who answers for someone else's debts.
Someone to whom money is owed, for example a bank.
The person who actually has to pay the money back.
A contract is officially recorded by a public official, such as a notary.

gewusst: In 1798 Friedrich Schiller wrote the ballad “Die Bürgschaft” (The Pledge), in which a friend stands surety for another with his life.
In Switzerland, a guarantee given by a private individual ends after 20 years at the latest.
The saying “Bürgen soll man würgen” is several hundred years old and warns of the risks of giving a guarantee.

teile.einleitung: With a share you buy a small part of a company. Anyone who owns shares is a co-owner of the company and can earn from its success. But shares can also lose value, which is why they involve risk.
wichtigste: A share is a small part of a company.
Companies that issue shares are called public limited companies, AG for short in Switzerland.
Shares are traded on the stock exchange, in Switzerland mainly on the SIX Swiss Exchange in Zurich.
The price of a share changes all the time.
Many companies pay their shareholders a dividend once a year.
Shareholders may have a say at the annual general meeting.
With shares you can make money, but you can also lose it.

abschnitte.text: A **share** is a security that represents part of a company. Imagine a company as a large pizza that is divided into many small slices. Anyone who owns a slice is a **shareholder** and therefore a co-owner. Large companies such as Nestlé have billions of shares that belong to many different people.

Shares are bought and sold on the **stock exchange**. The most important stock exchange in Switzerland is the SIX Swiss Exchange in Zurich. The **price** of a share is set by supply and demand: if many people want to buy, it rises; if many want to sell, it falls. The Swiss Market Index, SMI for short, shows how the 20 largest Swiss shares are doing.

abschnitte.titel: How do you make money with them?
abschnitte.text: You can make money with shares in two ways. First, the price can rise, so that you sell the share later for more. Second, many companies pay part of their profit to shareholders as a **dividend**. But if the price falls, you lose money, and if a company goes bankrupt, the share can become almost worthless.

Shareholders are invited to the **annual general meeting** once a year. There they vote, for example, on electing the board of directors and on the size of the dividend. The more shares you own, the more votes you have. That is why small shareholders usually have little influence, while large investors have a lot.

The first public company in today's sense was the Dutch East India Company, founded in 1602. Its shares were traded in Amsterdam, which is regarded as the beginning of the modern stock exchange. Anyone who buys shares today should use money that they will not need for a long time. Experts advise spreading the money across many companies instead of putting all your eggs in one basket.

begriffe.erklaerung: A person who owns shares and is therefore a co-owner of a company.
A marketplace where shares and other securities are traded.
Part of a company's profit that is paid out to shareholders.
The current price of a share.

gewusst: For shares you need a special account at a bank, called a securities account.
Shares used to be beautifully designed pieces of paper; today they are almost always stored only electronically.
Rising prices are called a boom or bull market, and falling prices a slump or bear market.

teile.einleitung: Withholding tax (Quellensteuer) is a tax that is deducted directly from your wages before the money even reaches your account. In Switzerland it mainly affects foreign employees without a settlement permit. The employer deducts it and pays it to the state.
wichtigste: Withholding tax is deducted directly from wages.
The employer calculates it and pays it to the tax authority.
It mainly affects foreign employees without a C settlement permit.
Cross-border commuters also often pay withholding tax.
Swiss citizens, on the other hand, fill in a tax return every year.
The amount depends on wages, the canton of residence, marital status and the number of children.
People who earn a lot still have to do a tax return.

abschnitte.text: In German, **withholding tax** is called “Quellensteuer”, tax at source, because it is deducted directly at the source of the income, that is from the wages. The person only receives their wages after the tax has been deducted. The **employer** is responsible for deducting the correct amount. It then pays the money to the cantonal tax administration.

In Switzerland, withholding tax is mainly paid by foreign employees who do not yet have a C **settlement permit**. These include, for example, people with a B residence permit or short-term residents. **Cross-border commuters**, who live abroad and work in Switzerland, are also often affected. Anyone married to a Swiss citizen or to a person with a C permit normally does not pay withholding tax.

The amount is calculated using tables that each canton sets. What matters are the wages, marital status and number of children. A married person with children pays less than a single person on the same wage. The deduction usually combines the taxes for the federal government, canton, municipality and church.

Anyone who earns more than 120,000 francs a year must also fill in a **tax return**. Others can ask for a recalculation voluntarily, for example to claim deductions for pillar 3a. The deadline for this is the end of March of the following year. Swiss citizens and people with a C permit, on the other hand, always pay their taxes via the tax return.

Withholding tax makes sure that the state reliably receives the money. With people who may only stay in Switzerland for a short time, it would otherwise be difficult to collect the taxes later. It is also practical for the people affected, because they do not receive a big tax bill. The principle is similar to the **wage tax deduction** in Germany or Austria, where almost all employees are taxed this way.

begriffe.erklaerung: Money that everyone pays to the state so that it can pay for schools, roads and much more.
Permit C for foreign nationals who have lived in Switzerland for a long time and may stay here.
A person who lives in a neighbouring country and commutes across the border to work.
A form in which you tell the tax office about your income and assets.

gewusst: For withholding tax there are tariff letters, for example A for single people and C for married couples where both partners work.
In many countries, such as Germany, almost all employees are taxed directly through their wages in a similar way.
The employer receives a small payment from the canton for handling the withholding tax.

teile.einleitung: Quality describes how well something is made. An item of good quality lasts a long time, works reliably and does not break so quickly. That is why the cheapest is not always the best choice.
wichtigste: Quality means how well something is made and how long it lasts.
Cheap things sometimes break quickly.
Then you have to buy again and end up paying more.
Something good often costs more but lasts longer.
Expensive does not automatically mean good, so it is worth looking closely.

abschnitte.text: Imagine one toy car costs 5 francs and another costs 15 francs. The cheap car breaks after a week, and you buy a new one. After three cars you have also paid 15 francs. The good car might have lasted for years. That is why people say: **buy cheap, buy twice.**

You can often recognise good quality by the **material**: it feels sturdy and is neatly made. Seams hold, parts do not wobble, and nothing smells strongly of plastic. A **guarantee** also shows that the manufacturer trusts its product. Reviews from other buyers can also help. But a high price alone is not a sure sign of good quality.

Things that last a long time are also good for the **environment**. If you have to buy new things less often, less rubbish is produced. Making them requires fewer raw materials and less energy. If you also look after your things well, you can use them even longer.

gewusst: In Switzerland there is a legal warranty for faulty goods. Many retailers also give their own guarantee.

teile.einleitung: Anyone in Switzerland against whom debt enforcement proceedings are started receives a payment order from the debt enforcement office. If you do not agree with the claim, you can raise an objection (Rechtsvorschlag). This stops the debt enforcement for the time being.
wichtigste: An objection is a challenge to a **payment order**.
You must raise it within **10 days** of receiving the payment order.
You can declare it verbally when the order is handed over.
No reason has to be given.
The objection stops the debt enforcement, but it does not cancel the debt.

abschnitte.titel: Debt enforcement and the payment order
abschnitte.text: If someone does not pay a bill, the **creditor** can start debt enforcement proceedings at the **debt enforcement office**. The office then serves the **debtor** with a **payment order**. It states how much they are to pay. This is governed by the Federal Act on Debt Enforcement and Bankruptcy, **SchKG** for short.

If you think that you owe nothing or less, you raise an **objection**. This can be done verbally when the order is handed over or in writing at the debt enforcement office. The deadline is **10 days**. You do not have to explain why you disagree. The objection is an important right for defending yourself against unjustified claims.

After the objection, the debt enforcement comes to a standstill. If the creditor wants to continue, they must ask the **court** to set aside the objection (**Rechtsöffnung**). If, for example, they have a signed acknowledgement of debt, the court can set the objection aside. Then the debt enforcement continues. So the objection stops things, but it does not cancel the debt.

gewusst: In Switzerland you can start debt enforcement proceedings without first having to prove that the claim is correct. That is why the objection is so important.

teile.einleitung: With leasing, you pay an amount every month to use a car or another product. But it does not belong to you. Leasing often looks cheap, but it can end up more expensive than you think.
wichtigste: With leasing you pay for using something, not for owning it.
The leasing company remains the owner.
That is why you may not simply sell a leased car.
If you drive more kilometres than agreed, you have to pay extra.
Ending the contract early often costs a lot of money.
Total costs: instalment times months plus the deposit, plus insurance and servicing.

abschnitte.text: Leasing is similar to renting. The **leasing company** buys the car and lets you have it for a certain time, for example 48 months. For this you pay a **leasing instalment** every month. Often the company also asks for a **deposit** at the start. The car belongs to the company the whole time. At the end you usually give it back.

The leasing contract states a **mileage limit**, for example 15,000 kilometres a year. If you drive more, at the end you pay a fixed amount for every extra kilometre. The car must be looked after and well insured, usually with **fully comprehensive insurance**. Damage that goes beyond normal wear and tear has to be paid for when you return it.

The instalments are calculated over the whole term. If you end the contract early, you get a new statement. The car is then often worth less than what is still to be paid. That is why high **extra payments** often arise. In Switzerland, leasing for private individuals counts as a **consumer loan**. The company must check beforehand whether you can afford the instalments.

An instalment of 350 francs looks small. But over 48 months that comes to 16,800 francs. With a deposit of 3,000 francs you pay 19,800 francs altogether. On top of that come insurance, servicing, tyres and petrol. And at the end you own nothing. That is why it is worth adding up all the costs before signing and comparing them with buying.

gewusst: The word “leasing” comes from the English “to lease”, which means to rent.
It is not only cars that are leased, but also phones, machines or photocopiers in companies.

teile.einleitung: Have you ever noticed that on the internet you are shown adverts for things you recently searched for? That is personalised advertising. It happens because websites and apps collect data about how you behave.
wichtigste: Personalised advertising is tailored to one individual person.
Websites and apps analyse searches, clicks and preferences.
Cookies and other techniques are often used for this.
The aim is to get you to buy something.
In many apps and browsers you can limit the collection of data.
In Switzerland, the Data Protection Act protects personal data.

abschnitte.text: When you surf the internet, you leave **traces**. Websites store small files on your device, known as **cookies**. Apps remember what you look at, search for and click on. Advertising companies analyse this **data**. That way they know what you are interested in. If you have searched for trainers, you suddenly see adverts for trainers everywhere.

Advertising costs money. That is why companies only want to show it to people who are likely to be interested. Personalised advertising is **targeted**: it matches your wishes and is meant to get you **to buy**. Many free apps and social networks earn their money exactly like this. That is why people say: if something costs nothing, you often pay with your data.

Personalised advertising can be very convincing. It often appears just when you are thinking about something. Then it is good to pause for a moment: **Do I really need this?** It also helps to recognise advertising as advertising. On social networks it is often marked “Sponsored” or “Ad”. Influencers sometimes advertise things too, and they are paid for it.

In many browsers and apps you can set which **cookies** are allowed. You can often switch off personalised advertising or refuse **tracking**. It is worth not giving every app every permission. In Switzerland, the **Data Protection Act** governs how companies may handle personal data. A new, stricter version has applied since September 2023.

gewusst: The English word “cookie” means a biscuit.
In Switzerland, the Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner makes sure that the Data Protection Act is followed.

teile.einleitung: Sometimes you see something and want it straight away. Then a simple trick helps: **wait**. If you wait a few days, you will notice whether something really matters to you.
wichtigste: Sudden wishes are often less strong after a few days.
If you wait, you can think things over calmly.
If you still want something after a while, it really matters to you.
Waiting protects you from buying things you regret later.
Sleeping on it for a night is a good start.

abschnitte.text: In shops, in adverts or at friends' houses, you often see great things. Then a strong wish arises: “I want that now!” Such **sudden wishes** are completely normal. Shops know this and like to put sweets and toys near the till. But not everything you want straight away is something you need.

A good trick is to **wait** a few days. You can write the wish down and look at it again after a week. Often the wish is smaller by then or gone altogether. But if you still want it, it really matters to you. Then you can calmly think about whether you have enough money.

If you wait, you buy fewer things that end up lying in a corner after a short time. That leaves more money for things that really make you happy. Some people also save up for a bigger wish. Looking forward to something while you wait can even be nice. Adults call this “sleeping on it”.

gewusst: Many adults use the same trick when shopping online: they put something in their basket and only buy it a few days later if they still want it then.

teile.einleitung: Payslips often show a deduction marked “BVG” or “PK”. This is the contribution to the **pension fund**, the **occupational pension**. It is the second pillar of the Swiss pension system.
wichtigste: BVG stands for the Federal Act on Occupational Retirement, Survivors' and Disability Pension Plans.
PK is short for Pensionskasse, the pension fund.
The occupational pension is the second pillar of the pension system.
The employer pays at least as much as the employee.
A separate savings balance is built up for each person.
On retirement you receive a pension or the capital from it.

abschnitte.text: The Swiss pension system stands on **three pillars**. The **first pillar** is the AHV, which is meant to secure the minimum needed to live. The **second pillar** is the **occupational pension** with the **pension fund**. Together, the AHV and the pension fund are meant to help people roughly keep their usual standard of living in old age. The **third pillar** is voluntary private saving.

The “BVG” or “PK” deduction goes to the employer's **pension fund**. BVG is short for the **Federal Act on Occupational Pensions**. The **employer** must pay in at least as much as the employee. Many employers even pay more. How high the contribution is depends on the wages, the age and the pension fund.

Anyone who earns more than a certain **minimum salary** a year from one employer is compulsorily insured. This limit is called the **entry threshold**. From 1 January after your 17th birthday you are insured against death and disability. **Saving for old age** begins from 1 January after your 24th birthday. People who earn very little are often not in a pension fund.

Unlike the AHV, the pension fund saves a **separate balance** for each person. The money is invested and earns **interest**. On retirement you can draw a monthly **pension** from it or take part of it as a lump sum of **capital**. Anyone who changes jobs takes their balance with them to the new pension fund.

gewusst: In Switzerland, occupational pensions have been compulsory for employees since 1985.
In certain cases you can draw money from the pension fund earlier, for example to buy your own home.

teile.einleitung: A loan is borrowed money that you have to pay back with interest. Anyone who borrows money promises to give it back by a certain time. Loans come from banks, but also happen in everyday life, when you lend a friend some money.
wichtigste: A loan is borrowed money that you have to pay back.
You usually pay interest for the loan.
The one who lends money is called the creditor; the one who owes money is called the debtor.
Before giving a loan, banks check whether you can pay it back.
Well-known types of loan are mortgages, consumer loans and leasing.
If you lend a friend money, you may not get it back.
A loan can help, but it can also lead into the debt trap.

abschnitte.text: The German word for loan, **Kredit**, comes from the Latin “credere”, which means “to believe” or “to trust”. Anyone who lends money trusts that they will get it back. The **creditor** gives the money; the **debtor** takes it and pays it back later. Usually a contract records how much, by when and at what interest rate.

**Interest** is the price of borrowed money. If you borrow 1000 francs at 5 per cent for a year, you have to pay back 1050 francs at the end. Many loans are paid off in monthly **instalments**; this is called repayment or amortisation. The longer the term, the more interest adds up altogether.

The biggest loans in Switzerland are **mortgages**, with which people buy a house or a flat. With a consumer loan you buy furniture, cars or holidays. Companies take out loans to buy machines or open new branches. States also borrow money, for example through bonds.

Before a bank lends money, it checks the **credit rating**, that is the person’s creditworthiness. It looks at how much someone earns, what expenses they have and whether there are already debt enforcement proceedings against them. Anyone considered not very reliable gets no loan or has to pay higher interest. In Switzerland, consumer loans are also recorded in central databases.

Friends sometimes lend each other money too, for example for a cinema ticket or a game. You should be careful, because you may not get the money back. In the worst case, even the **friendship** suffers. That is why it helps to agree clearly when the money will come back, and only to lend as much as you could manage without if necessary.

begriffe.erklaerung: The person or company that lends money.
The person or company that has to pay money back.
A large loan for buying a house or a flat.
Creditworthiness, meaning how reliably someone pays back debts.

gewusst: More than 4000 years ago, loans were already being recorded on clay tablets in Mesopotamia.
Switzerland is one of the countries with the highest mortgage debt per person in the world.
The word “credit” literally means “trust”.

teile.einleitung: A discount code is a sequence of letters or numbers that lets you pay less when shopping online. Influencers often share codes like these in their videos. Usually they earn money from every purchase.
wichtigste: With a discount code, the price becomes lower when you buy online.
Each influencer often has their own code.
That way the company can see who brought about the purchase.
The influencer often receives a **commission** for this, meaning a share of the sale.
A discount code is therefore a form of advertising.

abschnitte.text: When paying in an online shop, there is often a box for a **voucher code**. If you type the code in there, the price is reduced, for example by 10 %. Special **links** that you click on work in a similar way. That way the company can count exactly how many purchases come through a particular code or link.

Companies pay influencers to show their products. With discount codes they often receive a **commission** for every sale. The more people buy, the more they earn. That is why some praise a product more than it deserves. This is not forbidden, but you should know about it.

Paid posts should be labelled as **advertising**, for example with “advertising” or “advert”. That way viewers know that money is involved. Before buying with a code, it is worth asking: Do I really need this? A discount on something unnecessary is not saving.

gewusst: This kind of advertising, where someone is paid per sale, is called **affiliate marketing**.

teile.einleitung: The Consumer Credit Information Office, IKO for short, is a database in Switzerland. Current consumer loans and leasing contracts are reported to it, so that nobody takes on too much debt.
wichtigste: IKO stands for the Consumer Credit Information Office (Informationsstelle für Konsumkredit).
It is provided for in the Consumer Credit Act.
Lenders must report consumer loans and leasing contracts to the IKO.
Before a new loan, they can see what commitments already exist.
This is meant to prevent over-indebtedness.

abschnitte.text: The **IKO** is an office that collects information about consumer loans. The **Consumer Credit Act** requires it to exist. The lenders in Switzerland run it together. It stores who has a loan or a lease and how high the instalments are.

What is reported includes, for example, **cash loans**, **leasing contracts** and, under certain conditions, credit cards with a credit facility. If someone is seriously behind with their payments, this is recorded too. Once a loan has been paid back, the entry is deleted after a certain time. Anyone can ask the IKO what data is stored about them.

Before a bank grants a loan, it must check the person’s **creditworthiness**. To do this, it looks up at the IKO which loans are already running. That way it can see whether the person can still afford another instalment. This protects people from taking on more debt than they can bear.

gewusst: Besides the IKO, Switzerland also has the ZEK, a private central office for credit information.

teile.einleitung: When bread, rents or train tickets become more expensive, this is called inflation (in Switzerland “Teuerung”). So that people know exactly how much prices are rising, the federal government calculates the Swiss Consumer Price Index every month.
wichtigste: The Swiss Consumer Price Index is abbreviated to LIK in German (CPI in English).
It is calculated by the Federal Statistical Office (FSO).
It is based on a basket of goods with many typical goods and services.
The prices are collected again and compared every month.
If the index rises, life becomes more expensive: this is called inflation.
The CPI helps with wage negotiations, rents and pensions.

abschnitte.text: The **basket of goods** is not a real basket, but a long list. It contains the things that households in Switzerland spend money on: food, clothes, rent, electricity, transport, phone, free time and much more. Important expenses such as rent count more than rare ones. This **weighting** comes from surveys in which households write down their spending. That way the basket of goods matches people’s everyday lives.

Every month the FSO records the prices of the products in the basket of goods, in shops, online and from providers all over the country. It then compares the new total price with the price in a **base month**. This base month is given the value 100. If the index stands at 103, prices have risen by 3 per cent since then. The change compared with the same month of the previous year is called the **annual inflation rate**.

When prices rise, you can buy less with the same money. We say that **purchasing power** falls. If prices fall over a long period, this is called **deflation**. Both can be difficult for the economy. That is why the Swiss National Bank (SNB) has the task of ensuring stable prices. It considers inflation of less than 2 per cent a year to be stable.

abschnitte.titel: What the index is used for
abschnitte.text: The CPI matters in everyday life. In **wage negotiations**, employers and trade unions look at how much prices have risen. Some tenancy agreements are linked to the index; then the rent may rise with inflation. Price changes also play a role when **AVS pensions** are adjusted. This is meant to stop people’s money simply losing value.

gewusst: An index is a number that shows a development, not a price in francs.
The basket of goods is adjusted regularly: in the past, for example, mobile phone contracts were not part of it, but today they are.

teile.einleitung: A free trial is an offer that lets you test a service for a short time for free or very cheaply. There are trials like this for streaming services, newspapers, apps or gyms. Often the subscription then continues automatically and costs money.
wichtigste: With a trial subscription you test a service for free or cheaply.
Many trials turn automatically into a paid subscription.
If you do not cancel in time, you have to pay afterwards.
It is best to note down the end date straight away.
Read the terms before you start: how long is it free, what does it cost afterwards, how do you cancel?

abschnitte.text: Companies want to win new customers. Once people have tried a service, they often stay with it. Many also simply forget to cancel the subscription. That is why some providers ask for a **payment method**, for example a credit card, even at the free start. After the trial period, the full price is then charged automatically.

Every subscription has **terms** that you should read before signing up. They state when the trial period ends and how to **cancel**. Sometimes you have to cancel a few days before the end. An entry in your calendar or a reminder on your phone helps. With many services you can also cancel straight after starting and still use the free month to the end.

A single subscription may only cost a few francs a month. But if you have several subscriptions, you quickly pay a lot of money in a year. That is why it is worth checking regularly which subscriptions you really need. Children and teenagers should always ask their parents first before taking out a subscription.

gewusst: For subscriptions that renew without you noticing, there is the term **subscription trap**.
If you keep a subscription costing 10 francs a month for a year, you pay 120 francs.

teile.einleitung: Board money (Kostgeld) is an amount that apprentices or young adults with their own wages give to their parents. With it they contribute to the costs of food and living at home.
wichtigste: Board money is a contribution towards food and housing.
It is often paid when you have your own wages and still live at home.
The amount is agreed within the family.
It depends on your wages and your expenses.
Paying board money teaches you to take on responsibility.

abschnitte.text: When you do an **apprenticeship**, you earn your own wages for the first time. If you still live with your parents, you still need food, electricity, water and a room. With **board money** you pay part of these costs yourself. It is not a law, but an agreement within the family.

The amount depends on the **apprentice’s wage**, which is often still small in the first year of the apprenticeship. Spending on the journey to work, your phone, clothes and free time also plays a role. Advice services such as Budgetberatung Schweiz give guideline figures. It is important that after paying board money there is still enough money left to live on and to save.

It is best for parents and apprentices to discuss together how much the board money is and what it covers. Does it include lunch, for example? Who washes the clothes? A clear agreement prevents arguments. If the wage goes up, the board money can be adjusted.

Board money shows that housing and food cost something. When you move out later, you already know these costs. That makes the step into your first flat of your own easier. So board money is also practice for life as an adult.

gewusst: In Switzerland, apprentices’ wages usually rise with each year of the apprenticeship.
Some parents secretly put part of the board money aside and give it back later as a present for the first flat of one’s own.

teile.einleitung: Deflation is the opposite of inflation. In deflation, prices fall generally and over a long period. That sounds good at first, but it can harm the economy.
wichtigste: Deflation means that the general price level falls over a long period.
In inflation prices rise, and in deflation they fall.
In deflation you can buy more with the same amount of money.
People put off purchases because they hope for lower prices.
Companies then sell less and take on fewer people.
The Swiss National Bank aims for inflation between 0 and 2 per cent.

abschnitte.text: We speak of **deflation** when not just a few things become cheaper but almost everything. If only one mobile phone becomes cheaper, that is not deflation. In Switzerland, price changes are measured with the **Swiss Consumer Price Index**. It is calculated by the Federal Statistical Office. If it falls over a long period, there is deflation.

If everyone expects prices to keep falling, they **wait** before buying. Companies then sell less and earn less. They save, invest less and take on fewer people. Then people have even less money and buy even less. In this way a **downward spiral** can develop. Debts also become harder to bear, because the amount owed stays the same while wages may fall.

abschnitte.titel: The role of the National Bank
abschnitte.text: The **Swiss National Bank** has the task of ensuring **price stability**. By this it means inflation of less than 2 per cent a year, but no deflation. To prevent deflation it can, for example, lower **interest rates**. Then saving is less worthwhile and buying or investing becomes more worthwhile.

There was severe deflation during the **Great Depression** in the 1930s. At that time prices, wages and production fell sharply in many countries. From the 1990s **Japan** experienced a long period of slightly falling prices. In Switzerland too, prices fell slightly in some years, for example in 2015, when the franc rose strongly in value.

gewusst: The word deflation comes from the Latin “deflare”, which means “to blow away”.
Many experts consider slightly rising prices healthier for the economy than falling ones.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland there are seven different coins. They differ in size, picture and value. If you know them, you can quickly find the right coin when paying.
wichtigste: There are coins worth 5, 10 and 20 centimes (Rappen).
There are also coins worth 1/2, 1, 2 and 5 francs.
One franc has 100 centimes.
Half a franc is 50 centimes, so more than 20 centimes.
The biggest and most valuable coin is the 5-franc piece.
The coins are made by Swissmint in Bern.

abschnitte.text: The smallest coins count in **centimes** (Rappen). There is the **5-centime piece**, the **10-centime piece** and the **20-centime piece**. They show the head of a woman who represents freedom. The 5-centime piece is golden, the others are silver. There used to be 1-centime and 2-centime pieces too. These are no longer used today.

There are four **franc coins**: 1/2 franc, 1 franc, 2 francs and 5 francs. The half-franc, the one-franc and the 2-franc pieces show **Helvetia**, a woman who represents Switzerland. On the 5-franc piece you can see the head of an Alpine herdsman. The greater the value, the bigger the coin usually is. One exception is the half-franc: it is smaller than the 20-centime piece.

One franc has **100 centimes**. So **half a franc** is 50 centimes. That is why the half-franc is worth more than a 20-centime piece, even though it is smaller. Two half-francs make one franc. So when you compare coins, it is better to look at the number than at the size.

gewusst: The 10-centime piece has looked almost the same since 1879. It is one of the oldest coins in the world that are still in circulation.
The edge of the 5-franc piece bears the words “DOMINUS PROVIDEBIT”, which means “The Lord will provide”.

teile.einleitung: Swiss franc banknotes are among the most colourful and most secure notes in the world. They come in six values from 10 to 1000 francs, and each note has its own colour. The current 10-franc note is yellow.
wichtigste: There are Swiss banknotes of 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 and 1000 francs.
The current 10-franc note is yellow.
The 20 note is red, the 50 green, the 100 blue, the 200 brown and the 1000 purple.
The current ninth series of banknotes was introduced from 2016 to 2019.
The notes are issued by the Swiss National Bank.
They show the theme “The many facets of Switzerland” with hands and a globe.
Old notes of the eighth series can be exchanged at the National Bank with no time limit.

abschnitte.text: Each Swiss banknote has its own **colour** so that you can recognise it quickly. The 10 note is yellow, the 20 red, the 50 green and the 100 blue. The 200 is brown and the 1000 purple. The higher the value, the longer the note, which also helps people with visual impairments.

The current **ninth series of banknotes** was designed by the graphic designer Manuela Pfrunder. Its theme is “The many facets of Switzerland”, and each note represents a characteristic of Switzerland. The 10 note stands for organisational talent, the 20 for creativity and the 50 for a love of experiences. On all the notes you can see a **hand** and a globe as linking motifs.

The new series was introduced step by step, first the 50 note in 2016. The 20 and 10 notes followed in 2017, and the 200 note in 2018. In 2019 the 1000 note and finally the 100 note came out. The previous eighth series, with portraits of famous people, was withdrawn in 2021 and is no longer official legal tender.

Swiss banknotes are considered especially **hard to forge**. They have a special base material made of several layers. When you move the note, pictures and colours change, for example a shimmering globe. When you hold it up to the light, you can see a Swiss cross and other hidden features.

In Switzerland, banknotes may only be issued by the **Swiss National Bank**, SNB for short. It has its headquarters in Bern and Zurich. Coins, on the other hand, are minted by Swissmint in Bern on behalf of the Confederation. The Swiss franc is regarded around the world as a very stable currency.

begriffe.erklaerung: A note of money made of paper or another material.
The state's bank, which issues banknotes and makes sure the franc stays stable.
A special detail on a note that makes forgery more difficult.
A group of banknotes with a shared design.

gewusst: The 1000-franc note is one of the highest-value banknotes in the world.
On all the notes of the ninth series, the value is written in four national languages, including Romansh.
The 10 note of the eighth series showed the architect Le Corbusier, who was born in La Chaux-de-Fonds.

teile.einleitung: In shops you often see signs saying “Aktion” (special offer). This usually means that something is **cheaper for a short time**. But a special offer is only worth it if you need the product anyway.
wichtigste: With a special offer, a product is cheaper for a while.
It often says how many per cent you save.
A special offer is only worth it if you really need the product.
Shops also run special offers so that more people come into the shop.
It is worth comparing the price per kilo or per litre.

abschnitte.text: With a **special offer**, the price is lowered for a certain time. The sign then often shows the old and the new price or a **discount** in per cent. Sometimes it says “3 for 2”: you take three and only pay for two. After the offer, the product costs the same as before again.

A special offer only saves money if you would have bought the product **anyway**. Anyone who buys something just because it is cheaper ends up spending more. Shops know that special offers attract customers. Once people are in the shop, they often buy other things as well. That is why a **shopping list** helps you stick to your plan.

A large pack on special offer is not always cheaper than a small one that is not on offer. That is why it is worth comparing the **unit price**, meaning the price per kilo or per litre. In Switzerland it is often shown in small print on the price label. And with food: only buy as much as you can eat before it goes off.

gewusst: In Switzerland, the unit price per kilo or litre must be shown for many packaged goods so that people can compare prices more easily.

teile.einleitung: Health insurance covers costs when you fall ill or have an accident. In Switzerland, everyone who lives here must take out basic insurance with a health insurance fund. For this you pay a premium every month, and in return the insurance helps with visits to the doctor, medicines and stays in hospital.
wichtigste: Everyone who lives in Switzerland must take out basic insurance.
The rules are set out in the Health Insurance Act (KVG), which has applied since 1996.
The benefits of basic insurance are the same with all health insurance funds.
You pay a monthly premium and contribute to the costs with a deductible and a co-payment.
People who earn little can receive a premium reduction.
Supplementary insurance is voluntary and covers further benefits.
You can change health insurance fund every year.

abschnitte.text: **Health insurance** is insurance that covers the costs of the doctor, hospital and medicines. In Switzerland, **basic insurance** is compulsory, which means everyone must have it. This is laid down in the Health Insurance Act, which voters approved in 1994 and which came into force in 1996. Anyone who moves to Switzerland or is born here must be insured within three months.

Every month you pay the health insurance fund a **premium**. You also bear part of the costs yourself: first the **deductible**, for adults at least 300 francs a year. After that you pay a co-payment of 10 per cent, for adults at most 700 francs a year. If you choose a higher deductible, you pay a lower premium but bear more yourself if you are ill.

Basic insurance covers treatment by doctors, medicines prescribed by a doctor and stays in the general ward of a hospital in your home canton. Its benefits are exactly the same with all health insurance funds. For dental treatment, glasses or a single room in hospital you usually need **supplementary insurance**. This is voluntary, and the health insurance fund may turn people down for it.

For children up to 18, premiums are considerably lower than for adults. As standard there is no deductible for children, and the co-payment is limited to at most 350 francs a year. Young adults aged 19 to 25 often pay reduced premiums. Families with a low income receive a **premium reduction** from the canton.

In Switzerland there are several dozen health insurance funds that offer basic insurance. Premiums vary greatly depending on the fund, the canton and the model chosen. With models such as the **family doctor model** or the Telmed model you save on premiums, but you commit to contacting a particular service first. You can change your basic insurance at the end of each year; the notice must arrive by the end of November.

begriffe.erklaerung: The amount you pay every month for the insurance.
The amount per year that you first have to pay yourself.
A share of the costs that you bear yourself in addition to the deductible.
A contribution from the canton for people with little money.

gewusst: Before the KVG was introduced in 1996, health insurance was not compulsory in all cantons.
For many Swiss families, health insurance premiums are among the biggest expenses after the rent.
Every autumn the premiums for the following year are announced, and many people then compare the offers.

teile.einleitung: A loan costs money, because you have to pay back more than you borrowed. You can easily work out the cost of a loan if you know the instalments.
wichtigste: The cost of a loan is the amount you pay on top of what you borrowed.
You calculate: number of instalments times the instalment, minus the amount borrowed.
Example: 24 instalments of 230 francs make 5520 francs.
With a loan of 5000 francs, the loan therefore costs 520 francs.
The effective annual interest rate helps you compare loans.

abschnitte.text: First you work out how much you pay back in total: **number of instalments times the instalment amount**. Lukas pays 24 instalments of 230 francs; that makes 5520 francs. From this you subtract the amount borrowed. 5520 minus 5000 gives **520 francs in loan costs**.

The cost of a loan consists mainly of **interest**. Sometimes there are fees as well, for example for processing or for insurance. All of it together is the price for having the money sooner. For this amount you get nothing extra to buy.

In Switzerland, the loan agreement must state the **effective annual interest rate**. It shows the total costs as a percentage per year. That way you can compare different offers. The longer the term, the higher the total costs usually are, even if the instalment looks small.

If Lukas had saved 230 francs a month for two years, he would have had the 5000 francs without a loan and even some left over. He would just have had to wait longer. For things that are not urgent, waiting is almost always worth it.

gewusst: A small monthly instalment can be deceptive: with a long term you often pay much more in total.
The Consumer Credit Act requires the loan agreement to be made in writing.

teile.einleitung: When you buy on invoice, you get the goods first and only pay for them afterwards. This is practical, but it means you must not forget the payment deadline.
wichtigste: When you buy on invoice, you only pay after delivery.
The invoice shows a payment deadline, often 30 days.
If you pay late, you get a reminder and often reminder fees.
If you do not pay, debt enforcement proceedings can follow.
You can check the goods first before you pay.
Many shops check beforehand whether you are able to pay.

abschnitte.text: When shopping online, you choose “buy on invoice” as the payment method. The shop sends the goods together with an **invoice**, or sends the invoice by email. You then have a certain time to pay. In Switzerland this is usually done with a **QR payment slip**.

You can look at the goods and try them out first. If they are broken or wrong, you do not pay for something you do not want. You do not have to give any credit card details. That is why buying on invoice is very popular in Switzerland.

Because you do not pay straight away, it is easy to lose track. Several unpaid invoices can add up to a lot of money. If you miss the **payment deadline**, you get a **reminder**, often with extra fees. If you still do not pay, the shop can start **debt enforcement proceedings**.

It is best to pay an invoice straight away if the goods are fine. You can also put a reminder in your calendar. If you only buy what you can already afford now, you will not get into difficulties. Minors usually need their parents’ consent for purchases like these.

gewusst: For buying on invoice, some shops work with specialised companies that take over the invoice.
An entry in the debt enforcement register can later make it harder to find a flat.

teile.einleitung: A savings reserve is money you put aside so that you can pay unexpected expenses later. It is also called an emergency reserve or emergency fund. If you have a reserve, you do not have to get into debt when there is a surprise, and you stay calm.
wichtigste: A reserve is saved money for hard times or unexpected expenses.
It is also called an emergency reserve or emergency fund.
It helps you pay bills without getting into debt.
Experts recommend adults have a reserve of about three to six months’ expenses.
The reserve should be quickly available, for example in a savings account.
Children can also build up a small reserve from their pocket money.
Companies and states also build up reserves.

abschnitte.text: A **reserve** is a cushion of money that you do not spend on everyday things. It is meant for situations you are not expecting. That could be a broken washing machine, a high dentist’s bill or a flat tyre on your bike. Because the reserve is there for emergencies, it is also called an **emergency reserve**.

Without a reserve, you have to borrow money when an unexpected bill arrives. This quickly leads to **debt** and often to extra costs such as interest. With a reserve you can simply pay the bill. That gives you security and saves your nerves.

For adults, budget experts usually recommend a reserve of three to six months’ expenses. So anyone who needs 3000 francs every month should put aside about 9000 to 18,000 francs. That way you would be covered for a while if, for example, you **lost your job**. For children, a small amount is enough, such as a few weeks’ pocket money.

The reserve should be safe but easy to get at quickly. A separate **savings account**, apart from your everyday account, is a good choice. That way you are not tempted to spend the money on the side. For children, a separate money box or envelope can also be a good solution.

It is best to put a fixed amount aside every month as soon as your wages or pocket money arrive. Many people do this with a **standing order**, which transfers the money automatically to the savings account. If the reserve has been used, you top it up again afterwards. Even small amounts grow over time into a good cushion.

It is not only families that build up reserves, but also businesses, municipalities and states. A company, for example, puts money aside for difficult years or new machines. The **Swiss National Bank** holds large reserves of foreign currency and gold. In nature, squirrels do something similar when they hide nuts for the winter.

begriffe.erklaerung: An old German word for money kept for emergencies.
A plan of how much money you take in and what you spend it on.
An instruction to the bank to transfer money automatically at regular intervals.
Something you keep for later in case you need it.

gewusst: The Groschen used to be a small coin, which is where the word Notgroschen comes from.
The AVS has its own compensation fund, which works like a huge reserve for pensions.
Even in the Bible there is the story of Joseph, who had grain stored during seven good years for seven bad years.

teile.einleitung: An overdraft facility (Kontokorrentkredit) is credit on your bank account that lets you spend more money than there actually is in the account. It is also called an overdraft or arranged overdraft. You have to pay the overdrawn money back with interest, and this interest is usually quite high.
wichtigste: With an overdraft facility you can overdraw your account up to a limit.
So you spend more money than there is in the account.
The bank charges interest on the overdrawn amount.
This interest is usually higher than with other loans.
The bank sets a credit limit up to which you may overdraw.
With youth accounts, an overdraft is usually not possible.

abschnitte.text: A **current account** (Kontokorrent) is an account where money comes in and goes out, for example a salary account or private account. If the bank allows the balance to fall below zero, this is called an **overdraft facility**. The balance then becomes negative; you are “in the red”. At that moment the bank is lending you money.

The bank sets a **credit limit**, for example 2000 francs. Up to this amount you can pay bills or withdraw money, even if the account is empty. As soon as money comes into the account again, such as your next wages, the minus is balanced out. For the time you are in the red, the bank charges **debit interest**.

Overdraft interest is usually considerably higher than interest on other loans. In Switzerland, under the Consumer Credit Act, it may be at most 12 per cent a year for overdrafts on accounts. Anyone who overdraws without an agreed limit often has to pay extra fees. Because an overdraft is so convenient, many people only realise late how much it costs.

For businesses, the overdraft facility is an important tool for everyday operations. A joinery, for example, has to pay for wood and wages before its customers pay their bills. With the overdraft facility it bridges this **payment gap**. So it secures **liquidity**, which means the ability to keep paying.

Youth and apprentice accounts usually do not allow a minus, which protects you from debt. If you later have an account with an overdraft option, you should only use it in an emergency. A **budget** and a small emergency fund help you avoid slipping into the red in the first place. If you do end up in the red, you should pay off the amount as quickly as possible.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bank account in everyday use for payments in and out.
The highest amount by which you may overdraw your account.
The interest you pay when your account is in the red.
The ability to pay bills at any time.

gewusst: The word “Kontokorrent” comes from Italian and means “running account”.
On a bank statement you can often recognise an account in the red by a minus sign or the word “debit” (Soll).
Credit cards with part payment work in a similar way to an overdraft.

teile.einleitung: Online shopping means buying goods or services over the internet. You order comfortably on a computer or phone, and the parcel arrives at your home. But before buying online, you should check the seller and the reviews so that you do not fall for dodgy shops or fraud.
wichtigste: With online shopping you buy things over the internet.
You can shop at any time and compare prices easily.
Before buying, you should check the seller and the reviews.
There are fake shops that deliver nothing after you have paid.
In Switzerland there is no general right to return online purchases.
With orders from abroad, VAT and fees can be added.
Young people under 18 need their parents’ consent for bigger purchases.

abschnitte.text: With **online shopping** you choose products on a website or in an app, put them in a virtual **shopping basket** and pay online. The goods are then delivered by Swiss Post or a courier service. Well-known Swiss online shops include, for example, Digitec Galaxus or the online shops of Migros and Coop. International platforms are also widely used in Switzerland.

Online you can shop round the clock, even on Sundays. You can **compare** the prices and reviews of different sellers in a few minutes. This is especially practical for people who live far away from big shops. The choice is also often much bigger than in a shop.

Unfortunately there are also **fake shops**, which look genuine but deliver nothing after you have paid. Warning signs are extremely low prices, a missing legal notice with an address, and payment in advance as the only option. That is why you should read reviews on independent sites and check for a secure connection with “https”. If you are unsure, a quick search for the shop’s name together with the word “scam” helps.

A safe way to pay is often by **invoice**; then you only pay once the goods have arrived. In Switzerland, credit cards and the payment app Twint are also common. Unlike in the EU, Switzerland has no general legal **right of withdrawal** for online purchases. Whether you may send something back therefore depends on the shop’s terms and conditions.

Young people under 18 should always talk to their parents about bigger online purchases. Never pass on passwords or card details by email or chat, because it could be **phishing**. With orders from abroad, VAT, customs duty and handling fees can make the price considerably higher. And just as in a shop: before clicking “Buy”, think for a moment about whether you really need the thing.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fake online shop that takes money but delivers nothing.
