Information on a website about who is behind it and how to contact the company (Impressum).
Fraud in which fake messages are used to get hold of passwords or card details.
The right to cancel a purchase within a set period without giving a reason.

gewusst: In Switzerland you are not automatically allowed to return goods bought online, but many shops allow it voluntarily.
The payment app Twint was developed in Switzerland and is used by millions of people.
Many parcels from online orders are sorted fully automatically in Swiss Post’s distribution centres.

teile.einleitung: By giving notice you end a contract, for example a subscription. So that you can prove later that you cancelled in time, the cancellation should be traceable.
wichtigste: Giving notice ends a contract.
The safest way to cancel is in writing, for example by registered post.
A confirmation from the provider also serves as proof.
The notice period must be kept to.
Simply no longer paying does not end a contract.
If you do not pay, you get reminders and fees.

abschnitte.text: The safest way is a **written cancellation**. It contains your name, address, customer or contract number and the end date you want. You sign the letter and keep a copy. With **registered post** from Swiss Post you have proof of when the letter arrived.

Many providers let you cancel in your customer account or by email. In that case you should definitely ask for a **confirmation** and keep it. A phone call is hard to prove. That is why it is worth putting the cancellation in writing afterwards as well.

Many contracts have a **notice period**. So the cancellation has to reach the provider a certain time before the end. If you cancel too late, you often have to pay for another term. That is why it is best to write the date in your calendar.

Some people think a subscription ends by itself if you stop paying. That is not true. The contract carries on, and the provider sends **reminders**. In the end **debt enforcement proceedings** can follow, and the debt grows even bigger because of the fees.

gewusst: With a registered letter you can track online when it was delivered.
Many subscriptions renew automatically if you do not cancel in time.

teile.einleitung: In the shop there are often two similar products side by side: one with a well-known name and one from the shop’s own brand. The branded product is usually more expensive. It is worth checking whether it is also better.
wichtigste: A branded product has a well-known name and a logo.
Own brands belong to the shop itself.
Own brands are often cheaper, with similar quality.
One reason for this: less advertising is done for own brands.
If you compare prices and contents, you can save a lot.
In Switzerland, brands are protected by law.

abschnitte.text: A **brand** is a name, a logo or a sign that a company uses to mark its products. You recognise it immediately. Companies can have their brand registered. In Switzerland this is done by the **Swiss Federal Institute of Intellectual Property** in Bern. After that, nobody else may use the same name for similar products.

Brand companies spend a lot of money on **advertising**, on television, on the internet or on posters. Attractive packaging and developing new products also cost money. These costs are included in the price. Many people are happy to pay more because they trust the brand or because they like it. But a well-known name can also simply be more expensive without the product being better.

Large retailers sell many products under their own name. These are called **own brands**. They are often right next to the branded product and cost less. In tests, own brands often do similarly well. Sometimes, though, the branded product tastes or works differently. It is best to try for yourself.

When shopping, it helps to look at the **list of ingredients** and the **unit price**. The unit price shows what, for example, a kilo or a litre costs. That way you can compare packs of different sizes fairly. If you choose the own brand for simple things such as flour, rice or salt, you often save quite a bit over the year.

gewusst: A **blind test** is so called because you cannot see which product you are trying. Then only the taste decides.
Some brand names are so well known that people use them for the whole product, for example “Tempo” for paper tissues in German-speaking countries.

teile.einleitung: Coins are small round pieces of money made of metal. In Switzerland you pay with francs and centimes (Rappen). Every coin shows how much it is worth.
wichtigste: Every Swiss coin shows its value.
Every coin is also stamped with the year in which it was made.
Swiss coins are made in Bern.
The company that makes them is called Swissmint.
There are coins from 5 centimes to 5 francs.
Larger amounts are paid with banknotes.

abschnitte.text: Every coin has two sides. On one side is the **value**, for example “1 Fr.” for one franc or “20” for 20 centimes. Next to it is the **year** in which the coin was minted. On the other side there is a picture, such as **Helvetia** or a woman’s head. It also says “HELVETIA” or “CONFOEDERATIO HELVETICA”. That is Latin and means Switzerland or Swiss Confederation.

Swiss coins are made by **Swissmint** in **Bern**. This is the federal mint. There, metal discs are **stamped** under great pressure. This creates the picture and the writing. On many coins you can see a small “B”. It shows that the coin was made in Bern.

With coins you pay small amounts, for example for a bread roll or chewing gum. For larger amounts there are **banknotes** made of paper and plastic. Coins are very sturdy and last for many years. Today many people often pay by card or phone. Even so, it is good to know coins and to be able to count with them.

gewusst: Coins are “minted” or “stamped”. In German the word for this is “prägen”, which is also where the word “Prägung” (imprint) comes from.
Swiss coins last a very long time. Some have been valid for more than a hundred years.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland, everyone who lives here must take out insurance with a health insurance fund. The premium differs according to age and rises sharply as you become an adult.
wichtigste: Basic insurance is compulsory for everyone in Switzerland.
There are three age groups: children, young adults and adults.
From the year in which you turn 19, you pay the premium for young adults.
This level applies up to 25; after that you pay the adult premium.
Anyone who does not pay the premiums can face debt enforcement.
People who earn little can get a premium reduction from the canton.

abschnitte.text: Since 1996 the **Health Insurance Act** has applied in Switzerland. It requires all residents to have **basic insurance**. It pays for visits to the doctor, hospital and many medicines. You can choose your health insurance fund freely, but the benefits of basic insurance are the same everywhere.

Health insurance funds have three **premium levels**. Children up to 18 pay the lowest premium. From the year in which you turn 19, the **young adults** level applies up to 25. After that you pay the full adult premium. The jump from the children’s premium to the adult premium is big and belongs in the budget.

As well as the premium, you pay part of the costs yourself. The **deductible** (Franchise) is the amount that adults first pay themselves each year. After that a **co-payment** of 10 per cent is added, up to a maximum. If you choose a higher deductible, you pay a lower premium but bear more of the costs yourself.

Basic insurance stays in place even if you do not pay the premiums. The health insurance fund first sends a **reminder**. After that it can start **debt enforcement proceedings**. If you have trouble paying the premiums, you should find out early from the canton about a **premium reduction**.

gewusst: Premiums differ from canton to canton and even within a canton.
For children there is no compulsory deductible in basic insurance; the choice starts at zero francs.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who takes out a loan has to pay back more than they received. The annual percentage rate shows how much a loan costs in total per year. It allows you to compare offers fairly.
wichtigste: The annual percentage rate shows the total cost of a loan per year as a percentage.
It includes interest and other costs such as fees.
It allows different loan offers to be compared fairly.
In Switzerland, lenders must state it for consumer loans.
The Consumer Credit Act sets a maximum interest rate.
The higher the interest, the more expensive the loan.

abschnitte.text: A **loan** is borrowed money. The bank or a credit company gives you an amount, and you pay it back later. For lending it, they charge **interest**. This is the price for the borrowed money. A **consumer loan** is a loan for private purchases, for example for a car or furniture.

The **nominal interest rate** is only the interest itself. But many loans have extra costs, for example **processing fees**. The **annual percentage rate** includes all these costs. That is why it is usually higher than the nominal rate. Because it includes everything, it shows honestly how expensive a loan really is.

Two offers can advertise a low interest rate and still cost different amounts. Only the **annual percentage rate** makes them truly comparable. That is why you always look at this figure. The **term** is also important: the longer you take to pay back, the more interest you pay in total.

In Switzerland, the **Consumer Credit Act** governs private loans. Lenders must state the annual percentage rate in the contract. The Federal Council sets a **maximum interest rate** that they may not exceed. Before a loan is given, it must be checked whether you can pay it back. This **creditworthiness check** is meant to prevent people from getting too deeply into debt.

gewusst: Credit cards and overdrafts also often come with high interest if you do not pay on time.
In Switzerland you can cancel a consumer credit agreement within 14 days of signing it.

teile.einleitung: The premium reduction is money from the canton that helps people with a low income pay for their health insurance. In Switzerland everyone must have basic insurance, and the monthly premiums are a heavy burden for many families. The reduction makes sure that everyone can afford health insurance.
wichtigste: In Switzerland, basic health insurance is compulsory for everyone.
The premiums do not depend on income, so they are hard to bear for families with little money.
The premium reduction is support from the canton for people on a low income.
The federal government and the cantons pay for the reductions together.
Each canton has its own rules on who gets how much.
For children from families with low and middle incomes, the premium must be greatly reduced.
In some cantons you have to apply; in others it happens automatically.

abschnitte.text: The **premium reduction** is a contribution with which the canton pays part of the health insurance premium. The money usually goes straight to the health insurance fund, which then sends a lower bill. The rule for it is in the **Health Insurance Act**, KVG for short, which has applied since 1996. It is also called IPV, which stands for individual premium reduction.

In Switzerland, every adult with the same health insurance fund in the same region pays roughly the same premium, no matter how much they earn. This is called a **per-person premium**. For families with low wages, health insurance can therefore take up a large part of the budget. The premium reduction balances this out, so that health care remains affordable for everyone.

The **federal government** gives the cantons money for the reductions, and the cantons add money of their own. Each canton decides from what income level you are entitled and how large the contribution is. It is usually based on the tax return. In some cantons you automatically receive a letter; in others you have to make an **application** yourself.

For children from families with low and middle incomes, the cantons must reduce the premium by at least 80 per cent. Young adults in education or training also receive special support. This is meant to ease the burden on families. Anyone doing an apprenticeship or studying should therefore check whether they are entitled.

Because premiums have been rising for years, the reduction is often debated. In June 2024 Switzerland voted on the **premium relief initiative**, which wanted to limit premiums to at most ten per cent of income. The people rejected it. Instead, the cantons will in future have to spend a minimum amount on premium reductions.

Anyone who earns little should look on their canton’s website to see whether they are entitled. There is often an online calculator there. The deadlines are important, because if you hand in the application too late, you may get nothing. Switching to a cheaper health insurance fund or a different insurance model can also save money.

begriffe.erklaerung: The amount you pay every month for an insurance policy.
The compulsory health insurance that everyone in Switzerland must have.
Everyone pays the same, no matter how much they earn.
A written request with which you ask an authority for something.

gewusst: In Switzerland, about one person in four receives a premium reduction.
A newborn baby also needs health insurance; the parents must register the baby within three months of the birth.
People who receive supplementary benefits or social assistance usually get the premium reduction automatically.

teile.einleitung: A debt collection agency is a company that collects unpaid bills from debtors who are behind with payment, on behalf of creditors. That is why someone who does not pay a bill sometimes gets a letter from a debt collection company. You should take such a letter seriously, but not panic.
wichtigste: Debt collection means recovering money that is owed.
A debt collection agency works on behalf of a creditor.
It sends reminders and demands payment of the unpaid bill.
A debt collection agency may not seize anything itself; that requires the debt enforcement office.
In Switzerland you often do not have to pay additional debt collection fees.
If you think a claim is wrong, you should object in writing.

abschnitte.text: The German word for it, **Inkasso**, comes from Italian and means roughly “into the cash box”. It refers to recovering money that someone is owed. A company that is waiting for bills and reminders to be paid can hand this work over to a **debt collection agency**. The agency then makes sure that the money is paid after all.

First the **creditor** sends a bill and usually one or more reminders. If payment still does not arrive, the creditor hands the claim over to a debt collection agency. The agency writes letters, phones or suggests **payment by instalments**. Sometimes the agency also buys the claim and then collects it for itself.

abschnitte.titel: What it may and may not do
abschnitte.text: In Switzerland, a debt collection agency may not take money or belongings away from anyone. To do that, it has to start debt enforcement proceedings at the **debt enforcement office**; the debtor then receives a payment order. If you dispute the claim, you can raise an **objection** against it within 10 days. Threats or pressure using false claims are not allowed.

Debt collection agencies often charge high additional fees for their work. Under Swiss law, you usually only have to pay the original bill, any **default interest** of 5 per cent a year and the debt enforcement costs. Further collection fees are often only owed if they were expressly agreed beforehand. Debt advice centres help to check such claims.

It is best to pay bills on time; then it never gets as far as debt collection. If you do receive a letter, you should check whether the claim is correct. If it is justified, you pay the basic amount as quickly as possible or agree on **instalments**. If you are unsure, the free advice centres of Schuldenberatung Schweiz can help.

begriffe.erklaerung: Someone who is owed money.
Someone who owes money.
A notice that a bill has not yet been paid.
A challenge to debt enforcement proceedings that you can lodge within 10 days.

gewusst: In Switzerland, anyone can start debt enforcement proceedings against someone else, even if the claim is not correct at all.
An entry in the debt enforcement register can make it harder to find a flat.
Some debt collection firms buy old claims for a fraction of their value.

teile.einleitung: The gross salary is the pay stated in the employment contract before anything is deducted. But what is paid out is the net salary, meaning what is left after deductions such as AHV and the pension fund. If you know the difference, you can plan your budget better.
wichtigste: The gross salary is the agreed pay before any deductions.
The net salary is what is paid out after deductions such as AHV and the pension fund.
Typical deductions are AHV, IV, EO, unemployment insurance, accident insurance and the pension fund.
In Switzerland, the net salary is usually about 85 to 90 per cent of the gross salary.
All deductions are shown on the monthly payslip.
In Switzerland, taxes are usually not deducted from pay but paid separately.
Many employers pay a 13th month's salary.

abschnitte.text: The German words **brutto** (gross) and **netto** (net) come from Italian. “Brutto” means roughly “raw” or “unrefined”, and **netto** means “clean”, in other words what is left over. The gross salary is the figure in the employment contract or in a job advert. But what lands in your account is the net salary, which is noticeably lower.

In Switzerland, contributions to the **social insurance schemes** are deducted from the gross salary. For AHV, IV and EO, employees pay 5.3 per cent, and the employer pays the same again. For unemployment insurance, another 1.1 per cent is added. On top of this come contributions to non-occupational accident insurance and the **pension fund**, which vary depending on age and company.

Let us take a gross salary of 5000 francs a month. Of this, 265 francs go to AHV, IV and EO and 55 francs to unemployment insurance. The pension fund and accident insurance often add another 300 to 400 francs. Roughly 4300 to 4400 francs are then paid out.

Unlike in many countries, **taxes** in Switzerland are usually not deducted directly from pay. You fill in a tax return every year and pay the taxes yourself. One exception is **withholding tax**, which is deducted directly from the pay of many foreign workers. You also pay the health insurance premium yourself and not through your wages.

Look closely at your **payslip** every month and check that everything is correct. Always plan your budget with the net salary, not the gross salary. Put some money aside for taxes right from the start so that the bill does not come as a nasty surprise. Apprentices also receive wages, from which social insurance contributions are already deducted.

begriffe.erklaerung: Pay before any deductions.
Pay that is paid out after the deductions.
A sheet showing how your pay is made up.
Tax that the employer deducts directly from pay.

gewusst: In job adverts and salary comparisons in Switzerland, the gross salary is almost always given.
On top of the gross salary, the employer pays its own contributions to the social insurance schemes, so an employee costs more than the contract says.
Whether a 13th month's salary is paid must be stated in the employment contract; it is not required by law.

teile.einleitung: Influencers are people who have a lot of followers on social media. Many of them earn money by showing and recommending products.
wichtigste: Influencers have many followers on platforms such as Instagram, TikTok or YouTube.
Companies pay them or give them presents so that they show products.
That is why their opinion is not always neutral.
Paid posts should be labelled as advertising.
If you know this, you can check recommendations more critically.

abschnitte.text: The word **influencer** is English and means someone who influences others. Influencers publish videos and pictures about fashion, games, sport or their everyday lives. Many people watch them regularly and trust them. That is exactly what makes them interesting for companies.

Companies pay influencers to show or praise a product. Sometimes they get the product as a present. Others earn money with **discount codes**: for every purchase made with their code, they receive a share. This kind of advertising is called **influencer marketing**.

Paid posts should be recognisable as advertising, for example with “advertising”, “advert” or “#ad”. In Switzerland, the **Swiss Commission for Fairness** requires advertising to be clearly marked as such. Not everyone sticks to this. That is why it is worth looking closely at enthusiastic recommendations.

Good questions are: Who earns money from this video? Would the person recommend the product even without being paid? It helps to read other opinions and tests. That way you only buy what you really want.

gewusst: Some influencers are still children or teenagers and are supported by their parents.
There are even computer-generated influencers who are not real people at all.

teile.einleitung: Bankruptcy means that a company or a person can no longer pay their debts and the remaining assets are realised through the courts. The money from the sale is then divided among the creditors. In Switzerland, the Federal Act on Debt Enforcement and Bankruptcy, SchKG for short, governs how this works.
wichtigste: Bankruptcy means that someone can no longer pay their debts.
The remaining assets are realised, that is sold, by the bankruptcy office.
The proceeds are divided among the creditors in a fixed order.
Companies listed in the commercial register usually go bankrupt if they become insolvent.
Private individuals can also declare themselves insolvent.
Whatever cannot be paid is recorded in a certificate of loss.
The rules are set out in the SchKG, which has been in force since 1892.

abschnitte.text: **Bankruptcy** happens when someone can permanently no longer pay their debts. You also say they are **insolvent** or broke. The German word “Konkurs” comes from Latin and means that the creditors “run together” to get their money. Instead of each creditor taking something separately, all the assets are realised together.

Companies listed in the **commercial register**, such as public limited companies or limited liability companies (GmbH), are usually put into bankruptcy if they become insolvent. A court opens the bankruptcy, and then the **bankruptcy office** takes over. It collects all the company’s assets, such as money, machines, buildings or goods. The company is then usually wound up and removed from the commercial register.

The bankruptcy office sells the assets, often at a public **auction**. The proceeds are distributed in a fixed order, which the law divides into classes. First, for example, the employees’ outstanding wages are paid. The other creditors often get only a small part of their money back.

A private individual can also declare to the court that they are insolvent. This is called **personal bankruptcy** or a declaration of insolvency. For the debts that could not be paid, the creditors receive a **certificate of loss**. With it they can demand money again later if the person comes into money again.

A well-known example from Switzerland is the airline Swissair. In October 2001 its planes had to stay on the ground because there was no money left for fuel; this is known as the **grounding**. Thousands of people lost their jobs, and the company was later wound up. Parts of it became the new airline Swiss.

begriffe.erklaerung: When someone can permanently no longer pay their bills.
The authority that manages and sells the assets in a bankruptcy.
A document recording how much money a creditor has not got back.
A public register of companies in Switzerland.

gewusst: The word “bankrupt” comes from Italian and means “broken bench”, because the table of a money changer who could not pay was once smashed.
In Switzerland, thousands of companies go bankrupt every year.
In Switzerland, a certificate of loss from a seizure only expires after 20 years.

teile.einleitung: Your first flat of your own is a big step. You are free, but you also have to pay for many things yourself. New items in the budget are above all rent, service charges and insurance.
wichtigste: With your first flat, rent, service charges and contents insurance come into the budget.
These fixed costs are often the biggest item in the budget.
Many landlords ask for a rent deposit.
In Switzerland, the deposit for a flat may be no more than three months' rent.
After moving, you register with the municipality.
A rule of thumb says that the rent should not be more than about a third of your income.

abschnitte.text: You pay **rent** for the flat every month. On top of that there are often **service charges**, for example for heating, hot water or cleaning the stairwell. Electricity is usually paid separately to the electricity company. Together these **fixed costs** are often the biggest item in the budget. That is why, before looking for a flat, you work out how much rent you can afford.

Many landlords ask for a **rent deposit**. This is a sum of money as security in case you leave damage or do not pay the rent. In Switzerland it may be no more than **three months' rent** for flats. It is paid into a blocked account in the tenant's name. When you move out, you get it back with interest if everything is in order.

**Contents insurance** pays if your own belongings are damaged by fire, water or theft. **Personal liability insurance** is also important. It pays if you accidentally damage something belonging to others, for example in the case of water damage in the flat below. Many landlords even require it. Both kinds of insurance are often available together in one package.

When you move in, you and the property management draw up a **handover report** listing any existing defects. After moving, you register with the **municipality**. New costs include the internet, household items, food and the radio and television licence fee. Furniture and the move itself also cost money. A budget helps you keep track.

gewusst: Switzerland has one of the highest proportions of tenants in Europe: more than half of households rent their home.
There is also insurance for the rent deposit, so that you do not have to put down the money all at once.

teile.einleitung: The real interest rate shows how much savings really gain or lose in value. To work it out, you compare the interest on the account with inflation. If prices rise faster than the interest, the money loses purchasing power.
wichtigste: The interest rate stated by the bank is called the **nominal interest rate**.
**Inflation** shows how much prices are rising.
The real interest rate is roughly the nominal interest rate minus inflation.
With 0.5 % interest and 1.5 % inflation, the real interest rate is about minus 1 %.
A negative real interest rate means: you can buy less with the money than before.

abschnitte.text: If you put money into a savings account, you receive **interest** for it. At the same time, many things become more expensive over time. This rise in prices is called **inflation** (in Switzerland also “Teuerung”). In Switzerland the Federal Statistical Office measures inflation with the **Swiss Consumer Price Index**. Whether saving is worth it depends on comparing these two figures.

A simple rule of thumb is: **real interest rate = nominal interest rate minus inflation**. If an account pays 0.5 % interest and inflation is 1.5 %, you calculate 0.5 minus 1.5. That gives **minus 1 %**. The savings do get bigger in francs, but you can buy about 1 % less with them. So purchasing power falls.

The real interest rate shows the **real gain** from saving. If it is positive, purchasing power grows. If it is negative, the money slowly loses value, even though there are more francs in the account. That is why savers do not only look at the interest rate, but also at inflation.

gewusst: The Swiss National Bank wants to keep inflation below 2 % a year.
Cash under the mattress earns no interest at all. So when there is inflation, it always loses purchasing power.

teile.einleitung: Many people think you can always send back things you have bought online. But in Switzerland there is no general legal right of withdrawal for online purchases. Whether you can return something is usually decided by the shop.
wichtigste: In Switzerland there is no general legal right of withdrawal for online purchases.
This is different from the EU, where you usually have 14 days.
Whether and how you can return something is stated in the shop’s **GTC**.
Many shops allow returns voluntarily.
If goods are broken or faulty, the rules on warranty apply.

abschnitte.text: If you buy something online in Switzerland, the **contract of sale** is valid as soon as you have ordered. There is no legal right to cancel the purchase without a reason. In the **EU**, on the other hand, customers usually have a **right of withdrawal** of 14 days for online purchases. So different rules can apply to shops abroad.

The **general terms and conditions**, **GTC** for short (AGB in German), are the shop’s rules. They state whether you can return something, for how long and who pays the postage. Many shops voluntarily offer returns, for example within 30 days. Some give the money back, others only a **voucher**. It is worth reading this before you buy.

It is different if goods have a **defect**. Then the legal **warranty** applies. You report the defect to the seller quickly. Depending on the case, the goods are repaired or replaced, or the price is reduced. Many retailers also set out the details of this in their terms and conditions.

gewusst: In Switzerland there is a legal right of withdrawal, for example, for doorstep sales, meaning when someone sells you something at your front door.

teile.einleitung: The maximum interest rate is the highest interest that lenders in Switzerland may charge for a consumer loan. It is set by the Federal Council to protect borrowers from interest that is too high.
wichtigste: The Federal Council sets a maximum interest rate for consumer loans.
The rule is laid down in the Consumer Credit Act.
It protects against usurious interest, meaning interest that is far too high.
A slightly higher rate applies to credit on credit cards and to overdrafts.
The Federal Council can adjust the maximum interest rate when interest rates on the market change.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland, the **Consumer Credit Act** governs loans to private individuals. A consumer loan is money that you borrow, for example, for a car, furniture or a holiday. The law gives the **Federal Council** the task of setting a maximum interest rate. No lender may charge more.

**Usurious interest** is interest that is much higher than usual. People in financial difficulty sometimes sign bad contracts because they urgently need money. The maximum interest rate prevents them from being exploited. Even so, a loan remains expensive, because even permitted interest costs a lot of money.

The maximum interest rate is linked to the general level of interest rates. In 2016 the Federal Council lowered it for cash loans from 15 to 10 per cent. For overdraft credit, for example on credit cards, a slightly higher maximum rate applies. The Federal Council reviews the figures regularly.

Even with a maximum interest rate, a loan can be expensive. At 10 per cent interest, 1000 francs cost about 100 francs extra in one year. If you save instead of taking out a loan, you pay no interest. That is why saving up for the things you want is usually the better choice.

gewusst: The interest on credit card debt is often higher than the interest on an ordinary cash loan.
Anyone who lends money in Switzerland must also state the effective annual interest rate in the contract.

teile.einleitung: A notice period is the time that must pass between giving notice and the end of a contract. If you know it, you can cancel in time and do not pay for longer than necessary.
wichtigste: The notice period is the time before the end of a contract within which you have to cancel.
Many subscriptions have notice periods of one to three months.
If an annual subscription ends on 31 December with 2 months’ notice, the cancellation must reach the provider by 31 October.
What usually counts is when the cancellation reaches the provider.
If you cancel too late, you often pay for another term.

abschnitte.text: Many contracts cannot be ended from one day to the next. You have to give notice a certain time beforehand. This time is called the **notice period**. It is stated in the contract or in the general terms and conditions, **GTC** for short (AGB in German).

An annual subscription ends on **31 December**, and the notice period is **two months**. You count back two months from the end date and arrive at **31 October**. By then the cancellation must have reached the provider. If you only post the letter on 31 October, you are usually too late.

Many subscriptions renew **automatically** if you do not cancel in time. The contract then often runs for another year. This applies, for example, to magazines, gym memberships or mobile phone contracts. That is why it is wise to note down the date early.

There are also notice periods at work and for flats. For a flat in Switzerland it is at least **three months**. For a job, under the Code of Obligations, it depends on how long you have been working there. During the probation period it is particularly short.

gewusst: In Switzerland, rented flats often have fixed termination dates, which differ depending on the canton or municipality.
If the end of the notice period falls on a Sunday, the deadline is not always moved, so it is better to cancel a few days early.

teile.einleitung: Phishing is a trick used by fraudsters on the internet. With fake emails, text messages or websites they try to get hold of passwords, card details or bank account details. If you know the tricks, you will not fall for them so easily.
wichtigste: Phishing is the attempt to get personal data with fake messages.
It is often about passwords, credit cards or bank accounts.
Messages about parcels, banks or prizes are typical.
Do not click on unknown links.
Banks never ask for passwords by email or text message.
Check genuine offers through the official website or app.

abschnitte.text: The word **phishing** comes from the English word “fishing”. The fraudsters cast out bait, so to speak, and hope that someone will bite. They send messages that look genuine, for example from a **bank**, a **parcel service** or an online shop. They contain a **link** to a fake website. Anyone who enters data there gives it straight to the fraudsters.

A common text message says: “Your parcel is waiting, pay 2 francs using this link.” Other messages claim that your account has been blocked or that you have won something. There is often **pressure**: “Today only!” Phishing by text message is also called **smishing**. There are also phone calls from fake bank staff.

Many phishing messages have **mistakes** in the language or a strange sender address. The address of the link often does not match the real company. You are addressed as “Dear customer” instead of by your own name. And they always ask for **data** or **money**. A real bank never asks for your password by email or text message.

Do **not** click on links in unexpected messages, and delete them. If you want to check whether a parcel really is waiting, open the official website or app of the parcel service yourself. Only enter passwords and card details on sites you have opened yourself. If you have entered something after all, tell your parents straight away and contact the bank. In Switzerland you can report suspicious messages to the **Federal Office for Cybersecurity**.

gewusst: The “ph” in phishing instead of “f” is a play on words from hacker slang.
Phishing fraudsters often send their messages to thousands of people at the same time.

teile.einleitung: As well as the AHV, the payslip shows another deduction: **ALV**. This is the **unemployment insurance**. It helps when someone loses their job and is looking for a new one.
wichtigste: ALV stands for unemployment insurance.
It pays a daily allowance in case of unemployment.
Employers and employees each pay half of the contributions.
In 2024 the contribution was 2.2 per cent of pay in total, up to a maximum salary.
The ALV is compulsory for employees in Switzerland.
The regional employment centres, RAV for short, help with the search for a job.

abschnitte.text: Sometimes people lose their job, for example because a company closes or has to save money. Then their wages suddenly stop. For this case there is the **unemployment insurance**, **ALV** for short. For a certain time it pays a **daily allowance**, meaning part of the previous wages. This way people can still pay their rent and food.

The ALV is **compulsory** for **employees** in Switzerland. The contribution is deducted directly from wages. The **employer** pays the same amount on top, so the costs are split in half. In 2024 the contribution was 2.2 per cent of pay in total. No contribution is charged on very high parts of a salary above a maximum amount.

Anyone who becomes unemployed registers with the municipality or with the **RAV**, the regional employment centre. The daily allowance is usually **70 or 80 per cent** of the insured wages. How long you receive it depends, among other things, on how long you paid contributions before. In return you have to make an active effort to find a new job.

The ALV does not only pay money. At the **RAV** you get advice and support when looking for a job. There are also **courses**, for example on job applications or languages. The aim is for people to find work again as soon as possible. The ALV also pays **short-time working compensation** when a company temporarily has less work.

gewusst: During the Covid pandemic, the ALV paid short-time working compensation for very many companies so that fewer people lost their jobs.
Self-employed people are not insured with the ALV.

teile.einleitung: If someone does not pay a bill, the creditor can start debt enforcement proceedings against them. Every such proceeding is recorded in a register at the debt enforcement office. This list is called the debt enforcement register.
wichtigste: Every debt enforcement office keeps the register for its district or municipality.
It lists all debt enforcement proceedings against a person or company.
Third parties are given information about proceedings from the last 5 years.
You can lodge an **objection** against a payment order.
If a debt enforcement is unjustified, you can ask after 3 months for it not to be disclosed.
The rules are in the Federal Act on Debt Enforcement and Bankruptcy, SchKG for short.

abschnitte.text: If a **creditor**, meaning someone to whom you owe money, wants to get their money by force, they submit a debt enforcement request to the debt enforcement office. The office then sends the **debtor** a **payment order**. This debt enforcement is entered in the register. Important: anyone can start debt enforcement, even if the claim is not correct at all. The office does not check this at the beginning.

If you do not agree with the claim, you lodge an **objection**. This must be done within 10 days of receiving the payment order. A short sentence is enough, and no reasons are needed. After that the debt enforcement is stopped for the time being. The creditor must prove in court or in another way that they are right.

Even an unjustified debt enforcement first appears in the register. That is why there is **non-disclosure**. If you have lodged an objection and the creditor has done nothing within 3 months to have it removed, you can submit an application to the debt enforcement office. The debt enforcement is then no longer shown to third parties. This way it does no harm, for example when you are looking for a flat.

Third parties only find out about debt enforcement proceedings from the **last 5 years**. Older entries no longer appear on the extract. In principle, a debt enforcement that has been paid also remains visible. However, if you pay the debt, the creditor can withdraw the proceedings. Then they are no longer disclosed to third parties.

gewusst: Anyone who wants information about another person must show a credible interest, for example as a landlord.
You may ask for information about yourself at any time.

teile.einleitung: Sometimes you are short of money, and someone helps you out. Then you have **borrowed** money. The important thing is: borrowed is not given, and you pay it back soon.
wichtigste: Anyone who borrows money must give it back.
It is best to pay it back soon and at the agreed time.
That way trust between people stays good.
If you do not get your money back, you remind the person kindly.
If that does not work, you can ask an adult for help.

abschnitte.text: If Lara borrows 2 francs from her brother, the money still belongs to him. She may only use it for a while. That is why she gives it **back soon**. It is best to agree straight away **when** that should be. Anyone who reliably pays back will be happy to get help next time too.

abschnitte.titel: When the money does not come back
abschnitte.text: Sometimes someone forgets to give the money back. Usually this is not meant badly. Then it helps to **remind the person kindly**, for example: “Do you remember the 5 francs from last week?” If it still does not work, you can ask an **adult** for help. Arguing or shouting usually only makes things worse.

Adults borrow money too, for example from a **bank**. This is called a **loan**. But the bank wants extra money for it, the **interest**. That is why a loan costs more in the end than you borrowed. If you only borrow as much as you can definitely pay back, you will not get into **debt**.

gewusst: The word “credit” comes from the Latin word for “to believe” or “to trust”: anyone who lends money trusts that they will get it back.

teile.einleitung: A reminder is a notice that a bill has not yet been paid. It is an important signal: if you do not react, you risk fees and, in the worst case, debt enforcement proceedings.
wichtigste: A reminder tells you about an unpaid bill.
Reminder fees are often added.
There are often several reminders one after another.
If you do not pay, debt enforcement proceedings can be started against you.
If you have no money, it is best to get in touch straight away.
You can often agree on instalments or a delay.

abschnitte.text: Every bill says by when you have to pay. Once this deadline has passed, the company sends a **reminder**. It states how much is still unpaid and by when you should pay. Sometimes the first reminder is also called a **payment reminder**. Perhaps you simply forgot the bill. Then it is best to pay it straight away.

Many companies send several reminders. Each one is usually worded more strictly. Often a **reminder fee** is added with each reminder, if this was agreed beforehand. **Default interest** can also be charged. If the bill still remains unpaid, the company can hand the claim to a debt collection agency or start **debt enforcement proceedings**.

Debt enforcement goes through the **debt enforcement office**. You receive a **payment order**. If you do not agree, you can raise an **objection** within 10 days. Debt enforcement proceedings are entered in the debt enforcement register. This can cause problems later, for example when looking for a flat, because landlords often ask for an extract.

If you have no money at the moment, you should not hide the reminder. It is best to phone the company or write to it. You can often agree on **payment by instalments** or a **payment delay**. That way further fees and debt enforcement can be avoided. Anyone with many unpaid bills can find help at a **debt advice service**. This advice is often free.

gewusst: If you pay your bills as soon as they arrive or by standing order, you will never get a reminder at all.
In Switzerland you can order an extract from the debt enforcement register at the debt enforcement office.

teile.einleitung: If you can count coins, you always know how much money is in your purse. You just have to add up the values of the coins. With a few tricks it is quick.
wichtigste: When counting, you add up the values of the coins.
Two 2-franc pieces and one 1-franc piece make 5 francs.
100 centimes make 1 franc.
Five 20-centime pieces make 1 franc.
Two 50-centime pieces make 1 franc.
For 2 francs you need four 50-centime pieces.

abschnitte.text: The easiest way is to **sort** the coins first. You put all the same coins in a little pile: the 2-franc pieces, the 1-franc pieces, the 20-centime pieces and so on. Then you start with the **biggest values**. Mia, for example, has two 2-franc pieces and one 1-franc piece. 2 plus 2 is 4, plus 1, so **5 francs**.

One franc has **100 centimes**. This helps when counting. Five 20-centime pieces are 5 times 20, so 100 centimes. That is **one franc**. Two 50-centime pieces are also 100 centimes. Ten 10-centime pieces also make one franc. If you make little groups like these, you count much faster.

How many 50-centime pieces are worth as much as a 2-franc piece? Two half-francs are 1 franc. So for 2 francs you need **four** of them. You can practise tasks like this at home with real coins. You can also play shop and give change. That way, counting with money will soon be really easy.

gewusst: Banks have machines that count and sort coins in seconds.
Banks often pack coins into rolls that always contain the same number of pieces.

teile.einleitung: With payment by instalments, you do not pay for a purchase all at once, but in several part payments. These part payments are called instalments. It sounds convenient, but it often makes things more expensive.
wichtigste: With payment by instalments, you pay in several parts instead of all at once.
Instalments often cost extra, for example through interest or fees.
12 instalments of 55 francs make 660 francs instead of 600 francs in cash.
Each instalment is a fixed expense for many months.
Several instalments at the same time can blow your budget.

abschnitte.text: When **buying in instalments**, you take the goods with you straight away but pay bit by bit. You commit to paying a certain amount every month. Basically, you are borrowing money that you do not have yet. That is why buying in instalments is a kind of **loan**. In Switzerland, the **Consumer Credit Act** governs many such contracts and requires a check of whether you can pay the instalments.

A phone costs 600 francs in cash. You can also buy it in 12 instalments of 55 francs. If you work out 12 times 55, you get **660 francs**. So buying in instalments costs 60 francs more. That is why you should always work out the **total price** and not just look at the small monthly instalment.

abschnitte.titel: Be careful with lots of instalments
abschnitte.text: A single instalment looks small. But if you are paying instalments for a phone, furniture and a bike at the same time, you have much less money free every month. If an unexpected bill then arrives, the money is no longer enough. That is how **debt** can build up. It is better to save up for something and then pay in cash.

gewusst: Offers like “buy now, pay later” when shopping online are also a form of payment by instalments or credit.

teile.einleitung: Honesty means telling the truth and not cheating others. When dealing with money, it shows, for example, when you give back change that you were given by mistake. Honesty creates trust, and without trust no economy would work.
wichtigste: An honest person tells the truth and does not deceive others.
If you get too much change in a shop, you say so and give it back.
Anyone who finds something must give it back to the owner or hand it in to the police or a lost property office.
In Switzerland the finder is entitled to a reasonable reward.
Honesty creates trust between people and in the economy.
An experiment with lost wallets showed that a particularly large number of finds are returned in Switzerland.
Dishonesty such as fraud or theft is a criminal offence.

abschnitte.text: **Honesty** means telling the truth, keeping promises and not taking anything away from anyone that belongs to them. In almost all cultures and religions it is seen as an important virtue. Honest people are reliable, which is why people are happy to trust them. Admitting mistakes is also part of honesty.

Sometimes someone at the till makes a mistake and gives back too much **change**. That money does not belong to you; you should tell the shop assistant and give it back. Otherwise money will be missing from the till in the evening, and the person often has to answer for it. Anyone who travels on the train without a valid ticket is also being dishonest and can expect to pay a surcharge.

Anyone who finds something may not simply keep it. Under the **Civil Code**, you must give it back to the owner or report it to the police or the **lost property office**. In return, the finder is entitled to a reasonable reward, usually around ten per cent. If nobody comes forward within five years, the finder may keep the item.

Researchers, including some from the University of Zurich, had more than 17,000 wallets handed in at hotels, banks and public offices in 40 countries. They contained a business card and in some cases money. Switzerland, together with countries such as Norway, was among the most honest countries. The surprising thing was that wallets with more money were returned more often than those without money.

In Switzerland many farms have small farm shops with an **honesty box**. Nobody guards it; you simply put the money in yourself. This only works because most people are honest. Banks, insurance companies and contracts also depend on people being able to rely on agreements.

begriffe.erklaerung: The money you get back when you pay with a larger amount.
A reward for someone who returns a lost item.
An office that keeps items that have been found.
An unguarded box into which you honestly pay by yourself.

gewusst: Every year tens of thousands of lost items end up in the SBB lost property offices, from umbrellas to braces for teeth.
The wallet experiment was published in the scientific journal Science in 2019.
In surveys, many people say that honesty is what they value most in friends.

teile.einleitung: Money comes as coins and as **banknotes**, meaning paper notes. In Switzerland there are six different notes, from 10 to 1000 francs. They are issued by the **Swiss National Bank**.
wichtigste: In Switzerland there are notes of 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 and 1000 francs.
The smallest note is the 10-franc note.
The largest note is the purple 1000-franc note.
There is no 5-franc note, but there is a 5-franc coin.
The notes are issued by the Swiss National Bank.
Today's notes belong to the 9th series and appeared between 2016 and 2019.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland there are six **banknotes**: 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 and 1000 francs. Each has its own colour. The 10 note is **yellow**, the 20 **red**, the 50 **green**, the 100 **blue**, the 200 **brown** and the 1000 **purple**. The higher the value, the wider the note. This means you can also tell them apart by touch.

abschnitte.titel: A coin instead of a note
abschnitte.text: The smallest note is the **tenner**. For 5 francs there is no note but a large **coin**, the “Fünfliber”. There is no 500-franc note in Switzerland. That is why the step from the 200 to the 1000 note is especially big.

In Switzerland, only the **Swiss National Bank**, **SNB** for short, may issue banknotes. It makes sure that there is enough money in circulation. Today's notes belong to the **9th series**. They were introduced between 2016 and 2019. Each note shows a theme that is meant to be typical of Switzerland, for example the humanitarian tradition on the 100 note.

Swiss banknotes are among the **most secure** in the world. They have many **security features** that are hard to copy. These include pictures that move when you tilt the note, a security thread and a Swiss cross that you can see when you hold the note up to the light. The paper is made of several layers. This makes it hard to produce fake notes.

gewusst: The 1000-franc note is one of the highest-value banknotes in the whole world.
Since 2021 the notes of the 8th series are no longer legal tender, but you can still exchange them at the National Bank.

teile.einleitung: Most Swiss coins are silver. Only one shines gold: the 5-centime piece. But its colour does not come from real gold, but from a special mixture of metals.
wichtigste: The 5-centime piece is the only golden Swiss coin.
All other Swiss coins are silver.
The 5-centime piece is not made of gold, but of aluminium bronze.
The silver coins are made of cupronickel.
The colour helps you tell the coins apart quickly.

abschnitte.text: The **5-centime piece**, also called the **Fünfräppler**, has a golden-yellow colour. It is made of **aluminium bronze**, a mixture of copper, aluminium and nickel. This mixture looks golden but is much cheaper than gold. The 5-centime piece has had this colour since 1981. Before that it was made of a different metal.

The 10- and 20-centime coins and the 1/2, 1, 2 and 5-franc coins are **silver** in colour. They are made of **cupronickel**, a mixture of copper and nickel. There is no real silver in them. In the past the franc coins were made of silver. Because the price of silver rose, they switched to cupronickel in the 1960s.

The special colour makes the 5-centime piece easy to recognise. That way you can find it quickly in your purse. **Size** and **picture** also help you tell coins apart. People who cannot see well often feel the coins by their edge and size.

gewusst: The 5-centime piece is the coin with the lowest value that is still minted in Switzerland today.
